q: A deliberative assembly is typically a small group of fewer than six people.
exp: Deliberative assemblies that need formal procedure usually have more than about a dozen members.

q: When a member disagrees with a decision the assembly made, the president should ask that member to leave the organization before the next regular meeting.
exp: Disagreeing with a decision is a member's right; it is not grounds for removal.

q: In a deliberative assembly, the members present at a properly called meeting normally decide the questions that come up.
exp: Decisions are made by the members present at a legal meeting, which binds the whole body.

q: In parliamentary terms, an "assembly" means a series of meetings.
exp: An assembly is the body of people; a series of connected meetings is a session.

q: A member of an assembly is someone with the right to take full part in its proceedings.
exp: Membership means the full right to participate: make motions, debate, and vote.

q: Making motions, debating, and voting are all rights of the members of a deliberative assembly.
exp: These three rights are the core of membership in a deliberative assembly.

q: A deliberative assembly that has adopted no rules of its own is governed by the constitution of its state.
exp: Without adopted rules, an assembly follows the rules and customs of general (common) parliamentary law.

q: Any deliberative assembly's actions must comply with its own bylaws and rules as well as all applicable local, state, and national laws.
exp: An organization's rules rank below applicable law, and its actions must respect both.

q: The basic rule of decision in a deliberative assembly is that every proposal needs a two-thirds vote to pass.
exp: The basic rule is that a proposition is adopted by a majority vote.

q: A majority vote means more than half of the members present and voting approve the motion.
exp: A majority vote is more than half of the votes cast by those legally entitled to vote, ignoring blanks and abstentions.

q: When a decision needs more than a majority, the usual requirements are a two-thirds vote and, in some cases, previous notice.
exp: Two-thirds votes and previous notice protect members' rights on major changes.

q: If previous notice wasn't announced at the meeting before, notice of the proposal must be included in the call of the meeting where it will be considered.
exp: Previous notice can be given orally at the preceding meeting or in writing in the call of the meeting.

q: The "call" of a meeting is a spoken announcement of an upcoming meeting.
exp: The call is a written notice of the meeting's time and place, sent or distributed to all members.

q: A committee is one of the principal types of deliberative assembly.
exp: The principal types are mass meetings, local assemblies of organized societies, conventions, legislative bodies, and boards; committees are not one of them.

q: A mass meeting is an unorganized group meeting about a particular problem, open to anyone interested.
exp: That is the definition of a mass meeting.

q: Attendance at a mass meeting can be restricted.
exp: Attendance can be limited, for example, to people who support the meeting's purpose.

q: At a mass meeting, only the elected officers and the parliamentarian may take part.
exp: Anyone who supports the purpose of the meeting may attend and participate.

q: A mass meeting can operate even if attendance is small.
exp: A mass meeting doesn't require a large turnout to do its work.

q: Most people gain experience with deliberative assemblies through groups like a local chapter of a permanent organization.
exp: A local club or chapter is the most common kind of deliberative assembly people encounter.

q: The bylaws of a local organization normally require it to hold special meetings every month.
exp: Bylaws usually set regular meetings at stated intervals; special meetings are called as needed.

q: In most local organizations, each meeting is its own separate session.
exp: In ordinary local societies, each regular meeting is normally a separate session.

q: A body of delegates chosen to meet for one session is called a "delegation."
exp: A body of delegates chosen for one session is a convention.

q: The voting members of a convention are usually delegates.
exp: Conventions are made up of delegates representing constituent units.

q: When a convention ends, the alternates hold an "Alternate Convention" of their own.
exp: When a convention adjourns sine die, the assembly is normally dissolved.

q: Lawmaking bodies such as Congress are classified as mass meetings.
exp: Lawmaking bodies are classified as legislative bodies.

q: A state legislature typically has a single chamber, and its sessions last no longer than a month.
exp: Most legislatures have two houses, and sessions can last for months.

q: A board is an administrative body whose members must always be appointed.
exp: Board members may be elected or appointed.

q: A board shares many of the characteristics of a deliberative assembly.
exp: Boards are deliberative bodies that generally follow assembly procedure, with some small-board exceptions.

q: A board must have at least four members.
exp: Boards have no minimum size; they are usually smaller than the assembly.

q: A board within an organization gets its authority from a source outside itself.
exp: A board's powers are conferred by an outside authority, such as the bylaws or the parent assembly.

q: Large boards and large committees follow parliamentary procedure only when the chair decides it will help.
exp: Large boards and committees normally follow the same procedure as any assembly.

q: An organization adopts certain rules that set its basic structure and how it operates.
exp: Examples include the bylaws and the rules of order in its parliamentary authority.

q: The corporate charter of a society that wants to incorporate should include its name, its object, and whatever else that state's law requires.
exp: The charter contains the name, object, and items required by state law.

q: A main advantage of incorporating is that officers and members can change the bylaws without a membership vote.
exp: A main advantage is protecting members from personal liability for the organization's obligations.

q: The first officers of an organization should write its corporate charter.
exp: A corporate charter should be drafted by an attorney.

q: In an incorporated organization, the constitution outranks every other rule.
exp: In an incorporated society, the charter is the highest document.

q: The document containing an organization's own rules about itself as an organization is its constitution or bylaws.
exp: The bylaws (or constitution) set out the society's own basic rules as an organization.

q: RONR uses the term "statutes" for a combined constitution and bylaws.
exp: RONR uses the single term "bylaws" for a combined document.

q: Bylaws generally spell out the organization's main characteristics, how it functions, and the rules it considers most important.
exp: These are the essentials that bylaws cover.

q: A memory aid for the standard articles of bylaws is "NO MOME C PA" ("No Mommy, see Pa"), where the two M's stand for Members and Meetings.
exp: This course mnemonic lists Name, Object, Members, Officers, Meetings, Executive board, Committees, Parliamentary authority, and Amendment.

q: In an unincorporated society, the first two articles of the bylaws are "Officers" and "Duties."
exp: The first two articles are the Name of the organization and its Object.

q: Bylaws do not normally include an article listing every member's legal name and address.
exp: Membership rolls are kept by the secretary, not written into the bylaws.

q: In an incorporated society, the bylaws usually leave out the articles on Name and Members.
exp: In an incorporated society, the Name and Object are in the charter, so the bylaws usually omit them.

q: An incorporated society should not keep its constitution separate from its bylaws.
exp: A society should normally combine them into one document called the bylaws.

q: Apart from an incorporated society's charter, the highest set of rules is the standing rules.
exp: The bylaws are the highest set of rules after the charter.

q: When an organization has a constitution and bylaws as separate documents, the constitution ranks higher.
exp: A separate constitution outranks the bylaws.

q: The written rules of parliamentary procedure an organization formally adopts are its rules of order.
exp: Rules of order govern the conduct of business in meetings.

q: "Rules of order" is another name for the bylaws.
exp: Rules of order are the parliamentary procedure rules, usually in the parliamentary authority, not the bylaws.

q: Most societies get their rules of order by naming a parliamentary manual in their bylaws, which then becomes their parliamentary authority.
exp: Many organizations name RONR as their parliamentary authority.

q: Rules of order that add to or change the rules in the parliamentary authority are called the "secondary parliamentary authority."
exp: They are called special rules of order.

q: A mass meeting or a body that hasn't yet organized can adopt a parliamentary authority at the start of its meeting.
exp: An unorganized body can adopt a parliamentary authority when it begins.

q: When a special rule of order conflicts with the parliamentary authority, the parliamentary authority wins.
exp: The special rule of order takes precedence over the parliamentary authority.

q: If an organization has adopted RONR as its parliamentary authority and another manual says something different, RONR is the binding source.
exp: The adopted parliamentary authority controls over other manuals.

q: Special rules of order should be written into the bylaws.
exp: Special rules of order should be adopted separately from the bylaws.

q: Special rules of order may be printed in the same booklet as the bylaws, as long as they are under their own heading.
exp: They are kept separate from the bylaws but may be printed with them.

q: It takes a two-thirds vote to suspend a rule of order, whether it is in the parliamentary authority or is a special rule of order.
exp: Rules of order can be suspended by a two-thirds vote.

q: A special rule of order kept separate from the bylaws can be adopted or amended by a majority of those present.
exp: It takes a two-thirds vote with previous notice, or a majority of the entire membership.

q: Standing rules deal with administrative details rather than parliamentary procedure.
exp: Standing rules cover administration, not procedure.

q: A standing rule commonly sets the hour when meetings begin.
exp: The meeting starting time is a typical standing rule.

q: Setting the organization's quorum is a typical example of a standing rule.
exp: The quorum belongs in the bylaws; a guest register is a typical standing rule.

q: Standing rules are usually adopted before the society is organized.
exp: Standing rules are adopted as needed after the society is organized and its bylaws adopted.

q: Adopting a standing rule at a business meeting takes a two-thirds vote when no notice was given.
exp: A standing rule can be adopted by a majority vote without notice.

q: A standing rule expires when the meeting ends.
exp: A standing rule stays in effect until it is rescinded or amended.

q: An assembly can temporarily suspend one of its standing rules at a meeting without any prior notice.
exp: Ordinary standing rules can be suspended for a meeting by a majority vote without notice.

q: The quorum is the number of members who always vote on the motions before the assembly.
exp: The quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for business to be validly done.

q: In both houses of the U.S. Congress, a majority of the members is a quorum.
exp: The U.S. Constitution sets the quorum as a majority.

q: If the bylaws don't say otherwise, the quorum of an organized society is a majority of all its members.
exp: Without a bylaw provision, the quorum is a majority of the entire membership.

q: The minimum officers needed to conduct business are a president and a vice-president.
exp: The minimum officers are a presiding officer and a secretary or clerk.

q: Officers who are members of the assembly count toward the quorum.
exp: Officers who are members count toward the quorum like any other member.

q: In RONR, the term used for both the presiding officer and the place where they preside is "the chairman."
exp: The term RONR uses is "the chair."

q: The presiding officer is usually addressed as "Mr. or Madam Presiding Officer."
exp: The usual forms are "Mr./Madam President" or "Mr./Madam Chairman" (or "Chair").

q: A woman who serves as president should be addressed as "Mrs. President."
exp: The correct form is "Madam President," whether or not she is married.

q: When the president is not on the platform, a vice-president who is presiding is addressed as "Mr. or Madam President."
exp: A presiding vice-president is called "President" unless the president is also on the platform.

q: Apart from a few exceptions like small boards and committees, a member always stands to speak.
exp: In regular assemblies, members rise to get the floor and speak.

q: During a meeting, the presiding officer refers to themselves as "I."
exp: The presiding officer refers to themselves in the third person as "the chair."

q: The chair should mention a member's name only when calling that member to order.
exp: The chair also names members when assigning the floor and when announcing appointments.

q: "The meeting will come to order" is a proper way for the chair to open a meeting.
exp: This is a standard way to call a meeting to order.

q: The order of business sets the sequence in which general classes of business come up or may be introduced at a meeting.
exp: That is the purpose of an order of business.

q: A society that adopts RONR as its parliamentary authority must use RONR's standard order of business.
exp: A society may adopt its own order of business; RONR's applies only if it hasn't.

q: Right after the meeting is called to order, the next item is usually the reading and approval of the minutes.
exp: Minutes come first in the standard order of business, after any opening ceremonies.

q: In the standard order of business, reports of special committees come right after reports of officers, boards, and standing committees.
exp: Special committee reports are the second heading of reports.

q: In the standard order of business, officers report only if time permits.
exp: Officers' reports come right after the minutes are approved.

q: In the standard order of business, New Business comes immediately after Special Orders.
exp: Unfinished Business and General Orders comes immediately after Special Orders.

q: New Business is taken up after Unfinished Business and General Orders.
exp: New Business is the last regular heading in the standard order of business.

q: A mass meeting doesn't need an order of business because unfinished business always comes first.
exp: A mass meeting needs no order of business because only new business can come before it.

q: A convention usually adopts an order of business of its own.
exp: Conventions adopt their own program or agenda.

q: The call to order is not considered part of the order of business.
exp: The order of business starts after the call to order.

q: A convention's order of business is called its agenda or program.
exp: A convention's order of business is its agenda or program.

q: A member brings business before the assembly by making a formal proposal called an "order."
exp: The formal proposal is called a motion.

q: A primary amendment is the only motion whose introduction brings business before the assembly.
exp: Only a main motion brings business before the assembly.

q: The president normally reads aloud any letters sent to the organization.
exp: The secretary reads correspondence addressed to the organization.

q: Reading a letter at a meeting does not, by itself, put a motion before the assembly.
exp: A motion is still needed before the assembly can act on a communication.

q: The formal parliamentary term for discussing the merits of a motion is "argument."
exp: The term is "debate."

q: When a member who is entitled to the floor seeks it, the chair must recognize that member.
exp: The chair must recognize a member who is entitled to the floor.

q: To speak or make a motion, a member must first obtain the floor by rising, addressing the chair, and waiting to be recognized.
exp: These are the steps for obtaining the floor.

q: The chair recognizes a member who is entitled to the floor by announcing the member's name, title, or the unit they represent.
exp: Recognition is given by naming the member or how they are identified.

q: A member who "has the floor" has been recognized by the chair.
exp: Having the floor means you have been recognized and may speak.

q: In a meeting where the chair doesn't know members' names, a member seeking the floor should wait for the chair to ask for their name.
exp: The member should give their name and any identifying information when addressing the chair.

q: When a speaker sits down to yield the floor, the assembly immediately votes on the pending motion.
exp: Sitting down just means the speaker is finished; debate can continue.

q: "Privileges of the floor" means a person may enter the room where the meeting is held.
exp: The term means admission to the meeting hall (for non-members, sometimes also the right to speak).

q: When two members rise at about the same moment, the chair should recognize the one who raised a hand as well as stood.
exp: The chair recognizes whoever rose and addressed the chair first after the floor was yielded; raising a hand isn't required.

q: If several members seek the floor at once right after a motion is made, the chair should call on the motion's maker if they haven't spoken yet.
exp: The maker of a motion has first claim to the floor in debate on it.

q: During debate, the chair should alternate between the motion's maker and members who oppose it.
exp: When possible, the chair alternates between speakers for and against the motion.

q: If the chair gives the floor to the wrong member, any member can correct the mistake by immediately raising a Point of Order.
exp: A Point of Order is the way to correct an error in assigning the floor.

q: A member may raise a Point of Order when the chair overlooks a rules violation or fails to rule out of order a main motion outside the society's purpose.
exp: Points of Order enforce the rules when the chair misses a breach.

q: A motion comes before the assembly as soon as a member makes it and the chair states it.
exp: Normally a motion must be made, seconded, and then stated by the chair.

q: The terms "move," "make," and "offer" all describe the first step of bringing a motion before an assembly.
exp: Making the motion is step one in handling any motion.

q: Once a motion is seconded, the maker's debate on it is what places it before the assembly.
exp: The chair stating the question is what places a motion before the assembly.

q: A motion becomes pending once it has been made, seconded, and stated by the chair.
exp: After the chair states it, the motion is pending.

q: When the assembly agrees to do what a motion proposes, the motion is said to be "endorsed."
exp: The motion is said to be carried or adopted.

q: When the assembly decides against what a motion proposes, the motion is rejected, or lost.
exp: A defeated motion is said to be lost or rejected.

q: The proper way to begin a main motion is "I motion that..."
exp: The correct form is "I move that..."

q: A long or complex motion is usually offered in the form of a resolution.
exp: Resolutions are used for long, formal, or important motions.

q: Because resolutions tend to be long, they should be written out ahead of time and handed to the chair once offered.
exp: Long motions should be in writing for accuracy.

q: The member who proposes a main motion is entitled to speak last in debate.
exp: The maker of a motion is entitled to speak first.

q: A member should start debating a motion immediately after making it.
exp: After making the motion, the member sits down and waits for the second and the chair's statement.

q: If a member didn't hear a motion, the chair, the secretary, or the maker may repeat it.
exp: A motion may be repeated so everyone understands it.

q: Before making a main motion, a member may give a full, detailed speech explaining the reasons for it.
exp: Only a few words of explanation are allowed; the speech comes during debate.

q: A member who isn't sure how to word a motion may ask the chair for help.
exp: The chair can help a member phrase a motion.

q: In large assemblies, a motion must be seconded before it can be considered.
exp: Most motions need a second in a regular assembly.

q: A member must be recognized by the chair before seconding a motion.
exp: A second doesn't require obtaining the floor.

q: A member who wants a motion considered may say "I second the motion," "I second it," or simply "Second" without getting the floor.
exp: All are acceptable ways to second, and no recognition is needed.

q: In a large assembly, the best way to second is to call out "I second it" from your seat.
exp: In a large assembly, the seconder may need to rise and give their name, without waiting for recognition, so the second is noticed.

q: Some organizations use the word "subscribe" in place of "second."
exp: Some organizations use "support" instead of "second."

q: As chair of a large meeting, if a motion doesn't get a second right away, you should repeat it and ask, "Is there a second to the motion?"
exp: The chair calls for a second if none is heard right away.

q: Motions in small boards and committees must be seconded.
exp: In small boards and committees, motions don't need a second.

q: When no one seconds a main motion, the chair should ask the maker whether they will withdraw it.
exp: The chair announces, "Since there is no second, the motion is not before this meeting."

q: After announcing that a motion wasn't seconded, the chair moves on by saying, "The next item of business is..."
exp: The chair moves to the next business once a motion dies for lack of a second.

q: Seconding a motion signals that the seconder wants it adopted exactly as written.
exp: A second only means the member wants the motion considered.

q: A member who opposes a motion is allowed to second it.
exp: A second just means "let's discuss it," so an opponent may second.

q: In a committee of more than two members, motions require a second.
exp: Motions in committees generally don't need a second.

q: The requirement for a second exists mainly to guide the chair in deciding whether to state the question on a motion.
exp: A second shows the chair that at least two members want the motion considered.

q: The second keeps the assembly from spending time on a motion that only one member wants to bring up.
exp: That is the purpose of requiring a second.

q: Even if the chair is sure most of the assembly supports a motion, a second is still required before stating it.
exp: If support is obvious, the chair may state the question without waiting for a second.

q: If a controversial motion is stated without a second, a member should call for the orders of the day.
exp: The proper response is a Point of Order, raised before debate begins.

q: A motion that was adopted without ever being seconded is void and treated as lost.
exp: Once debate or voting has begun, the lack of a second doesn't affect the motion's validity.

q: "Stating the question" means the chair repeats the exact motion and announces that it is open to debate.
exp: Stating the question formally puts the motion before the assembly.

q: A debatable motion becomes open for debate as soon as it is seconded.
exp: It is open for debate once the chair states the question.

q: When the chair asks, "Are you ready for the question?" the members may begin or continue debating.
exp: The phrase invites debate on the pending question.

q: "It is moved and seconded that..." is a proper way for the chair to state a motion.
exp: This is the standard form for stating the question.

q: If a motion can't be debated or amended, the chair puts it to a vote right after stating it.
exp: With no debate or amendment possible, the chair moves straight to the vote.

q: As a rule, the chair states the question on a motion immediately after it is made, before any second.
exp: The chair states the question once the motion is made and seconded.

q: When a motion isn't in order, the chair should say, "You are out of order because..."
exp: The chair says, "The chair rules that the motion is out of order because..."

q: The secretary may reword a motion when writing it into the minutes after the meeting.
exp: The minutes record the motion as the chair last stated it before the vote.

q: The chair may require a main motion to be in writing before stating it to the assembly.
exp: The chair can also require amendments in writing.

q: A motion's maker may change or withdraw it freely until the chair states the question.
exp: Before it's stated, the motion still belongs to its maker.

q: No debate is in order after a main motion is made but before the chair states it.
exp: Debate begins only after the question is stated.

q: If the maker changes a motion before the chair states it, the seconder may withdraw the second.
exp: The seconder agreed to the original version, so they may withdraw.

q: The correct order for handling a main motion is: the chair puts the question, announces the vote, and then members debate.
exp: Debate comes first, then the chair puts the question, then announces the result.

q: Right after stating the question, the chair should look to the motion's maker to see if they want an immediate vote with no debate.
exp: The chair looks to the maker to see if they want the floor to speak first in debate.

q: The motion's maker is required to speak first in debate.
exp: The maker has the right to speak first but doesn't have to.

q: Unless a special rule says otherwise, each member may speak three times on the same motion in one day.
exp: The limit is two speeches per member per question per day.

q: A member who has "exhausted the right to debate" has already spoken twice on that motion that day and can't speak a third time.
exp: Two speeches per day is the standard limit.

q: Unless the assembly allows otherwise or a rule sets a different limit, each speech on a pending motion is limited to two minutes.
exp: The standard limit is ten minutes per speech.

q: Debate must stay on the merits of the immediately pending question.
exp: Remarks must be germane to the immediately pending question.

q: Members should direct their remarks in debate to the chair.
exp: Speakers address the chair, not each other.

q: In a large assembly, the presiding officer stays out of debate, remains seated while members speak, and doesn't cut off debate while members still want to speak.
exp: The chair stays impartial during debate.

q: The chair may interrupt a speaker for any reason at all.
exp: The chair may interrupt only for a breach of the rules or disorder.

q: "Putting the question" means the chair asks the motion's maker a question.
exp: Putting the question means taking the vote.

q: In a large group, the first vote on a main motion is usually a voice vote ("viva voce").
exp: A voice vote is the normal first method; small groups may use a show of hands.

q: The chair always takes the negative vote first.
exp: The affirmative vote is always taken first.

q: On a courtesy motion where the "ayes" are nearly unanimous, the chair doesn't have to call for the "noes."
exp: For complimentary motions the chair may skip the negative vote.

q: When taking a vote, the chair calls for abstentions last and uses them to figure the majority.
exp: The chair doesn't call for abstentions, and they don't count toward the majority.

q: A chair who says "All in favor, say 'aye'... Opposed?" has left out the proper cue for the negative vote.
exp: The negative should be called with "Those opposed, say 'no.'"

q: "All those in favor say aye," "As many as are in favor, say aye," and "Those in favor of the motion, say aye" are all acceptable ways to call for the affirmative.
exp: All are proper forms for the affirmative vote.

q: An uncounted rising vote is normally used on motions that need a two-thirds vote.
exp: A rising vote is the usual method for two-thirds votes.

q: When a rising vote is unclear, only the secretary can order a count to keep the minutes accurate.
exp: The chair or the assembly can order a count.

q: If a rising vote is inconclusive, the chair should just repeat the uncounted rising vote.
exp: The chair should retake it as a counted rising vote.

q: A show of hands can be used to settle an unclear vote in any size group.
exp: A show of hands is meant for small groups where everyone can be seen.

q: Members may change their votes up until the result is announced.
exp: After the result is announced, a change requires unanimous consent.

q: When announcing a voice vote, the chair should say which side has it, whether the motion passed or failed, and what effect the vote has.
exp: A complete announcement includes all three.

q: After a counted vote, the chair gives the count before saying which side prevails.
exp: The numbers come first, then the result.

q: When the ayes win a voice vote, the chair announces, "The ayes have it, and the motion is affirmed."
exp: The chair says, "The ayes have it, and the motion is adopted."

q: After a counted rising vote, the chair might say, "There are 20 in the affirmative and 10 in the negative. The affirmative has it, and the motion is adopted."
exp: This is a proper announcement of a counted vote.

q: When a motion needing two-thirds falls short, the chair says, "There are less than two-thirds in the affirmative, and the motion is lost."
exp: This is the proper announcement.

q: On a 26–26 tie on a main motion, the chair would have to vote no for the motion to pass.
exp: The chair would have to vote yes to break the tie in favor.

q: A counted vote on a main motion is 24 yes and 23 no, and the chair votes no. The result is a tie, so the motion passes.
exp: The 24–24 tie means the motion is lost, since a tie isn't a majority.

q: A chair who is unsure about a close voice vote should retake it as a division (rising vote).
exp: The chair may retake a doubtful vote by rising.

q: A member's demand that a vote be retaken by rising is called a "Division of the House."
exp: It is called a Division of the Assembly, or simply "a division."

q: A division may be demanded from the time the negative vote has been taken until the chair states the question on another motion.
exp: That is the window for demanding a division.

q: To have a voice vote retaken by rising, a member may call out without the floor, "I call for a division of the question."
exp: The member says "Division!" or "I call for a division"; Division of the Question is a different motion.

q: A member may move that a vote be counted; this motion needs a second and a two-thirds vote.
exp: A motion to count a vote needs a second and a majority vote.

q: After the chair announces a voice vote, a member who wants a counted vote should rise, address the chair, get recognized, and say, "I move that the vote be counted."
exp: A motion to count the vote is the correct method.

q: In a very small group where everyone is visible, an unclear voice vote must be checked by a rising vote.
exp: In very small groups, a show of hands may be used instead.

q: In a very small group, the chair may on their own initiative check an unclear voice vote by a show of hands.
exp: A show of hands is a proper way to verify a vote in a small group.

q: In a large assembly, the chair may vote when the vote would change the result, and may otherwise abstain.
exp: The chair votes only when it affects the outcome, or by ballot.

q: If a vote is tied and the chair doesn't vote, the chair should declare the motion adopted.
exp: A tie means the motion is lost.

q: Unanimous consent is also called general consent.
exp: The terms mean the same thing.

q: The rules of parliamentary procedure exist only to protect the majority.
exp: The rules protect everyone, including the minority, absentees, and individual members.

q: Adopting a motion without stating the question or taking a formal vote is called adopting by unanimous (general) consent.
exp: General consent skips the formal steps when no one objects.

q: To use unanimous consent, the chair may say, "Is there any objection to...? [pause] Since there is no objection, the motion that... is adopted."
exp: This is the proper form for general consent.

q: Correcting and approving the minutes is normally done by a main motion.
exp: The minutes are usually corrected and approved by general consent.

q: If a speaker's time runs out and they ask for two more minutes, the chair may say, "Is there any objection to extending the member's time by two minutes? [pause] Hearing none, it is so ordered."
exp: A time extension can be granted by unanimous consent.

q: A subject must be in the form of a privileged motion before the assembly can consider it.
exp: A subject must come in as a main motion.

q: Subsidiary, privileged, and incidental motions together are called "secondary motions."
exp: These classes are the secondary motions.

q: Of the five classes of motions, privileged motions make up the first class.
exp: Main motions, both original and incidental, are the first class.

q: Subsidiary motions belong to a different class from original main motions.
exp: Subsidiary motions are secondary motions; original main motions are main motions.

q: Original main motions, incidental main motions, and motions that bring a question back are all secondary motions.
exp: The secondary motions are subsidiary, privileged, and incidental motions.

q: No secondary motion may be made while a main motion is pending.
exp: Secondary motions are designed to be made while a main motion is pending.

q: Once a secondary motion is made and stated, it must be dealt with before the assembly can return to the main motion.
exp: The secondary motion has to be disposed of first.

q: After an amendment to a main motion is stated, the main motion is the immediately pending question.
exp: The amendment becomes the immediately pending question.

q: If motion B is properly made and seconded while motion A is pending, motion B takes precedence over motion A.
exp: A motion that can be made while another is pending ranks above it.

q: A main motion takes precedence over every other motion.
exp: A main motion takes precedence over nothing and yields to all applicable secondary motions.

q: When a main motion and two secondary motions are pending, the most recently stated motion is the immediately pending question.
exp: The last motion stated is voted on first.

q: If Amend, Adjourn, Commit, and a main motion are all pending, the main motion ranks lowest.
exp: The main motion is always at the bottom of the ladder.

q: The five privileged motions outrank only the subsidiary motions.
exp: Privileged motions outrank all other motions.

q: Incidental motions are ranked among themselves and have a fixed place in the order of precedence.
exp: Incidental motions have no rank among themselves.

q: Main motions can't be used to bring business before the assembly.
exp: Bringing business before the assembly is exactly what main motions do.

q: Incidental motions are the class that helps the assembly treat or dispose of a main motion.
exp: That describes subsidiary motions.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is the motion to use when you want to put off a motion until a later time.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely kills the motion without a direct vote; Postpone to a Certain Time delays it.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is not one of the incidental motions.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely is a subsidiary motion.

q: To change the wording of a main motion, you would propose the subsidiary motion to Amend.
exp: Amend modifies the wording of the pending motion.

q: A member who wants the pending question studied more closely can move to refer it to a committee.
exp: Commit (Refer) sends the question to a committee for study.

q: To take up a motion later in the same meeting, a member can move to Postpone to a Certain Time.
exp: Postpone to a Certain Time delays a question to a set time.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is used to delay a main motion until the next meeting.
exp: Postpone to a Certain Time (Postpone Definitely) delays to later in the meeting or the next meeting; Postpone Indefinitely kills the motion.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time is not classified as an incidental motion.
exp: It is a subsidiary motion.

q: To put a time limit on discussion of a main motion, you would get the floor and say, "I move to limit debate to twelve more minutes."
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: This is a proper form of the motion to Limit Debate.

q: The motion to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can be used to allow members more speeches than normal.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: Extending limits can add speeches or time.

q: To end debate and vote right away on a pending motion, you would move to Postpone to a Certain Time.
exp: The motion to close debate and vote now is the Previous Question.

q: To set a motion aside temporarily with no set time to resume it, a member would move to Lay on the Table.
exp: Lay on the Table sets aside a question temporarily when something urgent comes up.

q: Subsidiary motions have no place in the order of precedence.
exp: Subsidiary motions have a definite rank in the order of precedence.

q: Subsidiary motions can be applied to any main motion.
exp: All subsidiary motions apply to main motions.

q: Postpone Indefinitely can be amended.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely is not amendable.

q: Amend can be applied to some subsidiary motions even though Amend ranks below them.
exp: For example, Commit, Postpone, and Limit Debate can all be amended.

q: A motion to Lay on the Table is in order while a motion to Postpone to a Certain Time is the immediately pending question.
exp: Lay on the Table outranks Postpone to a Certain Time.

q: The motion to Amend is debatable in every case.
exp: Amend is debatable only when the motion it would change is debatable.

q: Lay on the Table, the Previous Question, and Limit or Extend Limits of Debate may be debated, but each member may speak only once.
exp: These three highest-ranking subsidiary motions are undebatable.

q: The Previous Question cannot be applied to the motion to Lay on the Table.
exp: Lay on the Table is undebatable and outranks the Previous Question.

q: Subsidiary motions don't relate to the pending business, but they are urgent enough to interrupt anything.
exp: That describes privileged motions.

q: There are four privileged motions.
exp: There are five: Call for the Orders of the Day, Raise a Question of Privilege, Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q: Every privileged motion has a place in the order of precedence.
exp: The privileged motions have a definite rank.

q: Privileged motions are also called "privileged questions."
exp: Both terms are used.

q: A member uses a Call for the Orders of the Day when they can't hear what's going on in the meeting.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It demands that the assembly follow its agenda; a hearing problem calls for a Question of Privilege.

q: One member can force a Call for the Orders of the Day, but a majority vote can set it aside.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: Setting aside the orders of the day takes a two-thirds vote.

q: Call for the Orders of the Day is the lowest-ranking privileged motion.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It is at the bottom of the privileged motions.

q: If the meeting room is stuffy and you want the ventilation fixed, you would Raise a Question of Privilege.
exp: Comfort of the assembly is a question of privilege.

q: A member may move to adjourn while business is pending, as long as a time for the next meeting has already been set.
exp: In that case, Adjourn is a privileged motion.

q: A member would move to Recess to set the date and hour of an extra meeting before the next regular meeting.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: That is the motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is the highest-ranking privileged motion.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It ranks highest of all motions.

q: Motions that relate in various ways to the pending business or other business at hand are called privileged motions.
exp: These are incidental motions.

q: Incidental motions usually deal with questions of procedure arising from another pending motion.
exp: That is the typical role of incidental motions.

q: Incidental motions usually relate to the pending question and must be decided right away before business continues.
exp: They must be settled before the assembly can go on.

q: Every incidental motion is debatable.
exp: Most incidental motions are undebatable.

q: To call the chair's attention to a rules violation, a member should immediately move to Suspend the Rules.
exp: The correct tool is a Point of Order.

q: A Point of Order is not a subsidiary motion.
exp: A Point of Order is an incidental motion.

q: Appeal is classified as an incidental motion.
exp: Appeal is incidental.

q: The motion to Repeal is used to put the chair's ruling to a vote of the assembly.
exp: That is the motion to Appeal.

q: A member who doesn't want a main motion discussed at all may raise an Objection to the Consideration of a Question.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: This objection can prevent consideration of an original main motion.

q: If a motion contains two parts that could each stand alone, a member can move for a Division of the Question.
exp: Division of the Question splits the motion into separate questions.

q: If you doubt the chair's announcement of a voice vote or show of hands, you can get a rising vote by making a Request for Information.
exp: The way to get a rising vote is a Division of the Assembly.

q: A single member can force a counted vote.
exp: One member can demand a rising vote (Division), but a count needs a majority vote or the chair's order.

q: Motions to close or reopen nominations can be made while an election is pending.
exp: These motions relate to the pending election.

q: A Parliamentary Inquiry asks the chair to make a ruling on a procedural question.
exp: An inquiry asks for the chair's opinion, not a ruling, on procedure as it relates to the business at hand.

q: A Request for Information can be addressed to the chair, or to another member through the chair.
exp: Questions to another member go through the chair.

q: A request to be excused from a duty is a privileged motion.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: It is an incidental motion.

q: A Point of Order outranks any pending motion, but only at the moment the breach happens.
exp: It must be raised promptly, at the time of the breach.

q: Incidental motions have no rank among themselves.
exp: Their rank depends on the motion they arise from.

q: A Point of Order arising from a motion to Recess would yield to a motion to Adjourn.
exp: An incidental motion takes the rank of the motion it arises from, and Adjourn outranks Recess.

q: Take from the Table is one of the motions that bring a question back before the assembly.
exp: It is a "bring-back" motion.

q: To cancel an entire main motion that has already been adopted, you could move to Rescind, Repeal, or Annul it.
exp: These are names for the same motion.

q: The motion to Discharge a Committee is used to charge a committee with neglecting its duty.
exp: Discharge takes a matter out of the committee's hands.

q: If you learn something new about an adopted motion that might change how members voted, you could move to Reconsider.
exp: Reconsider brings the vote back for a new decision.

q: Rescind is an original main motion.
exp: Rescind is an incidental main motion.

q: Amend Something Previously Adopted is an incidental main motion.
exp: It is an incidental main motion.

q: Discharge a Committee and Take from the Table both propose taking up a matter that is still "within the control" of the assembly or a committee.
section: Motions That Bring a Question Again Before the Assembly
exp: Both bring back a pending matter.

q: Reconsider can apply to a main motion whether it passed or failed, but Rescind applies only to a main motion that ended in a tie.
exp: Rescind applies only to a motion that was adopted.

q: Reconsider can't be made while other motions are pending.
exp: A motion to Reconsider can be made, though not always considered, while other business is pending.

q: RONR uses twelve standard characteristics to describe the rules for each motion.
exp: There are eight standard descriptive characteristics.

q: Because the main motion ranks lowest, it takes precedence over all other motions.
exp: Ranking lowest means it takes precedence over no other motion.

q: A main motion is amendable.
exp: Being amendable is one of its standard characteristics.

q: The other motions that can be applied to a motion are one of its standard descriptive characteristics.
exp: Applicable motions are one of the eight characteristics.

q: Which members may debate a motion is not one of the standard descriptive characteristics.
exp: The characteristics cover whether a motion is debatable, not who may debate it.

q: The voting characteristic of a motion tells which method of voting must be used.
exp: It tells what vote is needed for adoption.

q: A meeting is a single official gathering of an assembly's members.
exp: A meeting is one gathering with no separation except a short recess.

q: A session of an assembly is a caucus of members held outside the meeting room.
exp: A session is a meeting or series of connected meetings.

q: A session is usually devoted to at least two orders of business.
exp: A session is typically devoted to one order of business, program, or agenda.

q: A short break that doesn't end the meeting is called an adjournment sine die.
exp: A short break is a recess.

q: "Sine die" means "without ending."
exp: It means "without day."

q: Adjourning sine die ends a session of several meetings and is the assembly's final adjournment.
exp: It is the final adjournment of a session.

q: When the final meeting in a series of mass meetings adjourns sine die, the assembly is dissolved.
exp: Adjourning sine die dissolves a mass meeting.

q: The everyday use of "recess" for the time between regular sessions has nothing to do with its parliamentary meaning.
exp: In parliamentary terms, a recess is a short break within a meeting.

q: When a session runs for several days, the minutes are usually read at the end of each day's last meeting.
exp: They are read at the start of each day's first meeting.

q: If a meeting adjourns without ending the session, the next meeting can be set by adopting a motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: This sets an adjourned meeting that continues the session.

q: A standing rule adopted at one session doesn't tie the hands of later sessions, because it can be suspended by a two-thirds vote.
exp: An ordinary standing rule can be suspended for a session by a majority vote.

q: Bylaws and special rules of order contain the provisions members expect to stay stable from one session to the next.
exp: They are harder to change for that reason.

q: A regular meeting is also called an ad hoc meeting.
exp: A regular meeting is also called a stated meeting.

q: The bylaws should state both the day (such as the third Tuesday) and the hour of regular meetings.
exp: The day belongs in the bylaws; the hour is best set in a standing rule.

q: In a group that meets less often than quarterly, a main motion can be carried over to the next session by referring it to a committee to report then.
exp: Referring keeps the matter alive across sessions.

q: A meeting held at a time other than the regular meeting to deal with specific items is called an adjourned meeting.
exp: That is a special meeting.

q: Members must be notified in advance of a special meeting's time, place, and exact purpose.
exp: The call of a special meeting must state its purpose.

q: A special meeting may consider only the business named in its call.
exp: Only items in the call may be acted on.

q: Special meetings can be called only if the president approves.
exp: Special meetings may be called only if the bylaws authorize them.

q: The president may call a special meeting at any time with no notice.
exp: Notice of the time, place, and purpose must be sent to members a reasonable time ahead.

q: The bylaw authorizing special meetings should state how many days' notice is required.
exp: The bylaws should set the notice period.

q: A special meeting considers items that members learn about for the first time when the meeting opens.
exp: It considers only items listed in the call.

q: Business done at a special meeting that wasn't in the call becomes valid only if the organization later ratifies it.
exp: Ratification at a later meeting makes it valid.

q: A special meeting is a continuation of the regular or special meeting just before it.
exp: A continuation meeting is an adjourned meeting.

q: A society meeting on September 21 can't finish its business and votes to adjourn until October 21. The October meeting is an adjourned meeting.
exp: It continues the September meeting's session.

q: A special meeting is also known as a "stated meeting."
exp: A special meeting is a "called meeting"; a stated meeting is a regular meeting.

q: The minutes of the previous meeting are read at an adjourned meeting.
exp: The adjourned meeting starts with the minutes.

q: A society that holds only one general business meeting a year calls it the "calendar meeting."
exp: That yearly meeting is the annual meeting.

q: In a group that has regular meetings all year, the annual meeting's minutes are read and approved at the next regular meeting.
exp: They are approved at the next regular business meeting.

q: A meeting, or part of one, whose proceedings are secret is called a "confidential session."
exp: It is called executive session.

q: Disciplinary matters, especially trials, should normally be handled in executive session.
exp: Discipline is handled in executive session to protect everyone involved.

q: A motion to go into executive session is a question of privilege that needs a second and a majority vote.
exp: It is a question of privilege.

q: The organization can do nothing about a member who breaks the secrecy of an executive session.
exp: The member may be disciplined.

q: Minutes of an executive session are usually read and approved in another executive session.
exp: The minutes stay confidential.

q: An original main motion is one that amends the first main motion made at a meeting.
exp: An original main motion brings a new substantive subject before the assembly.

q: What sets an incidental main motion apart from an original main motion is that it brings up a new substantive subject.
exp: An incidental main motion never introduces a new substantive subject.

q: A motion to take a recess while business is pending is an example of an incidental main motion.
exp: A recess motion is an incidental main motion only when no business is pending; otherwise it is privileged.

q: The key rule difference is that an Objection to the Consideration of a Question can't be applied to incidental main motions.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: The objection applies only to original main motions.

q: A main motion can be applied to any other motion.
exp: A main motion can't be applied to any other motion.

q: Every subsidiary motion can be applied to an original main motion.
exp: All subsidiary motions apply to main motions.

q: A main motion may be made while another member has the floor.
exp: Main motions are out of order when another has the floor.

q: A main motion that puts a special limit on the number of speeches per member at a meeting needs a two-thirds vote.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: Limiting debate rights requires two-thirds.

q: As a general rule, avoid wording a main motion so that it asks the assembly not to do something.
exp: A negative motion is usually improper because voting it down has the same effect.

q: A member who gets the floor and says, "I move that this organization declare its opposition to the recent dues increase," is in order.
exp: Declaring a position is a proper main motion.

q: A motion to reaffirm a position already taken is in order.
exp: A motion to reaffirm an existing position is out of order.

q: A resolution should always be offered orally.
exp: A resolution should always be in writing.

q: When a resolution includes reasons, a preamble beginning with "Whereas" explains why it should be adopted.
exp: The preamble gives the reasons; the resolving clauses follow.

q: When a resolution has a preamble, the preamble is amended first.
exp: The preamble is amended last, after the resolving clauses.

q: After the Previous Question is ordered on a resolution with a preamble, the preamble may still be debated.
exp: The preamble is handled after the resolving clauses, so it can still be debated and amended.

q: In a written resolution, "Resolved" is never underlined or italicized.
exp: "Resolved" is customarily underlined or italicized.

q: A main motion may be offered even if it repeats a question already rejected earlier in the same session.
exp: A motion that repeats a question rejected earlier in the same session is out of order.

q: A main motion is out of order if it conflicts with law, conflicts with or repeats a question that is temporarily but not finally disposed of, or goes beyond the organization's purpose (unless two-thirds agree to consider it).
exp: These are the standard limits on main motions.

q: After a main motion is made but before the chair states it, any member may informally suggest changes to the maker.
exp: The motion still belongs to the maker until it is stated.

q: After the chair states the question, the maker may try to change the motion by asking for unanimous consent.
exp: Once stated, a motion belongs to the assembly, so changes need consent or an amendment.

q: If a motion clearly needs more time or study before it is ready, a member should move to Postpone Indefinitely.
exp: The right motion is to Commit (refer); Postpone Indefinitely kills a motion.

q: A member may speak in debate on a main motion and finish by moving an amendment.
exp: Members can debate and then offer an amendment.

q: A main motion and an amendment are pending, and a member moves to refer both to a committee. The main motion is voted on first.
exp: The motion to Commit is voted on first because it is the immediately pending question.

q: When a main motion and a motion to Postpone Indefinitely are both pending, the main motion is voted on first.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely is voted on first.

q: If a main motion, a primary amendment, and a motion to Commit are pending and Commit passes, the amendment goes to the committee along with the main motion.
exp: Pending amendments go with the main motion.

q: A member can bring up a main motion while another is pending by making a "Call for the Previous Order."
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: The correct motion is a Call for the Orders of the Day, which applies only to scheduled business.

q: Some questions can be brought up by the lowest-ranking privileged motion, Call for the Orders of the Day.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It brings up business scheduled as orders of the day.

q: When debate seems to be over, the chair checks whether anyone else wants to speak by asking, "Are there any questions?"
exp: The chair asks, "Are you ready for the question?"

q: "Previous notice" means that members are informed ahead of time that a particular motion will be brought up at a meeting.
exp: Notice protects members who might otherwise be absent.

q: Rescind, Amend Something Previously Adopted, and Discharge a Committee need no previous notice if they are to pass by a simple majority.
exp: To pass by a majority vote, these motions require previous notice.

q: Adopting special rules of order takes only a two-thirds vote, with no other requirement.
exp: It takes previous notice and a two-thirds vote, or a majority of the entire membership.

q: Any member present at a meeting may give previous notice.
exp: Notice isn't limited to officers.

q: Previous notice of a motion may be given orally at a meeting even while a question is pending, as long as no speaker is interrupted.
exp: Notice can be given when no one else has the floor.

q: Previous notice may be sent to members by mail.
exp: Notice can be given in writing, such as in the call of the meeting.

q: Ratify is a privileged motion.
exp: Ratify is an incidental main motion.

q: The motion to Ratify is used to delay action.
exp: Ratify confirms action already taken that needs the assembly's approval.

q: If adopted, a motion to Ratify makes valid an action already taken.
exp: Ratifying approves the action after the fact.

q: Ratification is the right procedure for emergency action taken at a regular meeting that lacked a quorum.
exp: The assembly can ratify it at a later meeting with a quorum.

q: Ratify should not be used to validate a voice-vote election when the bylaws require a ballot.
exp: An assembly can't ratify what it had no authority to do that way.

q: If emergency action is taken without a quorum, a motion to ratify can approve it, and the question can't be debated again.
exp: A motion to ratify opens the whole question to debate.

q: To kill a pending main motion and avoid voting on it for the rest of the meeting, you would move to Rescind.
exp: The motion to use is Postpone Indefinitely.

q: If Postpone Indefinitely passes, the main motion is dead for the rest of the session.
exp: It kills the main motion for the session.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is used when a member wants to avoid a direct vote on the question.
exp: It disposes of the question without a direct vote.

q: Postpone Indefinitely outranks all other subsidiary motions.
exp: It outranks only the main motion.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is the lowest-ranking subsidiary motion.
exp: It ranks just above the main motion.

q: Postpone Indefinitely can be applied to any debatable motion.
exp: It applies only to main motions.

q: If a main motion is pending and an amendment is being debated, a motion to Postpone Indefinitely is out of order.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely ranks below Amend.

q: Postpone Indefinitely may be moved while an amendment is the immediately pending question.
exp: It can be moved only when the main motion is immediately pending.

q: If the main motion is laid on the table, a pending motion to Postpone Indefinitely goes with it.
exp: Pending subsidiary motions adhere to the main motion.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is debatable, but debate can't go into the merits of the main question.
exp: Debate on Postpone Indefinitely may go fully into the main question.

q: A motion to Postpone Indefinitely is out of order while another member has the floor.
exp: The mover must obtain the floor.

q: A member moves to amend a motion to Postpone Indefinitely by adding "until our next regular meeting." As chair, you should rule this amendment out of order.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely can't be amended.

q: A motion to Postpone Indefinitely that failed can be reconsidered.
exp: Only an affirmative vote on Postpone Indefinitely can be reconsidered.

q: At a multi-meeting convention, a motion that was postponed indefinitely stays suppressed only for the meeting where that happened.
exp: It stays suppressed for the entire session.

q: Adopting Postpone Indefinitely rejects the main motion indirectly.
exp: It kills the main motion without a direct vote.

q: Opponents can test their strength on a motion by moving to Postpone Indefinitely, which shuts off debate on the main motion.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely actually opens more debate on the main motion.

q: If a main motion is referred to a committee while Postpone Indefinitely is immediately pending, the motion to Postpone Indefinitely does not go to the committee.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely is dropped when the main motion is referred.

q: If you're sure a pending motion would harm your organization and want to stop it now, you could get the floor and say, "I move that this motion be postponed indefinitely."
exp: This is the correct form to kill a motion.

q: The main purpose of the motion to Amend is to change the wording of a pending motion.
exp: Amend modifies the motion before it is voted on.

q: Adopting an amendment to a main motion also adopts the main motion.
exp: The main motion remains pending, as amended, and may be debated further.

q: If an amendment is rejected, the motion it would have changed is rejected too.
exp: The motion stays pending in its original wording.

q: In RONR terms, the assembly "makes" an amendment.
exp: Members move amendments; the assembly makes them.

q: Voting for an amendment commits a member to vote for the amended motion too.
exp: A member may vote any way on the amended motion.

q: An amendment must be germane to be in order.
exp: It must relate to the subject of the motion it would change.

q: When applied to a main motion, Amend outranks Postpone Indefinitely.
exp: Amend ranks above Postpone Indefinitely.

q: Amend can be applied to any main motion and to any motion with a variable element.
exp: Motions with a variable element (time, number, etc.) are amendable.

q: When Amend is applied to an amendment, the result is called a "special subsidiary amendment."
exp: It is called a secondary amendment.

q: A motion to Amend can be postponed indefinitely.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely applies only to main motions.

q: A motion to Amend needs a second.
exp: Amend requires a second.

q: A primary amendment to a main motion is undebatable.
exp: It is debatable whenever the motion it would change is debatable.

q: While an amendment is pending, members may freely debate the motion it would amend.
exp: Debate must be limited to the amendment, touching the main motion only as it relates.

q: The motion to Amend can be applied to itself.
exp: An amendment to an amendment is a secondary amendment.

q: As chair, you should rule out of order a motion to amend a secondary amendment.
exp: Third-degree amendments are not allowed.

q: A secondary amendment may be amended if its maker agrees.
exp: A secondary amendment cannot be amended.

q: An amendment to a primary amendment is called a "secondary motion."
exp: It is called a secondary amendment.

q: "Prime amendment" is the preferred term for an amendment to a main motion.
exp: The preferred term is primary amendment.

q: "Secondary amendment" is the preferred term for an amendment to an amendment.
exp: That is the correct term.

q: A third-degree amendment is never allowed.
exp: Only primary and secondary amendments are allowed.

q: Only one primary amendment and one secondary amendment may be pending at a time.
exp: This limit keeps amending manageable.

q: An amendment to a motion that needs two-thirds must itself get two-thirds to pass.
exp: An amendment needs only a majority, even then.

q: Adding words to the end of a sentence is the "add" form of amendment.
exp: Inserting at the end is called adding.

q: Filling a blank is not one of the forms of amendment.
exp: Filling blanks is a separate method, not one of the amendment forms.

q: To remove a paragraph and put in a new one, the proper form of amendment is "strike out."
exp: The proper form is "substitute."

q: Inserting, striking out, and striking out and inserting can all be used to change wording within one sentence.
exp: These are the three basic processes of amendment.

q: For an amendment to be germane, it must include the date and purpose of the change.
exp: Germane means the amendment relates to the motion it would change.

q: A motion "to commend" the basketball coach is pending, and a member moves to strike "commend" and insert "censure." The chair should accept the amendment and ask for a second.
exp: It is germane, even though it reverses the intent.

q: If the chair can't decide whether an amendment is germane, the chair should ask its maker to withdraw it.
exp: The chair can put the question of germaneness to the assembly.

q: A motion "to postpone the question until 1 p.m." is pending, and a member moves to strike "until 1 p.m." and insert "indefinitely." As chair, you should process this amendment.
exp: It's out of order because it would change one kind of motion into another.

q: A frivolous or absurd amendment is always out of order.
exp: Such amendments are not allowed.

q: The "insert" form of amendment always puts the new word at the end of the motion.
exp: Insert places words between others; "add" places them at the end.

q: With "to buy basketballs" pending, a correct way to amend by inserting is: "I move to amend by inserting the word 'three.'"
exp: You must say where: "...inserting 'three' before 'basketballs.'"

q: With "that we have a dance next Saturday" pending, you'd add the time by saying, "I move to amend by inserting 'from 9 p.m. to 11:30 p.m.'"
exp: Words placed at the end are added: "I move to amend by adding..."

q: As chair, after an amendment to the main motion is adopted, the next step is debate on the main motion as amended.
exp: The amended main motion becomes immediately pending.

q: An amendment can be adopted without a formal vote, by unanimous consent.
exp: Simple or widely accepted amendments are often adopted by general consent.

q: When striking out words scattered through a motion, the best approach is to strike out the whole clause containing them and insert a new clause.
exp: This is clearer than several separate amendments.

q: A substitute offered for a main motion is an incidental main motion.
exp: A substitute is a primary amendment.

q: When a motion to substitute is pending, debate is limited to the merits of the substitute alone.
exp: Debate may go fully into both the main motion and the substitute.

q: After one section of a resolution is substituted for another, the new section can still be amended by adding.
exp: A substituted section may only be added to.

q: A blank can be created only in motions that contain place names.
exp: Blanks can be used for names of persons, places, amounts, dates, and numbers.

q: A blank may be created by a member offering a motion with a blank, by a member moving to create one, or by the chair suggesting one.
exp: All three are proper.

q: A motion to create a blank is a main motion.
exp: It is an incidental motion.

q: A motion to create a blank doesn't need a second.
exp: It needs a second.

q: When the chair sees that a blank would help move a motion along, the chair may suggest creating one and ask for general consent.
exp: The chair can suggest a blank and use general consent.

q: Each proposal to fill a blank is debated and voted on separately until one gets a two-thirds vote.
exp: The first to get a majority fills the blank.

q: A blank can be filled with names, dollar amounts, places, dates, or numbers.
exp: These are the usual kinds of blanks.

q: A name proposed to fill a blank needs a majority vote to be chosen.
exp: A majority vote fills the blank.

q: If $125,000, $145,000, $149,000, and $151,000 are proposed to fill a blank for money to be spent, $151,000 is voted on first.
exp: For spending, amounts are voted on from the largest down.

q: The vote that fills a blank also decides the main motion.
exp: The main motion is voted on after the blank is filled.

q: Commit (Refer) sends a pending question to a committee so it can be studied and put in better shape for the assembly.
exp: That is the purpose of Commit.

q: A main advantage of committees is freer debate, meaning members may speak up to three times on each topic.
exp: In committees, members may speak as often as they like.

q: Considering informally, going into a committee of the whole, and going into a quasi committee of the whole are all forms of the motion to Commit.
exp: These are variations of Commit.

q: "Recommit" is the term used when the original motion to Commit fails.
exp: Recommit means referring a matter to a committee a second time.

q: Commit (Refer) outranks Amend.
exp: Commit ranks above Amend.

q: The motion to refer to a committee can be applied to main motions.
exp: Commit applies to main motions.

q: Commit can't be applied to a main motion that has amendments pending.
exp: The main motion and its pending amendments go to the committee together.

q: A motion to Commit can be postponed indefinitely.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely applies only to main motions.

q: Debate on a motion to Commit is limited to whether referring the question is a good idea.
exp: Debate can't go into the merits of the main question.

q: Commit needs previous notice and a two-thirds vote.
exp: Commit needs only a majority vote.

q: A motion to refer the main question to a standing committee should name the committee.
exp: The motion should say which committee.

q: When referring to a special (select or ad hoc) committee, the motion may set the number of members, how they're chosen, or name them.
exp: These details may be included in the motion.

q: Instructions in a motion to Commit may bind the committee on how to vote.
exp: Instructions may cover when to report, how to handle the question, or hiring an expert, not how to vote.

q: A special committee with "full power" may act for the society in all similar cases from then on.
exp: Full power applies only to the specific matter referred.

q: A committee may be given "full power" to act for the organization in a specific matter.
exp: Full power authorizes action on that matter.

q: As chair of a monthly meeting, a motion needing action by tomorrow is pending, and a member moves to refer it to a committee to report at the next regular meeting. You would rule the motion to refer dilatory.
exp: A motion that would defeat the purpose of the pending question is dilatory.

q: If someone makes an incomplete motion like "to refer the main motion to a committee," the chair may ask for amendments to fill in the details.
exp: Details like who serves and when to report can be added.

q: When the assembly suggests different kinds of committees for referring a main motion, the chair takes the vote on the committee of the whole first.
exp: The committee forms are voted on in a set order, beginning with the committee of the whole.

q: If several ways of choosing a committee are proposed, such as voice vote, floor nominations, ballot, and appointment by the chair, election by ballot is voted on first.
exp: Ballot election is taken first among selection methods.

q: The names of any non-members the chair appoints to committees must be approved by the chair of each committee.
exp: Such appointments must be approved by the assembly.

q: When the chair appoints a committee, the committee members pick their own chair.
exp: The appointing chair also names the committee chair.

q: When the presiding officer appoints a committee at a regular meeting, the committee chair is usually the member named last.
exp: The first person named is usually the committee chair.

q: If the chair didn't name the committee, the vice-president picks its chair.
exp: The body that elected the committee chooses its chair.

q: If a motion to Postpone Indefinitely was made before a member moved to refer the main motion, as chair you would declare that the motion to Postpone Indefinitely cannot be considered.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely applies only to a main motion that is immediately pending.

q: A vacancy on a committee the president appointed is filled by the committee's chair.
exp: Vacancies are filled by the president, who made the appointment.

q: The correct form is "I move to commit and refer the motion to a committee."
exp: A correct form is "I move to refer the motion to a committee."

q: "I move to commit or refer" is not a correct form of the motion to Commit.
exp: The motion should say "refer" or "commit," not both.

q: If you think a pending main motion needs further study, you could get the floor and say, "I move that the main motion be referred to a committee to be appointed by the chair."
exp: The motion can also set the size, appointing power, and reporting time.

q: "Postpone," "Postpone Definitely," and "Postpone to a Certain Time" all describe putting off action on a pending motion.
exp: These names mean the same motion.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time has the same effect as Postpone Indefinitely.
exp: One delays to a set time; the other kills the motion.

q: A motion to postpone business that isn't pending is a privileged motion.
exp: It is an incidental main motion.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time may be moved while a main motion and an amendment to it are pending.
exp: It outranks Amend.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time does not outrank the motion to Amend.
exp: Postpone to a Certain Time ranks above Amend.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time yields to a motion to Lay on the Table.
exp: Lay on the Table ranks higher.

q: A motion to Postpone to a Certain Time can by itself be postponed indefinitely, committed, or laid on the table.
exp: None of these can be applied to it alone.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time is in order while another member has the floor.
exp: It is out of order when another has the floor.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time is debatable.
exp: Debate is limited to the timing and reasons for postponing.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time can be amended and reconsidered.
exp: The time can be amended, and the vote can be reconsidered.

q: A motion to Postpone to a Certain Time can be amended to change where the question will be considered.
exp: It can be amended as to time, not place.

q: In an assembly that meets less often than quarterly, a question can't be postponed past the end of the next session.
exp: It can't be postponed past the end of the current session.

q: In an organization that holds weekly business meetings, a question can be postponed for up to a quarter (about three months).
exp: It can be postponed only to the next regular meeting, about a week.

q: In an assembly that meets at least quarterly, a question can't be postponed past the end of the next session.
exp: The next regular session is the limit.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time does not have the same effect as Postpone Indefinitely.
exp: One delays, the other kills.

q: The motion "that we play volleyball tonight" is pending, and a member moves to postpone it until tomorrow. As chair, you would rule that motion out of order.
exp: Postponing past the time the action could happen would kill it, so it's out of order.

q: As chair, if a member wants to postpone both officer and committee reports, you should suggest postponing each one as it is called for.
exp: Each report is postponed when it comes up.

q: When the bylaws require officers to be elected at a particular meeting, a pending election can be postponed by first adopting a motion to Adjourn.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: The assembly first adopts Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn, then postpones to that adjourned meeting.

q: Adopting Postpone Definitely always makes the postponed question an order of the day for a future meeting.
exp: It becomes an order of the day for whatever time it was postponed to, which may be later in the same meeting.

q: Orders of the day include both general orders and special orders.
exp: These are the two kinds.

q: General orders are taken up immediately after new business.
exp: They come under Unfinished Business and General Orders, before new business.

q: If business postponed to a meeting isn't finished before adjournment, it is generally laid on the table.
exp: It becomes unfinished business at the next regular meeting.

q: If a main motion is postponed while an amendment is pending, the amendment is lost.
exp: The amendment is postponed along with the main motion.

q: When an amendment is taken up on a different day than it was proposed, members who already spoke twice on it can't debate it again.
exp: On a new day, each member may speak twice again.

q: When a main motion postponed to a certain time comes up on a different day, each member may speak on it twice again.
exp: Speaking limits reset each day.

q: To make sure a question is considered at the next meeting without being crowded out, you could move "that the question be postponed to the next meeting and made a special order."
exp: A special order guarantees the question comes up.

q: To make a motion come up exactly at a given hour, even if that interrupts pending business, you would move "that the motion be postponed and made a special order for 3 p.m. tomorrow."
exp: A special order for a set time can interrupt pending business.

q: To put off a pending main motion until the next meeting, you would say, "I move to postpone the main motion indefinitely to our next regular meeting."
exp: The correct wording is "I move to postpone the main motion to our next regular meeting."

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate and the Previous Question are not allowed in committees.
exp: In committees, motions to close or limit debate generally aren't allowed.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can shorten speeches, reduce how many speeches are allowed, or set a time for debate to close.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: These are its main uses.

q: The motion to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can close debate instantly.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It can't close debate immediately; the Previous Question does that.

q: An order limiting or extending debate that no longer applies is said to have "expired."
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It is said to be "exhausted."

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate outranks every debatable motion.
exp: It ranks above all debatable motions.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can be applied to any debatable motion that is immediately pending.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It applies to any debatable motion.

q: When made with no question pending, a motion to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate needs only a majority.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It still needs two-thirds.

q: An order limiting debate on a main motion goes with the main motion if it is laid on the table.
exp: The order adheres to the main motion.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can be amended.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: The limits can be amended.

q: An amendment to a motion to Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is debatable.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: Amendments to it are undebatable.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate needs two-thirds mainly because it is really two separate motions.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It needs two-thirds because it limits members' right to discuss freely.

q: With three debatable motions pending, a motion "to limit debate to two minutes per member" affects only the immediately pending motion, unless it says otherwise.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
