exp: The unqualified form applies only to the immediately pending question.

q: As chair, if a member offers an amendment to the main motion while Limit or Extend Limits of Debate is pending, you should rule it out of order.
exp: Amend ranks below Limit Debate.

q: After a motion to close debate in ten minutes is adopted, it is in order to move to refer the matter to a committee.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: The key says referring isn't in order once that order is adopted.

q: After a motion extending debate to fifteen minutes per member passes, a member properly moves the Previous Question. As chair, you should allow debate on the Previous Question once it's seconded, then take a rising vote.
exp: The Previous Question is undebatable; take the vote right away after the second.

q: An order limiting or extending debate is exhausted when the affected questions are referred to a committee, when the meeting ends, or when all of them have been voted on.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: These end the order.

q: If debate is dragging and you want to limit each member to one speech, you should rise and, without getting the floor, say, "I move to limited debate."
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: Get the floor and say, "I move that debate be limited to one speech per member."

q: Unless it's adopted by unanimous consent, the chair of a large group puts a motion to limit debate to a vote by show of hands.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It needs two-thirds, so the chair uses a rising vote.

q: The "Privileged Question" is the motion used to stop debate immediately and vote on the pending question.
exp: That motion is the Previous Question.

q: If adopted, the Previous Question stops debate on the pending question and nothing else.
exp: It also stops further amendments.

q: The Previous Question is allowed in committees.
exp: It is generally not allowed in committees.

q: The Previous Question outranks Limit or Extend Limits of Debate.
exp: The Previous Question ranks higher.

q: The Previous Question doesn't prevent members from making privileged or incidental motions.
exp: Only debate and amendments are cut off.

q: The Previous Question can be applied to an immediately pending debatable or amendable motion, and to any consecutive series of pending motions starting with it.
exp: It may cover a consecutive series beginning with the immediately pending question.

q: The Previous Question can be applied to an undebatable motion to stop amendments to it.
exp: For example, it can be applied to a motion to Limit Debate.

q: The unqualified Previous Question applies only to the immediately pending motion.
exp: Unless it says otherwise, it covers only that motion.

q: "I move the previous question," with no qualification, applies to every pending question.
exp: The unqualified form applies only to the immediately pending question.

q: While a motion for the Previous Question is immediately pending, another may be made to cover more or fewer pending questions.
exp: These alternative versions are in order.

q: If ninety votes are cast on a motion for the Previous Question, it takes forty-six "yes" votes to pass.
exp: It needs two-thirds, which is sixty of ninety.

q: If a motion for the Previous Question fails, debate on the pending motion is stopped anyway.
exp: Debate continues as if the motion had never been made.

q: In the U.S. House of Representatives, the Previous Question can pass by a majority.
exp: The House uses a majority vote; ordinary societies need two-thirds.

q: After getting the floor, a member who wants to close debate now may say "I call for the question," "I call the question," or "I move we vote now."
exp: These are accepted informal forms.

q: "I move we vote now" follows different rules from the Previous Question.
exp: It is the Previous Question and follows all its rules.

q: If a member gets the floor and "calls the question" on a motion to Commit, as chair you should make sure it gets a second.
exp: Calling the question is a motion that needs a second.

q: When the Previous Question is ordered on a series of motions, they are voted on in the order they were made.
exp: They are voted on in reverse order, the most recent first.

q: The Previous Question is exhausted once every motion it covered has been disposed of.
exp: The order ends after those votes.

q: A vote ordering the Previous Question can be reconsidered at any time.
exp: It can be reconsidered only before any vote has been taken under it.

q: The form "I move the previous question" covers all pending questions.
exp: That form covers only the immediately pending question.

q: The proper way to call for the Previous Question is to shout "Question!" from your seat without recognition.
exp: Get the floor and say, "I move the previous question."

q: As chair, once the Previous Question is adopted on an amendment, you should immediately take the vote on that amendment.
exp: Ordering the Previous Question leads straight to the vote.

q: Lay on the Table lets an assembly set a pending question aside permanently when something urgent comes up.
exp: It sets the question aside temporarily.

q: Lay on the Table sets the pending question aside temporarily, with no set time to resume it.
exp: A motion to Take from the Table brings it back.

q: Lay on the Table is sometimes wrongly used in place of the motion to Commit.
exp: It is commonly misused in place of Postpone.

q: If a member moves to lay a question on the table until a specific time, as chair you should suggest it be offered as a motion to Postpone instead.
exp: Lay on the Table can't name a time.

q: Lay on the Table outranks every other motion.
exp: It outranks all subsidiary motions, but not privileged ones.

q: A motion to Lay on the Table is out of order when the real intent is to kill the motion.
exp: The proper way to kill a motion is Postpone Indefinitely.

q: When a main motion with a primary amendment pending is laid on the table, the amendment dies and comes up under unfinished business at the next meeting.
exp: The amendment goes to the table with the main motion.

q: No subsidiary motion can be applied to a motion to Lay on the Table.
exp: Lay on the Table can't be amended, referred, or postponed.

q: Lay on the Table can be applied only to a pending question.
exp: Only pending questions can be tabled.

q: Lay on the Table may be moved while another member has the floor.
exp: It is out of order when another has the floor.

q: The maker of a motion to Lay on the Table may never state a reason for it.
exp: The maker may briefly state the reason, such as the urgent matter.

q: A motion to Lay on the Table can be made after the Previous Question has been ordered.
exp: Lay on the Table outranks the Previous Question.

q: Lay on the Table can't be qualified in any way.
exp: It can't include a time or condition.

q: A motion to Lay on the Table can be amended.
exp: It can't be amended.

q: A negative vote on Lay on the Table can sometimes be reconsidered.
exp: The key says yes; RONR limits reconsideration here.

q: Take from the Table needs a majority vote.
exp: It is adopted by a majority.

q: A question may be taken from the table at a special meeting only with the chair's permission.
exp: It may be taken up if the call of the special meeting gave notice of it.

q: A question can't be laid on the table a second time on the same day, even after substantial debate.
exp: After substantial progress in debate, laying on the table again is in order.

q: In a group that meets at least quarterly, a tabled question stays there until it's taken up or until the end of the next special meeting.
exp: It stays until taken up or until the end of the next regular session.

q: Moving to lay a question on the table is out of order if no urgent matter requires attention.
exp: Lay on the Table is meant for urgent interruptions.

q: Lay on the Table is often misused to make room for non-urgent business, to cut off debate, or to kill a motion without a vote.
exp: These are all improper uses.

q: At a special meeting, the matter the meeting was called for can't be laid on the table.
exp: Tabling it would defeat the meeting's purpose.

q: Lay on the Table is the proper way to get rid of a motion without a direct vote.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely does that.

q: If an urgent matter comes up while a main motion is being debated, you would get the floor and say, "I move to lay the question on the table."
exp: This is the correct use of Lay on the Table.

q: Lay on the Table can say when the question will be taken up again.
exp: It can't be qualified with a time.

q: A member may mention the purpose for tabling when making the motion to Lay on the Table.
exp: Stating the urgent purpose is allowed.

q: Call for the Orders of the Day is mainly used to tell members when a point of order may be raised.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It is used to make the meeting follow its agenda.

q: Any member may call for the orders of the day.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: A single member can make the call.

q: Call for the Orders of the Day outranks all subsidiary motions.
exp: As a privileged motion, it ranks above them.

q: A member can Call for the Orders of the Day only when the assembly strays from its agenda.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It can also be used to bring up a general order that is due but isn't being taken up.

q: Call for the Orders of the Day needs no second and is neither debatable nor amendable.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: A single member's call is enough.

q: Any single member who objects can set aside the orders of the day.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: Setting them aside takes a two-thirds vote.

q: If a motion is made that departs from the proper order of business, a Call for the Orders of the Day must come before the chair puts the question.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It must be made before the chair states the motion.

q: As chair, if the orders of the day are called for but you sense the assembly wants to continue with the pending question, you may ask the assembly whether it wishes to proceed to the orders of the day.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: The chair can put that question to the assembly.

q: When the chair puts the question of proceeding to the orders of the day, a majority voting no is enough to keep the current business.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It takes a two-thirds negative vote to refuse to proceed.

q: If the assembly refuses to proceed to the orders of the day, they can't be called for again until the pending business is finished.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: The call can't be renewed until then.

q: In a large assembly, a member calling for the orders of the day doesn't need to be recognized.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: The call may be made without obtaining the floor.

q: The correct way to call for the orders of the day is to rise and, without recognition, say, "Order, order! I rise to call for the orders of the day."
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: The member says, "Mr./Madam President, I call for the orders of the day."

q: If the meeting has wandered so far from the agenda that important items may not be reached, you should rise and, without the floor, say, "Mr. or Madam President, I call for the orders of the day."
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: That is the proper use of this motion.

q: Raising a Question of Privilege is a device that can allow action that otherwise wouldn't be in order.
exp: It lets urgent matters affecting rights or comfort be dealt with right away.

q: When business is pending, a member raising a question of privilege needs the chair's permission to state it.
exp: The chair directs the member to state the question, then decides whether to entertain it.

q: Raise a Question of Privilege outranks the motion to Recess.
exp: It ranks just below Recess.

q: A member who has been assigned the floor may be interrupted for a question of privilege.
exp: The matter must be urgent, and ideally the member hasn't started speaking.

q: Raising a question of privilege needs a second and can be debated and amended.
exp: The request itself needs no second and isn't debatable or amendable.

q: The parliamentarian makes the first ruling on a question of privilege.
exp: The chair makes the ruling.

q: A member who rises without getting the floor and says, "I rise to a question of privilege affecting the assembly," may then ask that windows be opened for better ventilation.
exp: Room comfort is a question of privilege affecting the assembly.

q: Rumors attacking a member's character are not grounds for a question of privilege affecting the assembly.
exp: That is a question of personal privilege.

q: As chair, if a member rises without recognition and says, "I rise to a question of personal privilege," you should ask for a second.
exp: The chair asks the member to state the question, then decides whether to entertain it.

q: As chair, you should rule out of order a motion that was offered as a question of privilege and seconded.
exp: If admitted, the motion is handled with debate and a vote.

q: If construction next door makes the hall too noisy, you should rise and, without getting the floor, say, "Mr. President, I rise to a question of privilege affecting the assembly."
exp: Noise affecting the assembly is a question of privilege.

q: During debate on an urgent and controversial main motion, a member rises to a question of privilege and moves "that the meeting be closed and non-members be asked to leave." The chair should take an immediate vote on it.
exp: If the chair admits it, the motion needs a second and is open to debate.

q: A recess is a short break that ends the meeting for the day.
exp: After a recess, the meeting resumes exactly where it left off.

q: A recess may be taken only for informal discussion.
exp: A recess can also be taken to count ballots or get information.

q: A motion to recess made while another motion is pending is a main motion.
exp: It is a privileged motion.

q: A motion to Recess asks that the break start whenever the maker of the pending motion agrees.
exp: It calls for a recess to begin immediately.

q: A motion to recess made when no business is pending is privileged.
exp: When no business is pending, it is a main motion.

q: Recess is privileged only when it is moved while another question is pending.
exp: Otherwise it is a main motion.

q: During a regular meeting, a member moves that "the assembly recess for dinner after the vote on the pending motion." As chair, you should take a voice vote on it without a second.
exp: It is a main motion, so it is out of order while another motion is pending.

q: A motion to recess at a future time may be made only while another question is pending.
exp: It is a main motion, made when no question is pending.

q: Recess outranks the motion to refer to a committee.
exp: Privileged motions outrank subsidiary motions.

q: The privileged motion to Recess cannot be amended.
exp: It can be amended as to the length of the recess.

q: An amendment to a privileged motion to Recess is debatable.
exp: The amendment is undebatable.

q: If an adopted agenda schedules a recess, the chair declares it when the time arrives.
exp: No motion is needed for a scheduled recess.

q: If the chair forgets to announce a scheduled recess, a member should call for the orders of the day.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: The call enforces the agenda.

q: A scheduled recess can be postponed by two-thirds of the people in the room.
exp: It takes a two-thirds vote of the assembly (those voting), not of everyone present.

q: If a motion is being debated and you want to talk privately with a few members about it, you could get the floor and say, "I move to recess for ten minutes."
exp: A short recess allows informal discussion.

q: The gavel shouldn't be tapped to signal that a recess has been adopted.
exp: The gavel may be used to mark a recess, an adjournment, or to restore order.

q: Getting the floor and saying "I move to adjourn" is an example of the privileged motion to Adjourn.
exp: The unqualified form is privileged.

q: The privileged motion to Adjourn is unqualified, closes the meeting at once, and is made when no adjournment time has been set.
exp: These are the conditions for Adjourn to be privileged.

q: A motion to adjourn is always privileged when a time to adjourn has already been set.
exp: It is privileged when unqualified and no adjournment time has been set.

q: "I move to adjourn," made when no question is pending, is debatable.
exp: The privileged motion to Adjourn is undebatable.

q: A qualified motion to adjourn is classified as privileged.
exp: Qualifying it makes it a main motion.

q: A motion to adjourn at or to a future time is out of order while business is pending.
exp: That kind of motion is a main motion.

q: An unqualified motion "to adjourn" is always privileged.
exp: The key says yes; RONR treats it as a main motion in a few cases, such as when adjourning would dissolve the assembly.

q: Adjourn outranks every motion except Recess.
exp: Adjourn outranks everything except Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn.

q: A motion to Adjourn is out of order while the assembly is voting.
exp: Voting must be completed first.

q: When the privileged motion to Adjourn is pending, a motion to Recess is in order.
exp: Only Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn outranks Adjourn.

q: The privileged motion to Adjourn doesn't need a second.
exp: It requires a second.

q: The privileged motion to Adjourn passes by a majority vote.
exp: A majority is required.

q: If a motion to Adjourn fails, anyone who voted yes may move to reconsider the vote.
exp: A vote on Adjourn can't be reconsidered.

q: If a monthly meeting adjourns while a question is pending, the pending motion is lost.
exp: It comes up first under unfinished business at the next meeting.

q: "Adjourn sine die," which closes and dissolves an assembly's session, means "adjourn for one day."
exp: It means "adjourn without day."

q: When a committee of the whole finishes its work, it "rises" and reports, which is its version of adjourning.
exp: The motion to rise works like adjourning for the committee.

q: While a motion to Adjourn is pending, the assembly may be told about business needing immediate attention.
exp: Urgent announcements can be made before the vote.

q: A main motion is out of order while a motion to Adjourn is pending.
exp: Only higher-ranking or certain incidental actions are allowed.

q: While the motion to Adjourn is pending, members may give notice of a motion for the next meeting.
exp: Giving previous notice is permitted then.

q: A meeting is adjourned as soon as the chair takes the negative vote on the motion to Adjourn.
exp: The meeting isn't adjourned until the chair declares it adjourned.

q: If a motion to adjourn is clearly meant to obstruct, the chair should put it to the assembly for debate.
exp: The chair should refuse to entertain dilatory motions.

q: As chair, if a member calls out "I move to adjourn" without the floor, you may handle it by unanimous consent.
exp: Adjournment may be done by general consent.

q: At a convention, when the scheduled adjournment time arrives, the chair should ask a member to move to adjourn.
exp: The chair announces the time has come and declares the meeting adjourned.

q: No motion to adjourn is needed if the chair adjourns the meeting after asking whether there is further business.
exp: The chair can adjourn when no further business is offered.

q: When there seems to be no further business, the chair of an ordinary society only needs to say, "The meeting is adjourned."
exp: The chair should first ask, "Is there any further business?"

q: "I move to adjourn," "I move that we now adjourn to meet at 6 p.m. on May 5," and "I move that the meeting adjourn" are all correct ways to make the main motion to adjourn.
exp: Only the version setting a time to meet again is a main motion; the plain forms are privileged.

q: It's 11 p.m., and debate drags on over the last minor agenda item. To end the meeting, you should rise and, without getting the floor, say, "I move to adjourn."
exp: You must obtain the floor first.

q: With a seconded motion to adjourn and no other business, the chair may say, "If there is no objection, the meeting will now adjourn. [pause] Since there is no objection, the meeting is adjourned."
exp: This adjourns by unanimous consent; a gavel tap is optional.

q: The purpose of Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is to set up a special meeting.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It sets up an adjourned meeting.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn sets the time, and sometimes the place, of another meeting to continue the current one's business.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: That creates an adjourned meeting.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn changes when the current meeting will end.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It doesn't affect when the current meeting adjourns.

q: Depending on the situation, Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn may be a privileged motion or a main motion.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: Its classification depends on circumstances.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is privileged only when made with no question pending.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It is privileged when made while a question is pending, in an assembly with no other meeting set for the same or next day.

q: If Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is moved with no question pending, the chair should rule it out of order.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It is then a main motion and follows main-motion rules.

q: Moved when no question is pending, Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is debatable.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: As a main motion, it is debatable.

q: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn yields to a Point of Order.
exp: A Point of Order arising from it must be dealt with first.

q: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is debatable.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: The privileged form is undebatable.

q: The privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn can be amended only as to the date.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It can be amended as to date, hour, and place.

q: As chair, if an amendment to the privileged motion to Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is seconded, your next step is to vote on the amendment.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: The amendment is undebatable, so you go straight to the vote.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn outranks every motion and needs a two-thirds vote.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It outranks every motion but needs only a majority.

q: Adopting "I move that when this meeting adjourns, it adjourn to meet at 9 a.m. next Wednesday" creates an adjourned meeting.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: This is the standard form.

q: Adopting Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn adjourns the current meeting.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It sets up a continuation; the current meeting goes on.

q: At an adjourned meeting, business picks up where the last meeting left off, except that the minutes are read first.
exp: Minutes come first, then business resumes.

q: Fixing the time to which to adjourn is not the same as fixing the time at which to adjourn.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: One sets the next meeting; the other sets when this one ends.

q: During late-night debate on a main motion, to make sure the assembly meets again tomorrow to finish, you would get the floor and say, "I move that when this meeting adjourns, it adjourn to meet again at 9:00 a.m. tomorrow."
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: This sets an adjourned meeting.

q: A Parliamentary Inquiry is the way to require the chair to enforce a rule that was broken.
exp: A Point of Order does that.

q: A Point of Order yields to all privileged motions.
exp: Privileged motions outrank it unless it arises from them.

q: If a Point of Order is raised while an amendment is immediately pending, the amendment is settled first, then the point of order.
exp: The Point of Order is decided first.

q: A Point of Order may never interrupt someone debating a main motion.
exp: It may interrupt a speaker when necessary.

q: After a Point of Order is raised, the chair should always try to rule on it.
exp: The chair rules first, and may refer it to the assembly if in doubt.

q: The parliamentarian normally rules on points of order.
exp: The chair rules; the parliamentarian only advises.

q: Every Point of Order is put to a vote.
exp: It's voted on only if the chair refers it to the assembly or the ruling is appealed.

q: The usual reason for a Point of Order is to get information from the parliamentarian.
exp: A Point of Order is raised over a breach of the rules.

q: Members shouldn't raise points of order over trivial technical irregularities.
exp: Minor technicalities that harm no one are best ignored.

q: A Point of Order must be made right after the member who broke the rule sits down.
exp: It must be made at the time the breach happens.

q: A Point of Order is proper if the chair opens debate on a main motion that hasn't been seconded.
exp: Raised before debate begins, it corrects the error.

q: If a motion was never seconded but was debated and adopted, it's too late for a point of order about the second.
exp: Once debate has begun, the lack of a second doesn't matter.

q: A member who isn't sure whether a speaker has broken a rule may make a Parliamentary Inquiry.
exp: An inquiry asks the chair about procedure without making a charge.

q: A member is debating the main motion while an amendment is the immediately pending question. To stop them, you would rise and, without the floor, say, "I rise to a point of order."
exp: Debate must be germane to the immediately pending question.

q: As chair, after a member raises a Point of Order, you should immediately ask for a second.
exp: Ask the member to "state your point"; no second is needed.

q: When a member says, "I rise to a point of order," the person speaking should sit down at once.
exp: The speaker yields while the point is decided.

q: A member who raises and states a point of order should stay standing while the chair rules.
exp: The key says the member should be seated.

q: After hearing a point of order, the chair just says the member is "right" or "wrong."
exp: The chair rules that the point "is (or is not) well taken" and gives the reason.

q: A chair who is unsure how to rule on a point of order should consult the vice-president.
exp: The chair may consult the parliamentarian.

q: As chair, if you're unsure how to rule on a Point of Order, you may put it to a vote of the assembly.
exp: The chair may refer doubtful points to the assembly.

q: When a debatable point of order is put to the assembly, no one may speak more than once except the member who raised it.
exp: Only the chair may speak twice, first and last.

q: An Appeal is just a Point of Order stated another way.
exp: An Appeal challenges the chair's ruling.

q: An Appeal is used to get an accurate rising vote on a main motion.
exp: An Appeal puts the chair's ruling to a vote of the assembly.

q: An Appeal yields to all privileged motions.
exp: Privileged motions outrank it.

q: A ruling of the chair can be appealed at any time.
exp: The appeal must be made right when the ruling is made.

q: As chair, you make a ruling, several members then debate the pending motion, and then someone appeals your earlier ruling. You should rule the appeal too late.
exp: An appeal must be made immediately.

q: An Appeal may interrupt a speaker and needs no second.
exp: An Appeal must be seconded.

q: An Appeal is debatable unless the immediately pending question is undebatable, or the appeal concerns indecorum, the rules of speaking, or the priority of business.
exp: These exceptions make it undebatable.

q: The presiding officer must leave the chair to debate an Appeal.
exp: The chair may debate an Appeal without leaving the chair.

q: In debate on an Appeal, members may speak once each, and the presiding officer may speak three times.
exp: The chair may speak twice, first and last.

q: A tie vote on an Appeal reverses the chair's decision.
exp: A tie sustains the chair.

q: A member who disagrees with the chair's ruling on a Point of Order should appeal the decision.
exp: An Appeal lets the assembly decide.

q: You can't appeal the chair's answer to a parliamentary inquiry or request for information, or the chair's announcement of a vote result.
exp: These are opinions or announcements, not rulings.

q: As chair, if a member appeals your announcement of a vote result, you should retake the voice vote.
exp: Suggest that the member call for a Division instead.

q: If you disagree with the chair's ruling on your Point of Order, rise and, without getting the floor, say, "I appeal from the decision of the chair."
exp: That is the correct form.

q: When putting an Appeal to a vote, the chair should say, "All those in favor of my decision, say aye."
exp: The chair says, "Those in favor of sustaining the chair's decision, say aye."

q: When a member wants to do something that would break one or more of the assembly's regular rules, the assembly can adopt a motion to Suspend the Rules.
exp: That is the purpose of the motion.

q: Local, state, or national laws can be suspended.
exp: Laws, basic principles of parliamentary law, and rules protecting absentees can't be suspended.

q: Suspend the Rules doesn't need a second.
exp: It must be seconded.

q: Suspend the Rules usually takes a two-thirds vote.
exp: Most rules of order need two-thirds to suspend.

q: Suspend the Rules is meant to set aside one or more rules in the parliamentary authority, special rules of order, or standing rules.
exp: These kinds of rules can be suspended.

q: A motion to Suspend the Rules must say what it is for.
exp: It states its specific purpose.

q: Without unanimous consent, members may try up to twice more to suspend a rule after a failed vote at the same meeting.
exp: A failed suspension for the same purpose generally can't be renewed at that meeting without unanimous consent.

q: Rules that generally can't be suspended include those protecting absentees, those protecting basic rights of individual members, and those in the bylaws.
exp: These are beyond suspension.

q: By unanimous consent, members can skip the required previous notice of a bylaw amendment.
exp: Notice protects absentees, so it can't be suspended.

q: Rules found in an adopted parliamentary manual can be suspended by a majority vote.
exp: Suspending rules of order takes two-thirds.

q: Suspend the Rules can be used to set aside the regular order of business and jump to an item scheduled later in the meeting.
exp: Taking business out of order is a typical use.

q: A society's adopted order of business can't be suspended by a majority vote.
exp: Departing from it takes two-thirds or unanimous consent.

q: A local standing rule setting the meeting's start time can be suspended by a majority vote.
exp: Ordinary standing rules can be suspended by majority.

q: Suspending a standing rule without notice takes two-thirds.
exp: A majority is enough.

q: If a very undesirable original main motion is made, you should move to Dispense with the Question.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: The tool is Objection to the Consideration of a Question.

q: Objection to the Consideration of a Question must be raised before debate starts and before any subsidiary motion is stated.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: It is timely only at the start.

q: Objection to the Consideration of a Question can be applied to any motion.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: It applies only to original main motions and to communications not from a superior body.

q: Sustaining an Objection to the Consideration of a Question takes a two-thirds vote.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: Two-thirds must vote against considering the question.

q: The chair may raise an Objection to the Consideration of a Question.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: The chair may put the question of consideration on the chair's own initiative.

q: A member who rises without recognition and says, "I object to the consideration of the motion," is objecting that a motion was already considered and adopted.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: The objection aims to keep the pending motion from being considered at all.

q: If an objection to considering a main motion is sustained, the motion is dropped for that session.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: It can't be renewed in that session without a change in circumstances.

q: Once an undesirable main motion has been moved and seconded, you can keep it from coming before the assembly by getting the floor and saying, "I move that this motion be tabled."
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: Say instead, "I object to the consideration of the question."

q: When an objection to consideration is raised, the chair should say, "An objection has been raised. Is there any discussion?"
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: The chair asks, "The consideration of the question is objected to. Shall the question be considered?"

q: Division of a Question is used to get a rising vote on the pending motion.
exp: It separates a motion into distinct parts for debate and voting.

q: Adopting a Division of a Question splits the pending motion into separate parts to act on.
exp: Each part is then considered separately.

q: To split "I move that we buy our president a new lectern and a new gavel" into two motions, you would use Division of the Business.
exp: The motion is Division of a Question.

q: A Division of a Question on the main motion can't be made while an amendment to it is pending.
exp: The key treats it as out of order then.

q: A motion to divide a question must be seconded and isn't debatable.
exp: It is undebatable but amendable.

q: Amendments can never be divided.
exp: Dividing an amendment is allowed.

q: A member moves "to collect $10 from each member and give the money to the local high school." Someone moves to split it into "collect $10 from each member" and "give the money to the local high school." As chair, you should rule that out of order because the second part can't stand alone.
exp: Each part of a division must be able to stand as its own motion.

q: "I move we form a recreation committee and give it instructions" is a good candidate for division.
exp: The instructions can't stand alone without the committee.

q: If a member objects to part of a main motion that can't be divided, the member can move to strike that part out.
exp: An amendment to strike out is the alternative.

q: When one motion bundles several main motions on different subjects, a single member can demand that each be considered separately.
exp: Unrelated subjects must be separated if one member asks.

q: A motion proposes "that we send our president and all the other officers to Hawaii." To handle the president and the other officers separately, get the floor and say, "I move to divide the motion so as to consider separately 'sending our president to Hawaii' and 'sending all the other officers to Hawaii.'"
exp: This is the correct form for dividing.

q: The motion to open a long, multi-paragraph motion to debate one part at a time, without dividing it, is called Consideration by Paragraph or Series.
exp: It is called Consideration by Paragraph or Seriatim.

q: Consideration by Paragraph or Seriatim needs a two-thirds vote.
exp: A majority adopts it.

q: When a document is considered paragraph by paragraph, members can't debate each paragraph.
exp: Each paragraph can be debated and amended.

q: If the chair proposes going paragraph by paragraph and you'd rather save time by acting on the whole document, you would get the floor and say, "I move that it be considered as a whole."
exp: That motion keeps the document together.

q: A complicated multi-paragraph resolution is pending, and you'd like each paragraph handled separately. You should say "Division!" from your seat without getting the floor.
exp: Get the floor and say, "I move that the resolution be considered seriatim."

q: A single member can demand a Division of the Assembly.
exp: No vote is needed to order it.

q: At a seventy-member meeting, calling for a Division of the Assembly means retaking the vote by show of hands.
exp: The vote is retaken by rising.

q: A Division of the Assembly may be called from the time a voice vote is taken until the chair states the question on another motion.
exp: That is the window for demanding one.

q: A Division of the Assembly may be called without getting the floor, even when another member has the floor, right after a vote is announced.
exp: It doesn't require recognition.

q: A call for a Division of the Assembly needs no second.
exp: One member's demand is enough.

q: When a Division of the Assembly is demanded, the chair takes the "no" vote first.
exp: The affirmative is always taken first.

q: A Division of the Assembly is debatable if the vote will be counted and recorded in the minutes.
exp: It is never debatable.

q: If the voice vote was clearly one-sided, the chair may refuse a Division as dilatory.
exp: Demanding a division on an obvious result can be ruled dilatory.

q: After a close voice vote on an amendment, you would call out "Recount!" from your seat to force a rising vote.
exp: Say "Division!" or "I doubt the result of the vote."

q: Proper alternatives to a voice vote include ballot, roll call, and a rising vote.
exp: These are recognized voting methods.

q: A motion for a roll-call vote does not outrank the motion being voted on.
section: Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
exp: It outranks the motion it applies to.

q: Incidental motions about voting methods are undebatable.
section: Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
exp: They are undebatable.

q: Motions about voting methods and the polls can be applied only to amendments.
section: Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
exp: They apply to any motion being voted on.

q: Every incidental motion about voting methods needs only a majority.
section: Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
exp: Closing the polls needs two-thirds.

q: When different voting methods are proposed, they are handled like filling blanks, and the quickest method is voted on first.
section: Motions Relating to Methods of Voting and the Polls
exp: The most time-consuming method is voted on first.

q: Motions relating to nominations include how nominations are made and motions to close or reopen them.
exp: These are the nomination motions.

q: Incidental motions about nominations are never seconded.
exp: They require a second.

q: Incidental motions about nominations can be neither debated nor amended.
exp: They are undebatable but amendable.

q: Every incidental motion about nominations needs two-thirds.
exp: Most need a majority; closing nominations needs two-thirds.

q: When nomination methods such as floor, committee, ballot, or chair are proposed, they are treated as filling blanks, and nomination by the chair is voted on first.
exp: That follows the key's order for filling blanks.

q: The chair usually declares nominations closed.
exp: A motion to close is rarely needed.

q: Postpone Indefinitely can't be applied to a request to be excused from a duty.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: The key treats it as not applicable.

q: A request to be excused from a duty yields to every privileged motion.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: Privileged motions outrank it.

q: A request to be excused from a duty can be amended.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: The key says false, but the source explanation says it is amendable.

q: A request to be excused from a duty should never be handled by unanimous consent.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: It is often granted by unanimous consent.

q: An officer who can't serve should submit a written resignation, which the chair then puts to a vote.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: A resignation is accepted by the assembly.

q: The chair alone can excuse a member from a duty the bylaws require.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: It takes unanimous consent or a motion, if the bylaws allow it.

q: An officer who can't serve should resign by submitting a written resignation to the secretary or to whoever made the appointment.
section: Request to Be Excused from a Duty
exp: That is the proper procedure.

q: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, an assembly can fill an officer's vacancy right after the resignation.
exp: Notice is required before the vacancy is filled.

q: Parliamentary Inquiry, Request for Information, and Withdraw a Motion are ways to get information or permission from the assembly.
exp: These are requests and inquiries.

q: Call for the Orders of the Day is a kind of request or inquiry.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It is a privileged motion.

q: A Parliamentary Inquiry or Request for Information needs a second.
exp: Neither is seconded.

q: Requests for Information and Parliamentary Inquiries can't be debated or amended.
exp: They are simple requests.

q: A "Parliamentary Information Opinion" is used to ask the chair's opinion on a procedure question about pending business.
exp: That is a Parliamentary Inquiry.

q: The chair must answer any parliamentary inquiry except a hypothetical one.
exp: Hypothetical questions need not be answered.

q: If the Previous Question is pending and you aren't sure whether it can be amended, you could rise and, without getting the floor, say, "Madam President, I rise to a parliamentary inquiry."
exp: An inquiry asks the chair about procedure.

q: You can't appeal the chair's answer to a parliamentary inquiry because the assembly always votes on it.
exp: It can't be appealed because it is an opinion, not a ruling.

q: A Request for Information goes through the secretary.
exp: It goes to or through the chair.

q: A Request for Information asks the chair, or another member through the chair, about parliamentary procedure.
exp: It asks about facts of the business, not procedure.

q: If a main motion is pending and you have a question for its maker, rise and, without getting the floor, say, "Mr. Chair, I rise to a request for information."
exp: Questions go through the chair.

q: When a member makes a request for information of a speaker, the chair asks whether the speaker will yield, since the time comes out of the speaker's allotment.
exp: Answering uses the speaker's time.

q: Before the chair states a motion, its maker may withdraw it without anyone's consent.
exp: Until it is stated, the motion belongs to the maker.

q: You moved "to have a dance next Saturday." After it's seconded but before the chair states it, you realize the club picnic is that day. You could rise and, without getting the floor, say, "Mr. President, I withdraw the motion."
exp: A motion not yet stated can be withdrawn freely.

q: A change another member suggests before the chair states the motion must be approved by the assembly.
exp: Only the maker needs to accept it.

q: If the seconder withdraws the second after the maker accepts a change, no new second is needed because the member who suggested the change effectively seconds it.
exp: The suggester's support serves as a second.

q: Withdrawing a motion after the chair has stated it requires the assembly's permission.
exp: Once stated, it belongs to the assembly.

q: Once the chair states a motion, it belongs to the assembly, so anyone may withdraw it without a vote.
exp: Only the maker may ask, and the assembly must consent.

q: Permission to withdraw a motion may be requested any time before voting on it starts.
exp: Even after an amendment, withdrawal can be asked before the vote.

q: If a main motion, Postpone Indefinitely, Limit Debate, and a request to Withdraw are all pending, the request to Withdraw is the immediately pending question.
exp: The request to withdraw is taken up first.

q: A withdrawn motion can't be made again at the same meeting.
exp: It can be renewed, since it was never voted on.

q: As chair, if the maker "accepts" an amendment someone offers to a pending motion, you ask for a second and then declare the amendment adopted.
exp: Once a motion is stated, the amendment must be decided by the assembly, by vote or unanimous consent.

q: If a member wants to read from a book during debate and someone objects, as chair you should put the question of granting permission.
exp: The assembly decides by vote.

q: Take from the Table is used to bring back a motion that was postponed.
exp: It brings back a motion that was laid on the table.

q: Take from the Table brings a question back before the assembly.
exp: The question becomes pending again.

q: Take from the Table can be moved while another motion is pending.
exp: It is in order only when no question is pending.

q: Take from the Table can be moved under unfinished or new business, and in the same session the question was tabled.
exp: It is also in order at the next session in some cases.

q: Take from the Table is in order at any time.
exp: Some business must have happened since the question was tabled.

q: Take from the Table must be seconded.
exp: It requires a second.

q: Take from the Table requires a two-thirds vote and previous notice.
exp: A majority is enough.

q: A question taken from the table can't be laid on the table again.
exp: It can be tabled again when there's a new reason.

q: A main motion tabled by a group that meets only once a year can't be taken from the table at the next annual meeting.
exp: It dies at the end of the session.

q: Once the urgent matter that caused a question to be tabled is settled, the question may be taken from the table right away.
exp: Settling the interrupting business counts as intervening business.

q: If no one moves to Take from the Table within the time limit, the tabled motion automatically moves to "Unfinished Business."
exp: A question left on the table past the limit dies.

q: When a tabled question is taken up on a different day, each member may debate it only once more.
exp: On a new day, each member may speak twice again.

q: If you tabled a motion "to have a car wash next Saturday" early in a regular meeting, you could bring it back later that meeting by getting the floor and saying, "I move to take from the table the motion about the car wash."
exp: Taking it from the table is in order later in the same meeting.

q: Rescind is a subsidiary motion.
exp: It is an incidental main motion.

q: Amend Something Previously Adopted is an incidental main motion.
exp: It is one of the motions that bring a question again before the assembly.

q: Annul, Repeal, and Rescind can all cancel an earlier action.
exp: These are different names for the same motion.

q: To change part of an adopted text, or to replace it with a different version, you use Amend Something Previously Adopted.
exp: Rescind cancels; this motion modifies.

q: Rescind can be applied to an adopted secondary amendment.
exp: Rescind normally applies to adopted main motions.

q: Rescind and Amend Something Previously Adopted are debatable, but debate can't go into the merits of the original action.
exp: Debate may cover the merits of the original question.

q: Rescind may be moved only when no other motion is pending, and it applies to most adopted main motions.
exp: It is a main motion.

q: Rescind needs a second and is debatable and amendable.
exp: It follows main-motion rules.

q: Rescind passes by a majority of the people present.
exp: It takes two-thirds of those voting, a majority with previous notice, or a majority of the entire membership.

q: Both Reconsider and Rescind must be moved by someone who voted on the prevailing side.
exp: Only Reconsider has that limit; anyone may move to Rescind.

q: To cancel a motion adopted at last month's meeting, you would get the floor and say, "I move to rescind the motion about ... adopted at last month's meeting."
exp: This is the proper form.

q: Rescind and Expunge from the Minutes needs two-thirds of the entire membership.
section: Rescind and Expunge from the Minutes
exp: It needs a majority of the entire membership.

q: To show strong disapproval, an assembly may Rescind and Expunge from the Minutes. If it's adopted, the secretary draws a single line through the words, writes "Rescinded and Ordered Expunged" with the date and a signature, and leaves the material out of any published minutes.
section: Rescind and Expunge from the Minutes
exp: The original words stay legible but are marked.

q: Discharge a Committee is used to formally dismiss a committee after its final report.
exp: It takes a matter away from a committee before it reports.

q: Discharge a Committee needs a second, outranks nothing, and is moved only when no other question is pending.
exp: It is a main motion.

q: Discharge a Committee can be debated.
exp: It is debatable.

q: Discharge a Committee can apply to any referred main motion the committee hasn't yet reported on.
exp: Once the final report is in, the committee is done anyway.

q: Debate on discharging a committee can't touch the merits of the referred question.
exp: The merits may be debated.

q: Discharge a Committee needs a majority of the entire membership, two-thirds of those voting, or a majority with previous notice.
exp: These are its voting thresholds.

q: Discharging a committee is appropriate when it is slow to report, when the assembly wants to act without it, or when the assembly wants to drop the matter.
exp: These are common reasons.

q: A standing committee discharged from a matter stops existing.
exp: A standing committee continues; only that task is removed.

q: A special committee discharged from its matter ceases to exist.
exp: Its only purpose is gone.

q: If your group is unhappy with the Membership Standing Committee's recruiting and wants to take over, you should get the floor and say, "I move that we form a new plan to recruit new members."
exp: Say, "I move that the Membership Committee be discharged from further consideration of recruiting new members."

q: To discharge a special committee, get the floor and say, "I move that the committee to which the motion about ... was referred be discharged."
exp: That is the proper form.

q: Reconsider lets a majority bring back a motion that has already been voted on.
exp: The question is then before the assembly again.

q: The purpose of Reconsider is to withdraw a motion.
exp: It allows correcting hasty, ill-advised, or mistaken action.

q: At a regular society meeting, only someone who voted on the losing side may move to reconsider.
exp: It must be someone who voted on the prevailing side.

q: Reconsider may be moved only by someone who voted "yes" if the motion passed, or "no" if it failed.
exp: That is the prevailing side.

q: In a one-day session, Reconsider may be moved the day after the vote.
exp: It must be moved the same day.

q: Reconsider can't be applied to an affirmative vote on a contract once the other party has been told the result.
exp: The action can no longer be undone.

q: A motion to reconsider may be made after someone else has been given the floor, as long as that person hasn't started speaking.
exp: The time limits make this exception necessary.

q: The seconder of a motion to reconsider must also have voted on the prevailing side.
exp: The seconder may have voted either way.

q: Reconsider is debatable only if members speak in favor of the motion being reconsidered.
exp: It is debatable when the motion to be reconsidered is debatable.

q: Reconsider cannot be amended.
exp: It is not amendable.

q: At a regular meeting, Reconsider needs a two-thirds vote.
exp: A majority is enough.

q: Since debate rights on Reconsider are separate from the original debate, a member may speak to the merits twice more.
exp: Reconsideration starts fresh speaking rights.

q: Calling up a motion to reconsider requires no second.
exp: The motion was already seconded when made.

q: Anyone who spoke on the prevailing side may call up a motion to reconsider that couldn't be taken up when it was made.
exp: The key says the maker usually calls it up.

q: If reconsideration happens on a different day from the original vote, no one may debate it.
exp: Each member may speak twice again.

q: When debating a motion to reconsider an amendment to a pending main motion, members may discuss the amendment's merits.
exp: Debate covers the question being reconsidered.

q: To reconsider a primary amendment after the main motion is decided, only the amendment vote is reconsidered.
exp: The main motion vote must be reconsidered too.

q: In a committee, a vote may be reconsidered at any later time.
exp: Committees have no time limit for reconsideration.

q: In standing and special committees, Reconsider always passes by a majority.
exp: A majority is enough only if everyone on the prevailing side is present or was notified; otherwise it takes two-thirds.

q: You voted for an adopted motion "to have a picnic next Saturday," then remembered a conflict. To bring it back, get the floor and say, "I move to reconsider the vote on the motion about the picnic next Saturday. I voted in favor of it."
exp: The maker states which side they voted on.

q: If the maker of a motion to reconsider doesn't say how they voted, the chair asks the secretary to announce it.
exp: The chair asks the member to state it.

q: If the vote being reconsidered was taken by unanimous consent, and the maker doesn't say which side they were on, the chair should ask whether the member was present.
exp: Anyone present at a unanimous-consent vote counts as prevailing.

q: As chair, once a motion to reconsider a debatable motion is adopted, you put the original motion straight to a vote.
exp: The original motion is reopened for debate.

q: What makes Reconsider and Enter in the Minutes unusual is that it can't be called up on the day it's made.
section: Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes
exp: That delay is its purpose.

q: Unlike regular Reconsider, Reconsider and Enter in the Minutes can't be applied to votes where a one-day delay would defeat the purpose.
section: Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes
exp: It's barred when delay would cause harm.

q: A motion can be renewed in the same session only if a different member makes it.
exp: The question itself must have changed.

q: A main motion can't be renewed after significant progress in business or debate.
exp: Main motions can't be renewed in the same session.

q: Postpone Indefinitely may be renewed on the same main motion in the same session.
exp: It can't be renewed.

q: After the chair rules against a Point of Order, it can't come up again that meeting unless the chair raises it.
exp: It is settled unless an Appeal reverses the ruling.

q: A motion to adjourn may be renewed after meaningful progress in business or debate.
exp: A changed situation allows renewal.

q: Motions meant to obstruct the assembly's will are called disruptive motions.
exp: They are called dilatory motions.

q: Demanding a division on every vote, even when the result is clear, is a dilatory tactic.
exp: The chair may refuse such demands.

q: If a few members shout "Division!" on every voice vote, even unanimous ones, the chair should take a rising vote each time.
exp: The chair should refuse or rule the demands out of order as dilatory.

q: An improper motion is one that conflicts with the society's bylaws, the U.S. Constitution, or state or local law.
exp: Such motions are out of order.

q: A motion adopted in conflict with a previously adopted motion must be carried out.
exp: It is null and void.

q: A motion outside the society's stated purpose may be introduced only with the chair's permission.
exp: It takes a two-thirds vote to consider it.

q: A quorum is the number of voting members who happen to be present.
exp: A quorum is the number who must be present to do business.

q: The number that makes a quorum varies by organization.
exp: Each group sets its own.

q: An organization may set its quorum just before roll call by majority vote of those present.
exp: The quorum is set in the bylaws.

q: In a mass meeting, the quorum is a majority of those who said they would come.
exp: The quorum is whoever is present.

q: For a group with no dues or official membership list, the quorum at a regular meeting is whoever attends.
exp: Those present form the quorum.

q: In a convention with no bylaw provision, the quorum is a majority of the delegates registered as attending.
exp: It's based on registered delegates.

q: If the bylaws don't set a quorum, it is two-thirds of those present.
exp: The default is a majority of all members.

q: A volunteer organization with enrolled members should set a fairly small quorum, below a majority, so it can get work done.
exp: A realistic quorum prevents stalled meetings.

q: If the quorum clause is removed from the bylaws, the quorum becomes a majority of members by default.
exp: That is the default rule.

q: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, the quorum in a committee of the whole is a majority of those at the regular meeting.
exp: It is the same as the assembly's quorum.

q: If no quorum is set for boards and committees, a majority of their members must be present.
exp: Majority is the default.

q: Business conducted without a quorum must still be carried out.
exp: It is null and void.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is in order even without a quorum.
exp: It is one of the few actions allowed.

q: Without a quorum, the only legal action is to set the time to which to adjourn.
exp: The assembly can also recess, adjourn, and take steps to get a quorum.

q: A time for an adjourned meeting may be set even without a quorum.
exp: That action is allowed.

q: At a meeting with no quorum, members may act on an emergency at their own risk and have it ratified later.
exp: Ratification can approve it afterward.

q: Motions to obtain a quorum are main motions that need two-thirds.
exp: They are privileged and pass by majority.

q: The secretary must confirm a quorum before the meeting is called to order.
exp: That is the presiding officer's duty.

q: As chair, without a quorum you would take a vote on a motion to adjourn.
exp: Adjourning is allowed without a quorum.

q: As chair, if you see there is no quorum, you should announce it.
exp: The chair announces the lack of a quorum.

q: If there is no quorum, a member should move that the minutes record the absence of a quorum.
exp: A member should raise a point of order.

q: As chair, if the quorum is lost while someone is speaking, you should rule the speaker out of order and adjourn immediately.
exp: Let the speaker finish first.

q: A member may raise a point of order that a quorum is missing, as long as they don't interrupt a speaker.
exp: It waits until the speaker finishes.

q: A Call of the House is used in legislatures to force an immediate vote on the pending question.
exp: It compels absent members to attend so there is a quorum.

q: Once the roll has been taken under a Call of the House, no member may leave.
exp: Members are held so the quorum is kept.

q: "Agenda," "order of business," and "orders of the day" all concern the order in which business is taken up.
exp: They overlap in meaning.

q: A set sequence for taking up business in a session is called "the business ordered for the day."
exp: It is called an order of business.

q: "Roll Call" is not one of the headings in the standard order of business.
exp: The standard headings don't include roll call.

q: In a regular business meeting, unfinished business comes right before committee reports.
exp: It comes right before new business.

q: As chair, after the minutes are read you ask, "Are there any corrections?" If no one answers, you say, "There being no corrections, the minutes are approved as read."
exp: Minutes are usually approved by unanimous consent.

q: It's usually more efficient to approve and correct minutes through a formal motion.
exp: Unanimous consent is more efficient.

q: Minutes become the official record once the secretary approves them.
exp: The assembly approves them.

q: In most societies, reports from every officer, board, and standing committee are heard only at the annual meeting.
section: Reports of Officers, Boards, and Committees
exp: Full reports are typically annual.

q: Standing committees report in alphabetical order by name.
exp: They report in the order listed in the bylaws.

q: A motion arising from an officer's, board's, or committee's report is taken up under Unfinished Business at the next meeting.
section: Reports of Officers, Boards, and Committees
exp: It is taken up right after the report.

q: A suitable tabled item may be taken from the table, when nothing is pending, under Unfinished Business and General Orders, Reports of Special Committees, or Reports of Officers, Boards, and Standing Committees.
exp: These headings allow it.

q: Special committees report in alphabetical order.
exp: They report in the order they were appointed.

q: When the time for a special order arrives, the chair announces it and the business becomes pending.
exp: The chair announces the special order.

q: General orders are usually taken up under "Unfinished Business and General Orders."
exp: That is their place in the agenda.

q: A monthly club adjourned in January with a motion still pending. At the February meeting, it will be new business.
exp: It will be unfinished business.

q: Questions carried over because the previous meeting adjourned before finishing them are called "incomplete business."
exp: They are called unfinished business.

q: The chair should announce Unfinished Business and General Orders only if the minutes show there is some.
exp: Skip the heading if there's nothing under it.

q: Instead of asking, "Is there any unfinished business?", the chair should state the question on the first item under that heading.
exp: The chair knows the items from the minutes.

q: If a topic came up informally and a member suggested "bringing it up next meeting," the chair should announce that it is laid on the table.
exp: The chair should suggest introducing it as new business.

q: In the standard order of business, new business comes right after approving the minutes.
exp: It comes right after unfinished business and general orders.

q: After the chair asks, "Is there any new business?", members may bring up new items or move to take tabled motions from the table.
exp: Both are in order then.

q: Opening ceremonies include things like announcements and an open forum.
exp: They may include the Pledge of Allegiance.

q: Opening ceremonies, roll call, and announcements are optional parts of an order of business.
exp: An assembly includes them only if its rules or customs call for them.

q: A "consensus calendar" is the tool city councils use to clear large numbers of routine items at once.
exp: The correct term is consent calendar.

q: Under a heading like Good of the Order or Open Forum, members may share informal observations about the organization's work.
exp: This optional heading allows informal remarks without a pending motion.

q: A program, such as a guest speaker, is normally presented after the meeting has adjourned.
exp: A program is usually presented just before adjournment.

q: As chair, if a guest speaker must leave before their scheduled spot, you may ask the members for unanimous consent to let the guest speak early.
exp: Unanimous consent lets business be taken out of its normal order.

q: The chair can move an item out of its scheduled order just by announcing the change.
section: Taking Up Business Out of Order
exp: The assembly must agree, by suspending the rules or by unanimous consent.

q: Taking up an item out of its proper order requires only a majority vote.
section: Taking Up Business Out of Order
exp: It requires a two-thirds vote to suspend the rules, or unanimous consent.

q: A whole class of business cannot be postponed as a group.
exp: Postpone applies to a specific pending question, not to a category of business.

q: A chair departing from the order of business might say, "If there is no objection, the chair proposes we now take up . . ."
exp: This is the standard way to seek unanimous consent.

q: An order of the day can be taken up early by laying the rules on the table with a two-thirds vote.
exp: There is no motion to lay the rules on the table; the assembly suspends the rules by a two-thirds vote.

q: An order of the day is a list in the bylaws of all standing committee duties.
exp: An order of the day is an item of business set in advance for a particular session, day, or time.

q: The two classes of orders of the day are rules of order and calls to order.
exp: The two classes are general orders and special orders.

q: A motion to Adjourn, a motion to Recess, or a question of privilege can still interrupt a special order.
exp: These privileged matters outrank a special order.

q: When its time arrives, a special order can interrupt most pending business.
exp: That power to interrupt is what makes it special.

q: Postponing a main motion indefinitely makes it an order of the day.
exp: Postpone Indefinitely kills the motion; postponing to a certain time makes it an order of the day.

q: Lay on the Table is the motion that schedules a pending question as an order of the day for a later time.
exp: That is the job of Postpone to a Certain Time; Lay on the Table only sets a question aside temporarily for urgent business.

q: A general order set for a specific hour cannot be taken up before that hour unless the rules are suspended by a two-thirds vote.
exp: Taking it up early changes a schedule the assembly already set.

q: Orders of the day without a set hour are taken up under the headings Special Orders and Unfinished Business and General Orders.
exp: They come up in the regular order of business under those headings.

q: Once the hour for a general order arrives, it is taken up only when no other business is pending and no special order or reconsideration interferes.
exp: A general order cannot interrupt pending business.

q: When several general orders are set for the same time, the chair decides which comes first.
exp: They are taken up in the order in which they were made.

q: If an agenda has both postponed items and a special order set for a particular time, the special order set for that time is considered first.
exp: Special orders take priority over general orders and postponed items.

q: A special order automatically interrupts pending business, except a motion to Adjourn, a motion to Recess, or a question of privilege.
exp: Only privileged matters outrank it.

q: A special order was set for 2 p.m., and later another was set for 1 p.m. If the 1 p.m. item is still pending at 2 p.m., the chair interrupts it to take up the 2 p.m. item.
exp: When special orders conflict, the one made first takes precedence.

q: As chair, if a special order is pending when a scheduled recess time arrives, you let the pending business keep going.
exp: The chair announces the recess when its scheduled time arrives.

q: When a whole meeting is made a special order for one subject, that subject is taken up right after announcements.
exp: It is taken up right after the minutes are approved.

q: An adopted agenda can be changed only by a two-thirds vote or by unanimous consent.
exp: Once adopted, the agenda belongs to the assembly.

q: An order of business adopted for one specific session is called a privileged agenda.
exp: It is called an agenda or program.

q: To make a motion or debate, a member rises, addresses the chair, and asks permission to speak.
exp: The member must be recognized by the chair; they do not ask permission.

q: The chair can recognize a member by stating their name or title, naming the unit they represent, or simply nodding if only one person is seeking the floor.
exp: Any of these assigns the floor.

q: As chair, if a member rises while a privileged motion to Adjourn is immediately pending, you let them debate the motion to Adjourn.
exp: A privileged motion to Adjourn is undebatable, so you ask, "For what purpose does the member rise?"

q: A member who has the floor may debate the main motion and then end by making a secondary motion.
exp: For example, they may finish their remarks by moving an amendment.

q: If two members rise at about the same time, the chair recognizes the one who raised a hand.
exp: The chair recognizes whoever first rose and addressed the chair after the floor was yielded.

q: Member A stood before the floor was yielded, and Member B stood and addressed the chair after it was yielded. The chair should recognize Member B.
exp: Rising before the floor is yielded does not count.

q: A member recognized despite not rising first is said to have "precedence in assignment of the floor."
exp: The correct term is preference in recognition.

q: A member gets preference in recognition if they made a committee report and want to move its adoption, moved to take a motion from the table, or made the motion and have not yet spoken.
exp: RONR lists these as cases where a member has a stronger claim to the floor.

q: The chair should alternate between speakers for and against a motion when possible.
exp: This gives both sides a fair hearing.

q: When the pending question is undebatable and unamendable, a member may still get the floor to make a motion that outranks it.
exp: Higher-ranking motions remain in order.

q: After a motion is laid on the table, preference goes to any member who wants to debate why it was tabled.
exp: Lay on the Table is undebatable, so preference goes to the member who raised the urgent business.

q: A member who said in debate they would offer a different motion on the subject if the current one failed gets preference in recognition after it fails.
exp: RONR gives them a stronger claim to the floor.

q: If a referral passes without the committee's size, the member who moved to refer gets preference to fill in the details.
exp: The member who moved to refer gets no special preference here.

q: When the chair is unsure who is entitled to the floor, the officers should confer and decide.
exp: The chair can let the assembly decide by a vote.

q: If the chair gives the floor to the wrong member, the fix is a Request for Information.
exp: A member corrects it by raising a Point of Order.

q: Two members can usually appeal the chair's assignment of the floor, except in a convention.
exp: The original key says the exception is a mass meeting, not a convention.

q: In large conventions, members may be recognized at numbered microphones, in numerical order, or from a list given to the chair.
exp: Large bodies use these methods to manage recognition.

q: A Call for the Orders of the Day can interrupt a member who already has the floor and is speaking.
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: It is one of the motions that may interrupt a speaker.

q: During an interruption, the member who has the floor stays standing.
exp: They sit down but keep the floor while the interruption is handled.

q: A committee member who has the secretary read their report still has the floor when the reading ends.
exp: The reporting member keeps the floor and can move adoption.

q: When someone has the floor, a seated member may not call out "Question!", "I move to adjourn!", or "Table it!"
exp: Members must be recognized before making motions.

q: A majority vote can limit a member's right to speak on any debatable motion.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: Limiting debate takes a two-thirds vote.

q: The chair should not allow debate on a main motion that is not pending.
exp: Debate applies only to a pending question.

q: A motion can be debated as soon as it has been made and seconded.
exp: The chair must also state the question first.

q: As chair, if a member finishes debating a main motion by moving an amendment, you rule the amendment out of order.
exp: You ask for a second and process the amendment.

q: When the chair asks, "Are you ready for the question?", the chair is checking whether debate is finished.
exp: It invites any remaining debate before the vote.

q: "Gaveling through" means the chair calls the vote so fast that members can't get the floor.
exp: This improper practice denies members their right to debate.

q: When a vote is retaken because of a Division, debate cannot resume except by unanimous consent.
exp: Division only verifies the vote.

q: Unless the assembly allows more, a member may speak no longer than 10 minutes each time they have the floor.
exp: This is the default limit on each speech.

q: To speak past the time limit, a member moves to Extend the Limits of the Question.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: The motion is to Extend Limits of Debate.

q: Unused speaking time can be given to another member.
exp: Unused time cannot be transferred.

q: As chair, if a member tries to give their speaking time to someone else, you tell them time cannot be transferred.
exp: Each member's right to speak is personal.

q: If a member yields before using all 10 minutes, the leftover time is saved for their later speeches.
exp: The leftover time is given up.

q: Except on an Appeal, each member may speak three times on the same motion on the same day.
exp: The limit is two speeches per day.

q: On an Appeal, only the member who made the appeal may speak twice.
exp: Only the presiding officer may speak twice on an Appeal.

q: On an Appeal, everyone except the chair may speak only once.
exp: The chair may speak twice.

q: Asking a brief question or making a short suggestion does not count as a speech in debate.
exp: These are not counted against a member's speaking limit.

q: A member who has spoken twice on a main motion may speak only once on an amendment to it.
exp: Each motion has its own limit, so they may speak twice on the amendment.

q: The usual limits of debate can be changed with Limit Debate, Extend Limits of Debate, or the Previous Question.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: These motions change or close debate.

q: Limit Debate needs at least a three-fourths vote to reduce the number of speeches.
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It needs a two-thirds vote.

q: A two-thirds vote on the Previous Question closes debate immediately.
exp: It ends debate and goes straight to a vote.

q: To block all discussion of a subject, a member can raise an Objection to the Consideration of Debate.
section: Objection to the Consideration of a Question
exp: The motion is Objection to the Consideration of a Question.

q: In a committee of the whole, each member gets one extra speech.
exp: There is no limit on how many times members may speak.

q: When a question is considered informally, a member who has spoken twice may speak again the same day.
exp: Informal consideration removes the limit on the number of speeches.

q: Debate must be germane, meaning it must address whether the pending motion should be adopted.
exp: Off-topic remarks are out of order.

q: In debate, members address all their remarks to the chair.
exp: Members do not speak directly to each other.

q: If a member is called a "liar" or accused of "fraud" in debate, the chair should let that member answer back.
exp: The chair should stop it at once and not allow it to happen again.

q: When a member answers a Request for Information, the time comes out of the speaker's debating time.
exp: Time used for questions is charged to the member who has the floor.

q: In debate, members should say "the member who spoke last" instead of using a member's name.
exp: Avoiding names keeps debate impersonal.

q: Members may refer to themselves in the first person during debate.
exp: This is allowed.

q: The member who made a motion may vote against it and also speak against it.
exp: They may vote against it but may not speak against it.

q: When the chair stands to make a ruling, the member speaking stays standing.
exp: The speaking member sits until the chair finishes.

q: During debate, members should not disturb the meeting by whispering, walking across the floor, or similar behavior.
exp: These are basic rules of decorum.

q: To debate a motion, the presiding officer follows members' rules while speaking from the chair.
exp: The presiding officer normally hands the chair to the vice-president first.

q: A presiding officer who leaves the chair to debate a main motion returns once they finish speaking.
exp: They return only after the main motion is disposed of.

q: The presiding officer does not leave the chair to debate an Appeal.
exp: The chair may speak on an Appeal from the chair.

q: Speaking when no question is pending requires the assembly's permission.
exp: Debate otherwise requires a pending question.

q: A motion to Amend is always debatable.
exp: It is debatable only when the motion it amends is debatable.

q: Debate on a motion to Commit is limited to whether to refer, who serves on the committee, and its instructions.
exp: The merits of the main question are not debated.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate, the Previous Question, and Lay on the Table are undebatable.
exp: These motions are decided without debate.

q: The privileged motions to Adjourn, Recess, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn are debatable.
exp: Privileged motions are undebatable.

q: All incidental motions except two are undebatable.
exp: The exceptions are an Appeal (in most cases) and a Request to Be Excused from a Duty.

q: An Appeal is debatable unless it concerns indecorum, the rules of speaking, or the priority of business.
exp: These are the main exceptions.

q: Reconsider is debatable when it is applied to an undebatable motion.
exp: It is debatable only when the motion it applies to is debatable.

q: A "majority" means 51%.
exp: A majority means more than half.

q: An unqualified "majority vote" means more than half of the votes cast, not counting blanks or abstentions.
exp: Blanks and abstentions are ignored.

q: When 20 votes are cast, a majority is 13.
exp: A majority of 20 is 11.

q: With 51 votes cast, a majority requires at least 26 yes votes.
exp: 26 is more than half of 51.

q: At a meeting, 30 members vote and the presiding president does not. A main motion "to hold a dance next Saturday" needs 16 yes votes to pass.
exp: More than half of 30 is 16.

q: A society has 180 members and a quorum of 91, and 120 attend. If all 120 vote, a main motion needs at least 61 votes to pass.
exp: More than half of 120 is 61.

q: A society has 60 members and 40 attend. If 10 abstain on a motion "to hold a picnic next Saturday," 21 yes votes are needed to pass it.
exp: Only 30 vote, so 16 yes votes are needed.

q: In a society of 200 members, a majority of the entire membership is 100.
exp: It is 101.

q: With 21 votes cast and no fractional votes, a majority is 12.
exp: A majority of 21 is 11.

q: With 60 votes cast, a two-thirds vote requires at least 41 yes votes.
