exp: Two-thirds of 60 is 40.

q: At a meeting, 60 members vote and the presiding president does not. The Previous Question needs 40 yes votes to pass.
exp: It needs two-thirds, which is 40 of 60.

q: A vote of 24 to 12 passes a motion that needs a two-thirds vote.
exp: 24 is exactly twice 12.

q: A vote of 25 to 24 passes a motion that needs a two-thirds vote.
exp: It would pass only a motion that needs a majority.

q: An unqualified "two-thirds vote" means at least two-thirds of the votes cast by members entitled to vote.
exp: Blanks and abstentions are ignored.

q: With 33 votes cast and no fractional votes, a two-thirds vote requires at least 23 yes votes.
exp: Two-thirds of 33 is 22.

q: A motion to close, limit, or extend debate needs only a majority vote.
exp: It needs a two-thirds vote.

q: A motion to take away membership or office requires a two-thirds vote.
exp: This protects members' rights.

q: In a large assembly, the chair should use a show of hands to check for a two-thirds vote.
exp: The chair should use a rising vote; a show of hands is for small groups.

q: A society has 180 members and 120 attend. If all vote, the Previous Question needs at least 81 yes votes.
exp: Two-thirds of 120 is 80.

q: A society has 200 members and a quorum of 50. At a meeting with 60 present, 40 members take part in a counted vote. A majority of those voting is 21.
exp: A majority is more than half of the votes cast: more than 20 of 40, so 21.

q: Vote thresholds based on the number of members present are usually unwise because an abstention then has the same effect as a "no" vote.
section: Bases for Determining a Voting Result
exp: When the base is members present, anyone who doesn't vote effectively counts against the motion.

q: If two seats on a twelve-member board are vacant, a majority of the entire board is 7.
exp: With two vacancies the board has 10 members, so a majority of the entire membership is 6.

q: When three or more choices are possible, the largest number of votes received by any one option is called a "plural vote."
exp: The correct term is plurality.

q: As chair, if a main motion ends in a tie and you oppose it, you can simply not vote, and the motion fails.
exp: A tie vote is not a majority, so the motion is lost without the chair voting.

q: A chair who is a member may vote to break a tie, to create a tie, or to cause or prevent a two-thirds result.
exp: The chair may vote whenever the vote would change the outcome.

q: On a main motion that ties 20 to 20, the chair would have to vote yes for the motion to pass.
exp: A tie fails; the chair's yes vote would make it 21 to 20.

q: On a vote of 25 for and 24 against (majority required), the chair's vote could change the result.
exp: By voting no, the chair creates a 25-25 tie and the motion fails.

q: A main motion receives 30 yes and 29 no votes. If the chair then votes no, the motion is still adopted.
exp: The chair's no vote creates a 30-30 tie, so the motion is lost.

q: A rising vote on the Previous Question is 59 yes and 30 no. The chair should abstain so the motion is adopted.
exp: 59 of 89 is short of two-thirds; the chair must vote yes (60 to 30) for it to pass.

q: If the chair's vote creates a tie on an Appeal, the chair's ruling is overturned.
exp: A tie on an Appeal sustains the chair's ruling.

q: The chair may choose not to vote on a motion.
exp: Like any member, the chair can abstain, and usually does except when the vote is by ballot or would change the result.

q: Members who are behind on dues but have not been formally dropped from the rolls lose their right to vote.
exp: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, members in arrears keep their vote until formally dropped or suspended.

q: A member should vote no on a motion that would give them a direct personal financial benefit.
exp: A member should abstain on a question in which they have a direct personal or financial interest.

q: As chair, you should allow a member to vote for themselves in an election for president.
section: Voting on Matters of Personal Interest
exp: Members may vote for themselves in elections; the personal-interest rule does not apply there.

q: Members may not explain their vote while voting, because that would amount to debate.
exp: Explaining one's vote during voting is out of order; it is a form of debate.

q: Members may change their vote, without anyone's permission, until the chair states the next question.
exp: A member may change a vote freely only until the result is announced.

q: A rising vote is typically used to verify an unclear voice vote and to vote on motions needing a two-thirds vote.
exp: Standing makes the result easier to judge in both cases.

q: A show of hands is best suited to large assemblies.
exp: A show of hands works best in small assemblies, such as boards and committees.

q: On a voice vote, the chair always calls for the "no" votes first.
exp: The chair always calls for the affirmative first.

q: If a rising vote used to check a voice vote is still unclear, the chair may order a counted rising vote.
exp: The chair can have the vote counted to settle the result.

q: In a very large assembly, a member who thinks a vote should be counted can call out "I demand a count!" from their seat.
exp: A member may not demand a count; they must move that the vote be counted.

q: In a counted rising vote, the "no" side is counted first.
exp: The affirmative side is always counted first.

q: A ballot vote should be used only when the assembly orders it or the bylaws require it.
exp: Ballot votes are used when ordered or required by the rules.

q: A ballot vote is used when members want each person's vote made public.
exp: A ballot keeps each member's vote secret.

q: Ballots are typically used for electing officers, admitting members, and voting on charges after a disciplinary trial.
exp: These are the common cases where secrecy matters.

q: If the bylaws require a ballot vote, that requirement can be suspended by a two-thirds vote with previous notice.
exp: A bylaw requiring a ballot cannot be suspended at all.

q: In a ballot vote, members announce their vote aloud when their names are called.
exp: That describes a roll call; a ballot is marked on paper (or a secure electronic equivalent).

q: In a ballot vote, tellers typically hand out the ballots, count them, and report the result.
exp: These are the usual duties of tellers.

q: Making sure no member votes more than once is the chair's job.
exp: That is the tellers' responsibility.

q: The chair, if a member, may always vote in a ballot vote along with the other members.
exp: Because ballots are secret, the chair votes like everyone else.

q: After the polls close in a ballot vote, reopening them requires a two-thirds vote.
exp: Reopening the polls takes a majority vote.

q: Blank ballots are ignored when ballots are counted.
exp: Blanks are not votes and are not counted.

q: If a teller finds two filled-out ballots folded together, both are counted as legal votes.
exp: Two filled-out ballots folded together are counted as one illegal vote.

q: If a ballot leaves some offices blank, the offices that are filled in still count as legal votes.
exp: Each filled-in choice counts; the blanks are ignored.

q: Ballot entries that cannot be understood are treated as illegal votes.
exp: Unintelligible votes are recorded as illegal.

q: Illegal votes are counted only to determine the total used to compute the majority.
exp: Illegal votes by legal voters count toward the total but are not credited to anyone.

q: The tellers' names are not part of the tellers' report.
exp: The report lists vote totals; it does not list the tellers' names.

q: The teller who reads the report declares the result of a ballot vote.
exp: Only the chair declares the result.

q: Ordering a recount of a ballot vote requires a two-thirds vote.
exp: A recount is ordered by a majority vote.

q: A roll call vote puts each member's vote on the record.
exp: That is the purpose of a roll call (yeas and nays).

q: In the U.S. Congress, one-third of those present can order a roll call vote.
exp: The Constitution sets the requirement at one-fifth of those present.

q: In a roll call vote, members who support the resolution answer "aye," "yes," or "yea."
exp: These are the accepted affirmative answers.

q: In a roll call vote, members against the resolution may answer "reject," "disapprove," or "oppose."
exp: Members voting against answer "no" or "nay."

q: In a roll call vote, the secretary calls names in alphabetical order, calling the chair's name last.
exp: The chair's name is called last, and only if the chair wishes to vote.

q: A member not ready to vote in a roll call who wants to be called again later answers "abstain."
exp: The member answers "pass" and is called again after the roll.

q: The minutes should record how each member voted in a roll call vote.
exp: Recording each vote is the point of the roll call.

q: In a roll call vote, members may change their vote only with the chair's permission.
exp: Members may change their vote freely until the result is announced.

q: When the bylaws allow it, mail voting is often used to amend bylaws, elect officers, or get a vote of the whole membership.
exp: Mail voting reaches members who cannot attend.

q: Preferential voting is especially useful and fair in an election by mail.
exp: It avoids repeated rounds of mail balloting.

q: A proxy is a form of power of attorney that lets someone vote for an absent member.
exp: Proxy voting is not allowed in ordinary societies unless the bylaws or law require it.

q: Letting another member vote on your behalf is called preferential voting.
exp: That is proxy voting.

q: Technically, a nomination is a proposal to fill a blank.
exp: Nominations work like filling the blank in "that ___ be elected."

q: Making a nomination by phone is acceptable.
exp: Nominations are made in a meeting or by an authorized method, not by phone.

q: Nominations made from the floor are often called "oral nominations."
exp: They are commonly called "open nominations."

q: At a mass meeting, the vice-president usually nominates the chair.
exp: The person who calls the meeting to order usually nominates the chair.

q: A member does not need to be recognized to make a nomination from the floor.
exp: Members may call out nominations without obtaining the floor, though large assemblies may require recognition.

q: When nominating from the floor, the proper form is "I nominate Ms. Smith because..." followed by reasons.
exp: The proper form is simply "I nominate Ms. Smith."

q: In an organized society, the nominating committee should be elected by the organization or its executive board.
exp: The president should not appoint or serve on the nominating committee.

q: The nominating committee should contact every nominee before announcing the nomination.
exp: Nominees should agree to serve first.

q: Each organization decides when its nominating committee reports.
exp: The timing is set by the society's rules or custom.

q: A nominating committee is automatically discharged right after the members vote on the nominees.
exp: It is discharged when its report is formally presented, but revives if a nominee withdraws.

q: After the nominating committee reports and before voting, the chair must call for more nominations from the floor.
exp: Floor nominations are always in order after the committee reports.

q: As chair, after you call for more nominations and nobody responds, you should take a majority vote to close nominations.
exp: With no further nominations, the chair simply declares nominations closed.

q: Closing nominations requires a majority vote.
exp: A motion to close nominations requires a two-thirds vote.

q: Reopening nominations after they have closed requires a majority vote.
exp: A motion to reopen nominations needs only a majority.

q: If no rule sets the voting method for an election, a member may offer an incidental main motion to set it.
exp: The assembly can decide the method by majority vote.

q: Elections of officers should be held at the end of the meeting.
exp: Elections are best held early, so there is time for more ballots if needed.

q: A member elected by ballot as both president and secretary must take the higher office.
exp: If present, the member chooses which office to accept.

q: If more than two candidates run for one office, all stay on the ballot and voting continues until one gets a majority.
exp: No one is dropped unless the rules say so.

q: During repeated balloting for an office, all candidates' names stay on the ballot.
exp: Even the lowest candidate is not dropped unless a rule requires it.

q: If more candidates than open board seats receive a majority, the seats go to those with the most votes.
exp: The candidates with the most votes fill the seats.

q: Election by voice vote (viva voce) is especially suited to mass meetings.
exp: It is quick when secrecy isn't needed.

q: In an election by voice vote, candidates are voted on in random order.
exp: They are voted on in the order nominated.

q: In a voice-vote election with one nominee for president and one for vice-president, the chair may take a vote on each nominee or declare them elected.
exp: With only one nominee and no ballot rule, the chair may declare the nominee elected.

q: In an election by roll call, the secretary records each vote silently.
exp: The secretary records and repeats each answer aloud.

q: If they differ from the parliamentary authority, an office's qualifications, method of election, and term should be stated in the bylaws.
exp: These are bylaw matters.

q: If officers' duties differ from those in the parliamentary authority, the officers themselves decide what they are.
exp: Such duties are set in the bylaws.

q: An officer who has served ten percent of a term is considered to have served a full term.
exp: More than half a term counts as a full term.

q: An officer's term usually starts the January after they are elected.
exp: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, the term begins as soon as the officer is elected.

q: Without a special title, an assembly's presiding officer is usually called the chair or president.
exp: These are the general titles.

q: The presiding officer of a mass meeting is called the moderator.
exp: In a mass meeting the presiding officer is called the chair.

q: The term that means both the presiding officer and the presiding officer's place is "the bench."
exp: That term is "the chair."

q: The chair of a large assembly should be chosen mainly for their ability to preside.
exp: Presiding skill matters most in large bodies.

q: Enforcing the rules of debate and announcing the business in its proper order are duties of the chair.
exp: Both are core duties of the presiding officer.

q: One of the chair's duties is to slow down business.
exp: The chair's duty is to expedite business.

q: At every meeting, the chair should have the bylaws, the parliamentary authority, and a list of committees and their members.
exp: These references help the chair rule correctly.

q: In a large assembly, the chair should stand to call the meeting to order, put a question to vote, and explain a ruling on a point of order.
exp: The chair stands for these key moments.

q: The chair should remain standing while a member is speaking in debate.
exp: The chair sits while a member has the floor.

q: The chair should not hesitate to put the question on a motion electing officers, even if the chair is one of them.
exp: Routine motions involving the chair are still put by the chair.

q: The second vice-president comes before the first vice-president in the order of who presides.
exp: A president-elect, if any, comes before the first vice-president; otherwise the first vice-president presides first.

q: If the chair must leave and no vice-president is available, the chair may, with the assembly's approval, appoint a "chair pre term."
exp: The correct term is chair pro tem (pro tempore).

q: If neither the president nor vice-president is present, the parliamentarian calls the meeting to order.
exp: The secretary calls the meeting to order.

q: If the president and vice-president are absent, a chair pro tem should be elected.
exp: The secretary opens the meeting and the assembly elects a chair pro tem.

q: An elected chair pro tem's service ends when the vice-president or president arrives, or when another chair pro tem is elected.
exp: Any of these ends the temporary office.

q: A good chair should know more parliamentary procedure than any other member but should not be more technical than necessary.
exp: Knowledge plus good judgment makes meetings run smoothly.

q: A president who is an ex officio member of a committee may not vote in its meetings.
exp: An ex officio member has the same rights as other committee members, including voting.

q: A president elected a full term in advance is called the president pro tempore.
exp: That person is the president-elect.

q: After serving a full term as president-elect, a member becomes vice-president.
exp: The president-elect becomes president.

q: The vice-president fills in for an absent president.
exp: This is the vice-president's main duty.

q: Unless it would be confusing, a presiding vice-president is addressed as "Mr. President" or "Madam President."
exp: The presiding officer is addressed by the office being filled.

q: If the president resigns, the third vice-president moves up to first vice-president.
exp: The first vice-president becomes president and the second moves up to first.

q: A society's secretary must be able to serve as recording officer and keeper of the records.
exp: These are the secretary's core duties.

q: Another name for the secretary is the "transcribing secretary."
exp: Other names are clerk, recording secretary, or scribe.

q: When the president is absent, the secretary should not preside for the whole meeting.
exp: The secretary opens the meeting and presides only until a chair pro tem is elected.

q: The secretary should not change the bylaws in order to create an order of business for meetings.
exp: The secretary prepares an order of business for the chair under the existing rules.

q: If the secretary is absent, the vice-president takes over the secretary's duties.
exp: A secretary pro tem is elected.

q: The vice-president normally reads official correspondence.
exp: The recording secretary (or corresponding secretary) reads it.

q: Anyone interested may inspect a society's minutes at a reasonable time and place.
exp: Any member, not any outsider, has that right.

q: In larger societies, the corresponding secretary sends out meeting notices.
exp: Notices are among the corresponding secretary's duties.

q: The officer who keeps an organization's funds is the vice-president.
exp: The treasurer has custody of the funds.

q: A treasurer's specific duties vary with the size and complexity of the organization.
exp: Duties range from simple bookkeeping to managing large accounts.

q: Some organizations have a financial secretary, besides the treasurer, who bills and collects dues and keeps each member's account.
exp: A financial secretary handles member accounts.

q: The librarian writes the narrative history of the society's activities.
exp: The historian writes that account.

q: Members who serve on an executive board may be called directors, trustees, or managers.
exp: These are common titles for board members.

q: The officer who looks after the society's valuable objects (other than library materials) is called the "security master."
exp: That officer is the curator.

q: A sergeant-at-arms is sometimes called a curator.
exp: A sergeant-at-arms is sometimes called a warden or warrant officer.

q: The officer who helps the chair keep order and sometimes serves notice of fines is the "staff sergeant."
exp: That officer is the sergeant-at-arms.

q: At a members-only meeting, the doorkeeper may check credentials as people arrive.
exp: Checking credentials is a doorkeeper's duty.

q: Directors should always be appointed by the president.
exp: Directors should be elected.

q: An honorary office is a title of respect that may be given to members or nonmembers.
exp: It is complimentary and carries no duties.

q: An honorary office or membership must be renewed every year.
exp: It is permanent unless rescinded or limited by the bylaws.

q: Honorary officers and members normally cannot make motions or vote.
exp: Unless they are also regular members, they have no such rights.

q: Honorary presidents and vice-presidents should sit in the front row of the audience.
exp: They are seated on the platform.

q: An executive secretary runs the central office under the direction of the board and executive committee.
exp: The executive secretary is the society's chief staff officer.

q: A national organization's executive director may hire staff and set their salaries without board approval.
exp: Normally only routine day-to-day business may be handled without board approval.

q: The consultant who advises officers, committees, and members on parliamentary procedure is the parliamentarian.
exp: That is the parliamentarian's role.

q: An organization's parliamentarian should be appointed by the vice-president.
exp: The president appoints the parliamentarian.

q: The chair should meet with the parliamentarian before the meeting starts.
exp: Advance preparation heads off problems.

q: During a meeting, the parliamentarian may raise points of order whenever a member breaks a rule.
exp: The parliamentarian only advises the chair and members; they do not raise points of order.

q: At a regular meeting, the parliamentarian should sit somewhere out of sight.
exp: The parliamentarian sits next to the chair.

q: Once the parliamentarian gives an opinion, the chair must follow it.
exp: The chair makes the ruling and may disregard the advice.

q: A parliamentarian who is a member should vote only when the vote is by ballot.
exp: Voting otherwise would undermine the parliamentarian's impartiality.

q: The minutes of a legislative body are sometimes called "the record."
exp: They are often called the journal.

q: In an ordinary society, the minutes record what was done at a meeting.
exp: Minutes record actions, not what was said.

q: Minutes should note whether the previous minutes were read and approved, and should include all main motions and all notices of motions.
exp: These are required contents.

q: The first paragraph of regular meeting minutes should say that the vice-president and treasurer were present.
exp: It should say whether the regular president and secretary were present.

q: A skilled secretary rewords motions when writing the minutes.
exp: Motions are recorded in their exact final wording.

q: A secondary motion that was withdrawn must still be recorded in the minutes.
exp: Withdrawn secondary motions are left out.

q: The last paragraph of the minutes should give the time of adjournment.
exp: The hour of adjournment ends the minutes.

q: For a voice vote, the minutes should record the number of votes on each side.
exp: Vote counts are recorded only when a count is ordered or the vote is by ballot.

q: The minutes should include the name of the member who seconded a motion.
exp: The seconder's name generally is not recorded.

q: Proceedings in committee of the whole are not entered in the minutes.
exp: Only the committee's report to the assembly is recorded.

q: When a question is considered informally, the minutes should include the exact wording of adopted main motions, who made each, and how each was disposed of.
exp: Informal consideration still requires a record of actions.

q: If the assembly orders a committee report "entered in the minutes," the secretary may summarize it in their own words.
exp: The secretary must copy the full report into the minutes.

q: A summary of a guest speaker's remarks should not be included in the minutes.
exp: Minutes may note the speaker's name and topic but not summarize the talk.

q: Only the president should sign the minutes.
exp: The secretary signs; the president may also sign if the assembly wishes.

q: The secretary should always sign the minutes with "Respectfully submitted."
exp: That phrase is outdated and should not be used.

q: In most organizations, the minutes are read and approved early in the next regular meeting, after the call to order and opening ceremonies.
exp: This is the standard order of business.

q: If a motion is referred to a committee, the minutes must include the names of members the chair appoints to it.
exp: Committee appointments are recorded.

q: Minutes of an adjourned meeting of an ordinary society are approved at the next regular or adjourned meeting, whichever comes first.
exp: The next meeting of either kind approves them.

q: Corrections and approval of the minutes are usually handled by unanimous consent.
exp: No formal motion is usually needed.

q: Dispensing with the reading of the minutes (majority vote, no debate) means they never have to be read.
exp: It only postpones the reading to a later time.

q: If draft minutes were sent to members in advance, they are not read aloud unless someone asks.
exp: Members have already seen them.

q: At a five-day convention, each day's minutes are usually approved at the end of that same day.
exp: They are approved at the start of the next day's business.

q: After minutes are approved, the secretary writes "Approved," the date, and their initials.
exp: This marks the official copy.

q: An error found in minutes years after approval is fixed using the motion to Reconsider.
exp: It is corrected with the motion to Amend Something Previously Adopted.

q: A society may correct its minutes whenever a mistake is found.
exp: Corrections are possible at any time, by the proper motion.

q: Minutes intended for publication contain only a list of who spoke for and against each question.
exp: They also include summaries of speeches and committee reports as submitted.

q: Under the standard order of business, officers report whenever the secretary decides.
exp: Officers' reports come right after the minutes.

q: Any member other than the reporting officer may move to carry out an officer's recommendation.
exp: The reporting officer usually does not make the motion.

q: A treasurer's report at a regular meeting requires no action by the assembly.
exp: It is simply received for information.

q: The treasurer's annual report should always be audited.
exp: The annual financial report is referred to auditors.

q: The treasurer's report at a regular meeting must always list the date of every receipt and payment.
exp: At a regular meeting it may be as simple as a statement of the cash balance.

q: In ordinary societies, the financial reports are audited by elected members called "accountants."
exp: An auditing committee or auditors review them.

q: Adopting the auditors' report relieves the treasurer of all responsibility forever.
exp: It relieves the treasurer only for the period covered, except in case of fraud.

q: For a historian's account to become part of the society's official history, the assembly must formally adopt it.
exp: Adoption makes it official.

q: A board authorized by the bylaws to act for the society between meetings is called an "ex officio board."
exp: It is called an executive board.

q: Another name for the executive board is the board of directors.
exp: The titles are used interchangeably.

q: If a society wants an executive board, the bylaws should set the board's size, duties, powers, how members are chosen, and its meetings.
exp: These belong in the bylaws.

q: In organizations that meet monthly or more often, the board is given all the power.
exp: Frequent meetings mean the board is given less power.

q: The membership can override any board action except matters the bylaws place solely under the board's control.
exp: The assembly is superior to the board otherwise.

q: An ex officio board member must be a member of the society.
exp: An ex officio board member may be a nonmember.

q: A state governor serving ex officio on a private hospital's board is counted when determining a quorum.
exp: An ex officio member who is not under the society's authority is not counted for quorum.

q: In ordinary societies with an executive board, the society's president and secretary may hold the same roles on the board.
exp: They usually do.

q: A board generally cannot delegate its authority.
exp: It may not delegate unless the bylaws allow.

q: A board can do business as long as every board member was notified.
exp: It also needs a quorum and a regular or properly called meeting.

q: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, a board's quorum is a majority of its members.
exp: More than half is the default.

q: Approving an emergency action by calling board members one at a time has the same effect as a vote at a board meeting.
exp: Separate approvals are not valid; the action must be ratified at a meeting.

q: One way to let others see board minutes is to grant special permission.
exp: The board or assembly may permit inspection.

q: Society members can be allowed to inspect board minutes by a two-thirds vote, or a majority vote with previous notice.
exp: These are the thresholds to open board minutes.

q: In small boards (about a dozen members or fewer), members may speak three times on each debatable motion.
exp: They may speak as often as they like.

q: In a small board meeting, the chair should still stand when putting motions to a vote.
exp: The chair may stay seated.

q: In a small board of about a dozen members or fewer, the chair may make motions.
exp: Small board rules allow it.

q: When a board's membership changes periodically, unfinished business falls to the ground, and any committees the board appoints are chosen again.
exp: The new board starts fresh.

q: In a small board, the chair must step down from the chair to speak in debate.
exp: The chair may speak without leaving the chair.

q: A committee may be assigned a specific task and may consist of only one person.
exp: A one-person committee is allowed.

q: A key difference between a board and a committee is that a board has more authority to act independently of the assembly.
exp: Committees usually act under close assembly direction.

q: A committee appointed "with power" may add its own members and decide all related future matters on its own.
exp: "With power" lets it take the steps needed to carry out its instructions.

q: A committee with a continuing existence that is named in the bylaws is a "standard committee."
exp: It is a standing committee.

q: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, standing committee members usually serve until successors are chosen, or for the same term as officers.
exp: Their terms track the officers'.

q: If the bylaws list certain standing committees, others can be created only with the president's permission.
exp: Others can be created only by amending the bylaws.

q: A standing committee reports to the president.
exp: It usually reports to the assembly.

q: Special, select, and ad hoc committees are the same thing.
exp: These are three names for one kind of committee.

q: A committee formed for a specific task that ends once it gives its final report is called a special, select, or ad hoc committee.
exp: That is the definition.

q: After its final report, a special committee becomes a standing committee listed in the bylaws.
exp: A special committee ceases to exist after its final report.

q: How members are chosen for a special committee is usually stated in the motion creating it.
exp: The motion sets the method.

q: A committee fills its own vacancies.
exp: Vacancies are filled by the appointing power, usually the chair.

q: A standing committee with broad powers is usually elected by voice vote.
exp: It is usually elected by ballot.

q: In large assemblies, special committees are usually appointed by the secretary.
exp: They are usually appointed by the chair.

q: When the chair names a committee, the last member named is usually the committee chair.
exp: The first person named is the committee chair.

q: Some bylaws say the president "shall appoint all committees."
exp: Many bylaws include this clause.

q: Subcommittees appointed by a standing committee report directly to the assembly.
exp: They report to the committee that appointed them.

q: If the committee chair does not call a meeting, at least three committee members are needed to call one.
exp: Two members can call a meeting.

q: Unless a rule says otherwise, a standing committee's quorum is all of its members.
exp: The quorum is a majority of its members.

q: A brief memo for the committee's own use is enough for the minutes of a large committee.
exp: Brief notes suffice for small committees; large committees keep fuller minutes.

q: In small standing and special committees, the chair should not debate motions.
exp: In small committees the chair may debate.

q: Committees of an organized society normally follow the society's parliamentary authority.
exp: Committees use the same authority, with small-body relaxations.

q: When society members come before a committee to share views on a subject it is studying, the session is called a mass meeting.
exp: It is called a hearing.

q: During a hearing, only committee members may be present while the committee deliberates.
exp: Others leave when the committee deliberates.

q: When a special committee finishes its assigned work, it may adopt a motion to "rise," which adjourns it sine die.
exp: "Rise" ends the special committee's meeting for good.

q: The motion to "rise" is used in standing committees.
exp: It is never used in standing committees.

q: Standing committee members generally serve until they make a report.
exp: They serve until replaced, usually along with new officers.

q: Standing committees are generally required to report at least once a year, at the annual meeting.
exp: An annual report is the usual minimum.

q: A detailed committee report has four parts, with recommendations coming last.
exp: Task, findings, conclusions, then recommendations.

q: If the board chair is also the presiding officer, the board's report may be given by a co-chair, another board member, or the board secretary.
exp: Someone other than the chair presents it.

q: A committee report is usually presented by the committee secretary.
exp: It is usually presented by the committee chair.

q: "Receiving" a committee report means the assembly adopts it once it is read.
exp: Receiving a report just means hearing it.

q: When a committee report ends with recommendations, the reporting member should move to carry them out.
exp: The reporting member makes the motion to implement.

q: A motion made by the reporting member of a multi-member committee needs a second.
exp: A motion from a committee of more than one person needs no second.

q: A motion arising from an officer's, board's, or committee's report is taken up later, under new business.
exp: It is taken up right after the report.

q: If a regular member, not the reporter, moves to carry out a report's recommendations, the motion needs a second.
exp: Only motions from a multi-member committee skip the second.

q: Adopting a committee report means the assembly endorses every word of it.
exp: Adoption makes the whole report the assembly's own.

q: When the assembly approves a committee report, the best wording is "agree to."
exp: The best word is "adopt."

q: Adopting a motion "to accept" a committee report only means the assembly agrees to hear it and vote on it later.
exp: "Accept" means the same as adopt: it endorses the whole report.

q: A board's report is usually signed by every board member.
exp: It is usually signed by the board's president and secretary.

q: A written committee report is usually not addressed or dated and should begin by identifying the committee.
exp: It opens with the committee's name.

q: "The committee has studied... and we have decided..." is not proper wording to open a special committee report.
exp: Reports are written in the third person, without "we."

q: An important written committee report should be signed by the members who agree with it.
exp: Signatures by concurring members add weight.

q: When the committee authorizes its chair to sign a report, "Approved" is written after the chair's signature.
exp: "Chair" is written after the signature.

q: As chair, if no place in the order of business is set for a committee report, a member objects to receiving it, and the reporter still wants to give it, you put the question to the assembly.
exp: The assembly decides whether to receive it.

q: When a standing committee report ends by recommending a resolution, the reporting member moves its adoption.
exp: That puts the resolution before the assembly.

q: If a motion is referred to committee while Postpone Indefinitely is pending, Postpone Indefinitely comes back to the assembly when the committee reports.
exp: Referral drops the pending Postpone Indefinitely; it does not return.

q: When a committee report recommends several amendments, one motion can adopt them all.
exp: They can be adopted together in one motion.

q: When a committee recommends several amendments, the chair reads each one, opens it to debate, and takes a vote on it.
exp: Each amendment is handled in turn unless adopted together.

q: A committee report that only describes work completed is usually voted on.
exp: It is filed; no action is needed.

q: The main committees that organize a convention are Credentials, Standing Rules, and Program.
exp: These three set up the convention.

q: A formal statement from committee members who disagree with the committee report is called a "protesting report."
exp: It is called a minority report.

q: The report adopted by a majority of the committee is called "the majority report."
exp: It is simply the committee's report.

q: Presenting a minority report is a right that cannot be denied without the assembly's permission.
exp: It is a privilege the assembly may grant.

q: If the minority report ends with a proposed resolution, the minority may recommend amending or rejecting it, or another suitable motion.
exp: The minority can recommend alternatives.

q: As chair, if a member objects when you call for a minority report, you should not allow the report.
exp: The chair puts the question to the assembly.

q: A mass meeting is one of the alternate forms of the committee of the whole.
exp: The alternate forms are quasi committee of the whole and informal consideration.

q: In committee of the whole, quasi committee of the whole, and informal consideration, members may speak at most three times on any motion.
exp: Members may speak as often as they can get the floor.

q: Committee of the whole is suited to large assemblies.
exp: It is designed for large bodies.

q: The chair of a committee of the whole is elected.
exp: The chair is appointed by the presiding officer.

q: The president normally chairs the committee of the whole.
exp: The president presides over a quasi committee of the whole; the committee of the whole's chair is appointed.

q: Quasi committee of the whole suits groups of about 50 to 100 members.
exp: It is for medium-sized assemblies.

q: Informal consideration suits small meetings of an ordinary society.
exp: It is the simplest form.

q: In a quasi committee of the whole, the society's president normally presides.
exp: The presiding officer stays in the chair.

q: During informal consideration, members may debate amendments only once.
exp: They may speak as often as they get the floor.

q: Informal consideration lets members debate without being recognized by the chair.
exp: It only removes the limit on the number of speeches.

q: In committee of the whole, the chair is appointed, the body is technically not "the assembly," and it adopts a report to the assembly.
exp: All three are true.

q: To go into committee of the whole, a member says, "I move that we go into committee of the whole to consider the pending question."
exp: That is the proper form.

q: When the assembly votes to go into committee of the whole, the chair generally appoints the vice-president to preside.
exp: The presiding officer appoints someone, often the vice-president.

q: Proceedings in committee of the whole are entered in the assembly's minutes.
exp: They are not; only the report is.

q: For a committee of the whole, the regular minutes should include the motion to refer, the report, and the assembly's action on it.
exp: These are what is recorded.

q: A committee of the whole can adopt amendments on behalf of the assembly.
exp: It can only recommend amendments in its report.

q: An Appeal from the decision of the chair is not allowed in committee of the whole.
exp: Appeals are in order there.

q: In committee of the whole, subcommittees cannot be appointed, and motions to adjourn or recess cannot be made.
exp: The committee must rise instead.

q: A committee of the whole can refer a matter to a special committee.
exp: It cannot refer matters to another committee.

q: Unless the bylaws say otherwise, a committee of the whole sets its own quorum as its first item of business.
exp: Its quorum is the same as the assembly's.

q: If a committee of the whole loses its quorum, it must rise and report that to the assembly.
exp: It cannot continue without a quorum.

q: In quasi committee of the whole, the vice-president presides throughout.
exp: The regular presiding officer stays in the chair.

q: If a member moves "that the resolution be considered in quasi committee of the whole," the chair asks for a second, allows debate, then takes a vote.
exp: It is handled like other motions to commit.

q: In quasi committee of the whole, each member may speak three times on each motion.
exp: There is no limit on the number of speeches.

q: When a question is considered informally, there is no limit on how many times members may speak on main motions and their amendments.
exp: That is the point of informal consideration.

q: Proceedings under informal consideration are recorded in the minutes.
exp: The assembly is still in regular session.

q: Once a question considered informally is disposed of, informal consideration carries over to the next question.
exp: It ends automatically.

q: In parliamentary law, a mass meeting is a meeting of all the clubs in an organization.
exp: It is a meeting of an unorganized group called to act on a specific problem.

q: A mass meeting would not take place within an organized society.
exp: It is for unorganized groups.

q: A mass meeting is called to act only on a specific problem.
exp: Its purpose is limited.

q: Sponsors of a mass meeting may never limit who attends.
exp: They may limit attendance to people who support the meeting's purpose.

q: A mass meeting's chair should know many attendees, understand the meeting's purpose well, and be a skilled presiding officer.
exp: These qualities help the meeting succeed.

q: If uninvited people attend a mass meeting, the chair should welcome them and invite them to take part.
exp: The chair can ask them to leave.

q: At a mass meeting, a member may move to adopt a standard parliamentary authority, which takes a majority vote.
exp: Adopting an authority is a majority decision.

q: At a mass meeting, the officers usually elected are a chair and a vice-president.
exp: The usual officers are a chair and a secretary.

q: Those who attend may change the original purpose of a mass meeting.
exp: The purpose set in the call cannot be changed.

q: A mass meeting's chair and secretary are elected after the meeting is called to order.
exp: They are elected at the start.

q: In a mass meeting's elections, the sponsors' choice should be nominated first for each office.
exp: The sponsors' candidate is nominated first.

q: After a mass meeting elects its chair by voice vote, the chair next holds an election for parliamentarian.
exp: The next step is electing a secretary.

q: After elections at a mass meeting, the president reads the call of the meeting.
exp: The secretary reads the call.

q: At a mass meeting called to oppose a new landfill, a motion "to endorse the landfill site" should be ruled out of order.
exp: Motions contrary to the meeting's purpose are out of order.

q: At a mass meeting, members may usually speak up to thirty minutes at a time.
exp: The usual limit is ten minutes.

q: If resolutions were not drafted before a mass meeting, a committee should be named at the meeting to draft them.
exp: A resolutions committee is appointed.

q: All committees at a mass meeting should be appointed by the attendees.
exp: It is advisable for the chair to appoint them.

q: At a mass meeting with no further meeting scheduled, a motion to adjourn should not be made while business is pending.
exp: Adjourning would end the meeting for good.

q: At a mass meeting with no further meeting scheduled, adopting a motion to adjourn dissolves the assembly.
exp: There is no later meeting to return to.

q: If a mass meeting is organizing a permanent society and needs more meetings, the chair elected at the first meeting is called the "chair tro pem."
exp: The term is chair pro tem.

q: The first business at a meeting to organize a permanent society is electing a permanent chair.
exp: The first business is nominating a chair pro tem.

q: After a resolution to form a society is adopted, the next step is usually a motion for the secretary to draft bylaws.
exp: The next step is a motion for a committee, appointed by the chair, to draft bylaws.

q: A new society's first draft of bylaws is written by the chair pro tem and secretary pro tem.
exp: A committee drafts them.

q: After choosing a bylaws committee, the next step is a motion setting the date, time, and place of the next meeting.
exp: This sets up the second organizational meeting.

q: A committee drafting bylaws for an incorporated society should consult a professional parliamentarian and an attorney.
exp: Expert help avoids legal and procedural problems.

q: The first business at the second organizational meeting is reading and approving the first meeting's minutes.
exp: Minutes come first.

q: If no corporate charter is proposed, the bylaws committee reports at the second organizational meeting right after the call to order.
exp: It reports right after the minutes are approved.

q: Members who sign the permanent membership record of a new society are called "chapter members."
exp: They are called charter members.

q: After adopting bylaws and recessing to enroll members, the next business in forming a society is electing permanent officers.
exp: Elections follow enrollment.

q: When two societies merge, one continues and the other ceases to exist.
exp: That is a merger.

q: When organizations merge or consolidate, the new group must use parts of each old name.
exp: The new organization may take any name.

q: An unincorporated society that wants to end its existence should adopt a motion to disband.
exp: It should adopt a resolution to rescind its bylaws (dissolve).

q: Dissolving an unincorporated society requires the same vote and notice as amending the bylaws.
exp: Dissolution rescinds the bylaws, so the same rules apply.

q: A committee to draft bylaws is normally named at the second organizational meeting.
exp: It is named at the first organizational meeting.

q: A committee to draft proposed bylaws should be large.
exp: Key says a large committee.

q: When writing bylaws, the committee should word each sentence so it cannot be quoted out of context.
exp: Clear, self-contained sentences prevent misreading.

q: If the current bylaws require a three-fourths vote to amend, a full revision needs only two-thirds.
exp: A revision needs the same three-fourths vote.

q: Bylaws that create a new society are adopted by a two-thirds vote.
exp: They are adopted by a majority vote.

q: Bylaw articles are usually numbered with Roman numerals.
exp: Article I, II, III and so on.

q: The first article of an unincorporated society's bylaws lists its members.
exp: Article I gives the society's name.

q: When forming a new unincorporated society, Article II (Object) should be stated in general terms.
exp: A broad object avoids limiting future work.

q: The bylaw article on members usually covers classes of membership, eligibility, fees and dues, and when dues are payable.
exp: These are the usual contents.

q: Bylaws do not include an article listing the names of the current officers.
exp: Bylaws name offices, not the people holding them.

q: In the bylaw article on officers, the president should be listed last.
exp: The president is listed first.

q: Methods of nominating officers belong in the bylaw article on elections.
exp: They belong in the article on officers.

q: Article IV (Officers) should cover how officers are elected, their terms, and how they are nominated.
exp: These belong in the officers article.

q: An officer must serve exactly half a term for it to count as a full term.
exp: More than half a term counts as a full term.

q: Article V (Meetings) should set the regular meeting day and the annual meeting.
exp: These are fixed in the bylaws.

q: Article VI (Executive Board) should state only the board's powers.
exp: It should also give the board's composition and how often it meets.

q: Article VII (Committees) should name all the special committees.
exp: It names the standing committees, how they are chosen, and their makeup and duties.

q: Program, Finance, and Membership committees are typical standing committees listed in bylaws.
exp: These are common examples.

q: If the bylaws make the president "an ex officio member of all committees except the Nominating Committee," the president may debate in those committees.
exp: An ex officio member has full rights.

q: Article VIII (Parliamentary Authority) names a person to serve as the society's parliamentary authority.
exp: It names a manual, such as RONR.

q: If a society adopts Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised and another manual conflicts with it, RONR controls.
exp: The adopted authority is binding.

q: If the bylaws have no amendment clause, they can be amended by a two-thirds vote at any business meeting.
exp: Previous notice is also required (or a majority of the entire membership).

q: Bylaw articles are divided into "segments."
exp: They are divided into sections.

q: If a bylaw is unclear, the chair can change it at a special meeting of the officers.
exp: Only the members can change it, by amending the bylaws.

q: A motion to amend the bylaws is a privileged motion.
exp: It is a main motion.

q: A motion to amend the bylaws should require at least previous notice and a two-thirds vote.
exp: That is the standard protection for bylaws.

q: An affirmative vote on a bylaw amendment can be reconsidered.
exp: An affirmative vote on a bylaw amendment cannot be reconsidered.

q: A bylaws revision can be perfected with third-degree amendments.
exp: Only first- and second-degree amendments exist; third-degree amendments are never allowed.

q: When proposed bylaw amendments conflict, the vote is taken first on the least inclusive one.
exp: Key says least inclusive first.

q: Unless it is nearly unanimous, the final vote on a bylaw amendment should be counted and recorded in the minutes.
exp: A counted vote documents that two-thirds was reached.

q: Amendments to a proposed bylaw amendment may not increase the change beyond what the notice covered.
exp: They must stay within the scope of notice.

q: Notice of a bylaw amendment may be worded informally, and if written, it should be signed by the president and secretary.
exp: It should be formally worded and, if written, signed by the mover and seconder.

q: A member can give notice of a bylaw amendment only during new business.
exp: It can also be given just before adjournment, between other items, or before the chair declares adjournment.

q: A bylaw amendment with previous notice becomes a general order for the meeting where it will be considered.
exp: Notice places it on the agenda as a general order.

q: A bylaw amendment takes effect when the meeting adjourns.
exp: It generally takes effect immediately upon adoption.

q: While a bylaw amendment is pending, a motion to amend it may be made and needs a majority vote.
exp: Secondary amendments need only a majority.

q: Adopting a proviso to a bylaw amendment requires only a majority of those present and voting.
exp: A proviso is not part of the bylaws itself.

q: If the meaning doesn't change, renumbering articles, sections, and cross-references can be delegated to the secretary or a committee.
exp: These are clerical corrections.

q: Members chosen to represent their society at a convention are called "representatives."
exp: They are called delegates.

q: Delegates to a multi-meeting convention are usually chosen to represent their unit for a single meeting.
exp: They serve for the whole session.

q: "House of delegates" applies to delegates elected for a fixed term who meet in sessions from time to time.
exp: That is the definition.

q: In an established state, regional, or national society, the parent body's bylaws should authorize a periodic convention.
exp: The convention's authority comes from the bylaws.

q: In a society made up of constituent units, each unit's bylaws should set delegate qualifications.
exp: The parent organization's bylaws should set them.

q: The parent body's bylaws should set how many delegates and alternates there are, their qualifications, and how they are elected.
exp: These are bylaw matters.

q: Officers elected at a convention take office at the start of the next convention.
exp: They take office at the close of the convention.

q: If a state unit's president can't attend the national convention, the unit's secretary takes their place.
exp: The vice-president normally takes the president's place.

q: Alternate delegates usually sit together with the registered delegates.
exp: Alternates are seated apart.

q: To replace a delegate who withdrew, an alternate must register with the society's secretary.
exp: The alternate registers with the Credentials Committee.

q: A delegate who will miss the next business meeting asks her alternate to fill in. This is improper unless the rules allow it.
exp: Temporary substitution requires a rule permitting it.

q: When a group of delegates meets during a convention to plan how they will act on upcoming matters, it is called an "ad hoc meeting."
exp: It is called a caucus.

q: A caucus follows committee rules of procedure unless it is large.
exp: Small caucuses use committee rules.

q: A delegate under instruction must vote as instructed.
exp: Instructions bind the delegate.

q: "Caucus" sometimes refers to a standing committee that will support an issue.
exp: It refers to a strategy meeting of declared supporters of an issue.

q: The convention's Credentials Committee prepares and certifies the list of delegates, alternates, and officers.
exp: That is its main job.

q: The Membership and Officer committees are most directly involved in formally organizing a convention.
exp: Credentials, Standing Rules, and Program committees are.

q: At a convention, the Program Committee screens original main motions and recommends action on them.
exp: The Resolutions Committee does that.

q: A convention parliamentarian's most important work is rising to call members to order.
exp: The most important work may be consulting before the convention opens.

q: A convention must formally organize itself into a single voting body before doing business.
exp: It must first establish who may vote.

q: The first report taken up at a convention is from the Program Committee.
exp: The Credentials Committee reports first.

q: A convention is organized by adopting three committee reports, in this order: Credentials, Standing Rules, Program.
exp: That order is required.

q: The Credentials Committee sends each unit information on how many delegates and alternates it may send and who is eligible.
exp: This happens before the convention.

q: If a chapter lists a delegate who is ineligible for unpaid dues, the Credentials Committee should tell the chapter it may choose a replacement.
exp: The chapter may substitute an eligible person.

q: The Credentials Committee drafts the convention's standing rules.
exp: It arranges registration; the Rules Committee drafts standing rules.

q: The Credentials Committee records members as they register and verifies their credentials.
exp: Both are its duties.

q: For a multi-day convention, registration should begin the same day the convention opens.
exp: It should begin a day or two before.

q: A motion to Recess is out of order before the Credentials Committee reports.
exp: Recess is in order then.

q: After the Credentials report is given, the chair next asks for unanimous consent to approve it.
exp: The chair normally first asks if there are questions on the report.

q: Once adopted, the Credentials report becomes the official roll of voting members.
exp: It defines who may vote.

q: Voting members who register after the Credentials report, and whose status isn't questioned, may not take part.
exp: They may participate once added to the roll.

q: If no rule sets a convention quorum, it is a majority of registered delegates who have not left.
exp: It is a majority of those registered, regardless of departures.

q: Convention standing rules include both parliamentary rules for conducting business and nonparliamentary rules.
exp: They cover both kinds.

q: "The Standing Rules of the Convention" also apply to future conventions.
exp: They apply to that convention only.

q: A convention's standing rules expire when the session that adopted them adjourns.
exp: They last only for that session.

q: Voted on separately, a convention standing rule limiting speeches on resolutions to two minutes would need a majority vote.
exp: Limiting debate needs a two-thirds vote.

q: Voted on separately, a convention standing rule on the format of written reports would need a majority vote.
exp: It does not limit members' rights.

q: Amending a convention standing rule that was adopted by majority vote requires at least two-thirds.
exp: A majority suffices if notice was given at least the day before.

q: A convention standing rule naming the parliamentary authority cannot be suspended by majority vote for a particular purpose.
exp: Suspension needs more than a majority.

q: The convention's Program Committee prepares the proposed schedule of events, proceedings, and meetings.
exp: That is the program.

q: Once adopted, the convention program becomes the standing rules.
exp: It becomes the order of business.

q: If a convention opens with the national anthem, the Pledge of Allegiance, and an invocation, the anthem always comes last.
exp: Key: the anthem is not last; the source says the pledge is.

q: At a convention, the Ways and Means Committee reports right after the treasurer.
exp: The auditors report next.

q: Informational convention committee reports needing no action should be taken up one after another at the same point in the agenda.
exp: Grouping them saves time.

q: At a convention, announcements at each meeting come right before the minutes.
exp: They come right before adjournment.

q: Each day, the previous day's convention minutes are read at the first meeting, right after opening ceremonies.
exp: They start the day's business.

q: The minutes of a convention's last day are usually approved by the delegates at the next convention.
exp: A board or special committee usually approves them.

q: A convention day's unfinished business is normally taken up the next day after the minutes.
exp: It carries over.

q: Nominations and elections at a convention should be held near the end.
exp: They should be held fairly early.

q: Officers elected at a convention are often installed at the closing banquet.
exp: Installation is often ceremonial.

q: Adopting a convention program requires notice and a two-thirds vote.
exp: It takes a majority vote.

q: The best way to change the convention program for a routine matter is unanimous consent.
exp: The chair asks if there is any objection.

q: If nonvoters also sit on the convention floor, the Arrangements Committee should seat voting members in a separate section.
exp: Separate seating makes votes easy to verify.

q: The convention committee that takes up all unscreened original main motions or resolutions is called the "Standing or Special Committee."
exp: It is the Resolutions (or Reference, or Platform) Committee.

q: Arranging similar resolutions in a logical order is outside the Resolutions Committee's power.
exp: It is within its power.

q: The Resolutions Committee usually reports only resolutions it agrees with.
exp: It generally must report all resolutions referred to it.

q: A platform's preamble should begin with "Whereas."
exp: Platforms usually start with words like "Believing."

q: A convention called for one purpose, with no permanent organization, is like a mass meeting and has no officers when called to order.
exp: It must elect its own officers.

q: A convention not of a permanent society is sometimes called to order by the chair of the Convention Arrangements Committee.
exp: Someone from the sponsors opens it.

q: At a convention not of a permanent society, the vice-president is elected after the temporary chair.
exp: The secretary is elected next.

q: At such a convention, no business is done until the Credentials report is received, except authorizing or ratifying the appointment of the Credentials, Rules, and Program committees.
exp: Those steps set up the convention.

q: At a convention called to form a permanent organization, permanent officers are elected right after the chair pro tem opens the meeting.
exp: They are elected after the bylaws are adopted.

q: Formal discipline should be treated as a drastic step for serious situations.
exp: It is a last resort.

q: The most severe penalty a society can impose on a member is suspension.
exp: The most severe penalty is expulsion.

q: Nonmembers can be excluded from part or all of a meeting at any time, through a question of privilege or a motion to go into executive session.
exp: Nonmembers attend only by the assembly's permission.

q: Everyone attending a meeting must follow the chair's legitimate orders.
exp: This applies to members and guests.

q: The chair should never use the gavel to drown out a disorderly member.
exp: The gavel is not for overpowering speakers.

q: As chair, if a member's remarks aren't germane, you should loudly call them out of order and then reprimand them.
exp: Tap the gavel lightly, point out the problem, and ask them to stick to the topic.

q: A member who wants to call another member to order must rise, address the chair, and wait to be recognized.
exp: No recognition is needed to raise a point of order.

q: When the chair "names" a member, it means the member committed a serious breach, the chair is preferring charges, and the assembly may impose a penalty.
exp: Naming starts discipline in the meeting.

q: An offense in a meeting, such as using objectionable language, does not need a formal trial with witnesses.
exp: The assembly witnessed it directly.

q: A member who uses objectionable or disorderly language in a meeting can be removed by vote of the assembly.
exp: The assembly may order removal.

q: It takes two members to require that a vote on imposing a penalty be taken by ballot.
exp: Key says a single member can require it.

q: The chair may grant attending nonmembers rights such as voting and debating.
exp: Nonmembers have no such rights.

q: The sergeant-at-arms may order the removal of disruptive nonmembers.
exp: The chair orders removal; the sergeant-at-arms carries it out.

q: A formal trial of a member accused of harming the organization's name must be held at a special meeting.
exp: It must be held in executive session.

q: A society may tell anyone why an expelled member was found guilty.
exp: It has no right to publicize the reasons.

q: A society's trial can only decide whether the accused is fit for membership.
exp: It cannot rule on legal guilt.

q: The first step in fair discipline is a public announcement that a member has been accused.
exp: The first step is a confidential committee investigation.

q: If a member is suspected of misconduct, a standing committee should investigate confidentially.
exp: A special (select) committee should investigate.

q: A member accused of serious misconduct is entitled to due process, and investigation by outsiders like auditors, police, or detectives is not part of the procedure.
exp: The society's own committee investigates.

q: If the bylaws have no charge-and-trial process, a member should offer a resolution to appoint an investigating committee.
exp: That begins the process.

q: An investigating committee cannot force the accused to appear before it.
exp: It has no such power.

q: At a disciplinary trial, the "managers" present the case against the accused, acting as prosecutors.
exp: That is their role.

q: When a trial is ordered, the secretary only has to tell the accused the date, place, and time.
exp: The notice must also state the charges and order the accused to appear.

q: The accused may not call witnesses during a trial.
exp: The accused may call witnesses.

q: Nonmember witnesses should stay in the room for the entire trial.
exp: They are present only while testifying.

q: If the accused doesn't show up at the set time, the trial is canceled.
exp: The trial goes ahead without them.

q: As chair at a trial, you would first remind everyone that the meeting is in executive session and must be kept confidential.
exp: Secrecy comes first.

q: After the preliminaries, the chair has the secretary read the charges.
exp: The charges are then on record.

q: The second step in a trial is opening statements from both sides.
exp: The second step is asking the accused to plead guilty or not guilty.

q: If the plea is not guilty, the third step is witness testimony.
exp: Opening statements come third.

q: After closing arguments, each charge is opened to debate and voted on separately.
exp: Each specification and charge gets its own vote.

q: If the accused is found guilty, a motion to expel needs only a majority vote.
exp: Expulsion requires a two-thirds vote.

q: If a committee holds the trial, the assembly then votes in executive session on the committee's resolutions.
exp: The assembly decides the penalty.

q: Some professional societies have a standing discipline committee whose duties include imposing penalties.
exp: It may investigate and hear trials, but should not impose penalties.

q: A member may raise a point of order if a motion is made and seconded and the chair ignores it.
exp: The chair must state a seconded motion.

q: If the chair ignores a point of order raised because the chair refused to put a motion, the motion's maker may put it to a vote.
section: Chair Refuses to Put a Motion
exp: The maker can put the question from the floor.

q: A regular presiding officer who does not properly perform the chair's duties can be censured.
exp: Censure is available for officers.

q: If someone other than the regular presiding officer is in the chair and the assembly wants them out, it can move to "declare the chair vacant and elect a new chair."
exp: This applies to non-regular presiding officers.

q: If officers serve "for four years or until their successors are elected," a motion to Reconsider the election can remove an officer for misconduct.
exp: The removal is done by rescinding the election, not by reconsidering it.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time and Amend are both subsidiary motions.
exp: Both are subsidiary.

q: Adjourn, Recess, and Lay on the Table are all privileged motions.
exp: Lay on the Table is subsidiary.

q: Postpone Indefinitely, Postpone to a Certain Time, and Limit or Extend Limits of Debate are all subsidiary motions.
exp: All three are subsidiary.

q: Recess, Adjourn, and Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn are all in the same class.
exp: All are privileged motions.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn has the highest rank of all motions.
exp: It is the top-ranking privileged motion.

q: Lay on the Table has the lowest rank of all motions.
exp: The main motion ranks lowest.

q: Raise a Question of Privilege is the lowest-ranking privileged motion.
exp: Call for the Orders of the Day ranks lowest.

q: An amendment to a motion to Recess outranks a main motion.
exp: It takes the rank of the Recess motion.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time is the highest-ranking subsidiary motion.
exp: Lay on the Table ranks highest.

q: All privileged motions are debatable.
exp: Privileged motions are undebatable.

q: Call for the Orders of the Day is undebatable.
exp: It is a demand, not debated.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is debatable.
exp: It opens the main question to debate.

q: The Previous Question can be amended.
exp: It cannot be amended.

q: Commit (Refer) is amendable.
exp: Its details can be amended.

q: From lowest to highest rank: Main Motion, Amend, Adjourn.
exp: That order is correct.

q: From lowest to highest rank: Amend, Main Motion, Recess, Postpone Indefinitely.
exp: Correct order: Main Motion, Postpone Indefinitely, Amend, Recess.

q: From highest to lowest rank: Adjourn, Recess, Amend, Main Motion.
exp: That order is correct.

q: From highest to lowest rank: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn, Adjourn, Commit, Postpone Indefinitely.
exp: That order is correct.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is out of order while the privileged motion to Adjourn is pending.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It outranks Adjourn, so it is in order.

q: The Previous Question cannot be applied to a motion to Commit (Refer).
exp: It can be applied to Commit.

q: Adjourn, Previous Question, and Amend can all be moved while a main motion is pending.
exp: All outrank the main motion.

q: A motion to Limit Debate can be made while an amendment is pending.
exp: It is in order if the pending amendment is debatable.

q: With a main motion and an amendment pending, Postpone Indefinitely is out of order.
exp: It ranks below Amend.

q: With a main motion and the Previous Question pending, a motion "to recess for five minutes" is in order.
exp: Recess is privileged and outranks them.

q: If Postpone Indefinitely, Limit Debate, a main motion, and an amendment to a motion to Recess are all pending, Limit Debate is the immediately pending question.
exp: The amendment to Recess is immediately pending.

q: With a main motion, Postpone to a Certain Time, Commit, and Recess pending, Recess is the immediately pending question.
exp: The highest-ranking motion is immediately pending.

q: After the Previous Question is ordered on a pending amendment, a motion to Refer is out of order.
exp: Commit ranks below the Previous Question.

q: The Previous Question applies to every subsidiary motion except Refer to a Committee.
exp: The exception is Lay on the Table.

q: Lay on the Table outranks only main motions.
exp: It outranks all other subsidiary motions and main motions.

q: With a main motion pending and an amendment under debate, Postpone Indefinitely is out of order.
exp: It ranks below Amend.

q: If Postpone Indefinitely, Limit Debate, the Previous Question, and a main motion are all properly pending, the Previous Question is voted on first.
exp: It is the highest-ranking of them.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn is never in order while a Question of Privilege is pending.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It outranks it, so it is in order.

q: A main motion is out of order unless another motion is pending.
exp: A main motion can be made only when nothing else is pending.

q: The Previous Question is out of order when the immediately pending motion is undebatable and unamendable.
exp: There is nothing for it to close.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is out of order while a main motion is pending.
exp: It is in order when a main motion is immediately pending.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is out of order while a motion to Recess is pending.
exp: Recess outranks it.

q: Limit or Extend Debate may be moved when a motion to Recess is immediately pending.
exp: It is out of order then.

q: A main motion must be debated.
exp: Debate is allowed, not required.

q: A motion to adjourn made as a main motion is undebatable and unamendable.
exp: As a main motion it is debatable and amendable.

q: Adopting an ordinary standing rule needs a majority vote.
exp: Ordinary standing rules are adopted by majority.

q: Adopting parliamentary standing rules at a convention requires a two-thirds vote.
exp: They affect members' rights.

q: Amend is not a subsidiary motion.
exp: Amend is subsidiary.

q: A motion to amend an amendment does not need a second.
exp: It needs a second.

q: Amend is debatable only if the motion it would change is debatable.
exp: Debatability follows the motion being amended.

q: Both primary and secondary amendments need a second and a majority vote.
exp: Both follow the same rules.

q: One difference between Amend and Amend Something Previously Adopted is that the latter is always debatable.
exp: It is a main motion.

q: Amend Something Previously Adopted can be classed as a main motion.
exp: It is an incidental main motion.

q: Amending convention parliamentary standing rules when not pending takes at least two-thirds, or a majority of the registered voting members.
exp: These are the required votes.

q: An appeal on a question of priority of business is never in order when another member has the floor.
exp: It is in order then if made at the time of the ruling.

q: Adopting a proposal to fill a blank requires at least two-thirds.
exp: A majority is enough.

q: Consider Informally is a privileged motion.
exp: It is a subsidiary motion (a form of Commit).

q: Consider by Paragraph (Seriatim) is an incidental motion.
exp: It is incidental.

q: Considering a question informally requires a majority of the entire membership.
exp: It requires a majority of those present and voting.

q: A motion to consider informally can be amended.
exp: It cannot be amended.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate requires two-thirds of those present and voting.
exp: Changing debate rules needs two-thirds.

q: An incidental motion to change an adopted convention agenda on the spot is never debatable, amendable, or in order when another member has the floor.
exp: Key says True.

q: Limit Debate, Lay on the Table, Postpone Definitely, and the Previous Question are all debatable.
exp: Only Postpone to a Certain Time is debatable.

q: Refer to a Committee, Division of the Question, Reconsider, and Take From the Table are all incidental motions.
exp: Only Division of the Question is incidental.

q: Extend Debate, Point of Order, Postpone Indefinitely, and the Previous Question are never subsidiary motions.
exp: Only Point of Order is never subsidiary.

q: When debating a motion to Commit (Refer), debate must stay on the motion to Commit.
exp: Debate is limited to the referral.

q: A motion to limit or extend debate for an entire meeting is a main motion.
exp: With nothing pending, it is a main motion.

q: Discharging a committee requires a majority with previous notice, two-thirds of those voting, or a majority of the entire membership.
exp: These are the vote options.

q: A main motion to limit or extend debate for the whole meeting can never be adopted by a simple majority.
exp: It requires two-thirds.

q: A call for a Division of the Assembly does not need a second.
exp: It is a demand.

q: Division of the Assembly and Division of the Question are both debatable.
exp: Both are undebatable.

q: A member may call for a Division of the Assembly even when another member has the floor.
exp: It may interrupt.

q: Division of the Question needs two-thirds, needs no second, and cannot be amended.
exp: It needs a majority, a second, and may be amended.

q: Division of the Assembly, Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn, Lay on the Table, and Call for the Orders of the Day are all incidental motions.
exp: Only Division of the Assembly is incidental.

q: Division of the Assembly, the Previous Question, and Discharge a Committee all need a second.
exp: Division of the Assembly needs no second.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn, as a privileged motion, needs a majority of the entire membership.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: It needs a majority of those present and voting.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn made as a main motion is debatable.
section: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn
exp: As a main motion it is debatable.

q: A Request for Information is adopted by a majority of those present and voting.
exp: A Request for Information is not voted on.

q: Lay on the Table cannot interrupt another speaker.
exp: It needs the floor.

q: Motions to make, close, or reopen nominations are in order when another member has the floor.
exp: None of them is in order then.

q: A motion to approve the minutes is adopted by majority vote.
exp: Approval takes a majority (usually done by unanimous consent).

q: Dispensing with the reading of the minutes requires two-thirds.
exp: It needs a majority.

q: Lay on the Table, Postpone to a Certain Time, and Postpone Indefinitely have in common that none needs a second.
exp: All three require a second.

q: Closing nominations normally requires a two-thirds vote.
exp: It takes away members' right to nominate.

q: A Point of Order and a Parliamentary Inquiry can both be made when another member has the floor.
exp: Both may interrupt if urgent.

q: Objection to Consideration, Point of Order, Parliamentary Inquiry, and Call for the Orders of the Day are all privileged motions.
exp: Only Call for the Orders of the Day is privileged.

q: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question needs no second and is neither debatable nor amendable.
exp: Those are its rules.

q: A Call for the Orders of the Day cannot be amended.
exp: It is a demand.

q: A Call for the Orders of the Day is adopted by majority vote.
exp: It is not voted on; one member can enforce it.

q: Points of order and parliamentary inquiries are both voted on.
exp: The chair usually decides them.

q: Once the Previous Question is adopted, debate may begin on the motion it applies to.
exp: Debate is closed on that motion.

q: Postpone an Event or Action Previously Scheduled is an incidental main motion that brings a question again before the assembly.
exp: Key says True.

q: Postpone Indefinitely must be seconded.
exp: It needs a second.

q: A Question of Privilege that cannot be brought up as a main motion is an incidental motion.
exp: Raising a Question of Privilege is a privileged motion.

q: Postpone Indefinitely and Postpone to a Certain Time both must be seconded.
exp: Both need a second.

q: As chair, if a member debates the main motion's merits while Postpone to a Certain Time is immediately pending, you should allow it.
exp: Remind them that debate is limited to the postponement.

q: A Question of Privilege made as a main motion may be amended.
exp: As a main motion it is amendable.

q: A motion to Ratify is undebatable.
exp: Ratify is debatable.

q: The privileged motion to Recess needs no second.
exp: It needs a second.

q: A motion by one member to let another member read papers needs no second.
exp: Key says True.

q: The difference between the privileged motion to Recess and Recess as a main motion is that the main motion is debatable.
exp: With nothing pending, Recess is debatable.

q: A motion to Recess made when nothing is pending is a privileged motion.
exp: It is then a main motion.
