q: A motion to Recess made when nothing else is pending still needs a second.
exp: Every main motion needs a second.

q: A motion to Reconsider, used to bring a question back before the assembly, needs no second.
exp: It needs a second.

q: Annul, Repeal, and Rescind are incidental main motions.
exp: They are forms of Rescind.

q: Take From the Table is a main motion.
exp: It is a motion that brings a question again before the assembly.

q: Rescinding requires a majority with previous notice, two-thirds of those voting, or a majority of the entire membership.
exp: These are the vote options.

q: In a committee, a motion to Reconsider needs no second and cannot be amended.
exp: Committee rules waive the second.

q: Suspend the Rules normally needs two-thirds of those present and voting.
exp: That is the usual threshold.

q: Suspending ordinary standing rules requires at least two-thirds.
exp: A majority is enough.

q: Take From the Table needs no second.
exp: It needs a second.

q: After the chair states a motion, a motion granting permission to withdraw it must be seconded if made by the member asking to withdraw.
exp: Key says True.

q: A motion about voting made when no question is pending is undebatable.
exp: With nothing pending it is a main motion and is debatable.

q: A motion about voting made while a question is pending is debatable.
exp: While a question is pending it is undebatable.

q: The proper way to move to adjourn is to call out "Adjourn!" from your seat.
exp: The proper form is "I move to adjourn."

q: "I move the report be adopted" means the report is agreed to, accepted, or adopted.
exp: All three terms mean the same thing.

q: To add words at the end of a pending main motion, you say, "I move to amend by adding..."
exp: "Adding" is used for the end of a motion.

q: To appeal the chair's ruling on a point of order, you call out "Appeal!" from your seat.
exp: The proper form is "I appeal from the decision of the chair."

q: To let members speak as often as they can get the floor, you move "that the question be considered informally."
exp: That removes the limit on speeches.

q: The proper form for filling a blank is "I move that the blank be $500."
exp: You simply say, "I suggest $500."

q: With "give the president $500 to travel to a leadership workshop" pending, you create a blank by saying, "I move to create a blank by striking out '$500.'"
exp: That is the proper form.

q: To ask for a rising vote to verify a voice vote, a member calls out "Verification!"
exp: The member calls out "Division!"

q: If the chair doesn't order a counted vote on a division, a member may say, "I move that the vote on this motion be counted."
exp: A motion to count the vote is in order.

q: The proper form for a Request for Information is "I want to ask [member's name] a question."
exp: Use "Request for information," "I rise to a request for information," or "Will the member yield for a question?"

q: The form to lay a motion on the table is "I move to postpone the motion by laying it on the table."
exp: The form is "I move that the motion be laid on the table."

q: To hear the minutes later than scheduled when nothing is pending, you say, "I move that the reading of the minutes be dispensed with."
exp: Dispensing with the reading delays it until later.

q: The form for a nomination is "I move to nominate [name]."
exp: The form is "I nominate [name]."

q: "Order, order!" is the correct way to call a member to order.
exp: Say "Point of order," "I rise to a point of order," or "I call the member to order."

q: "I move that the member be allowed to read their statement" may be used to grant permission to read papers.
exp: That is an acceptable form.

q: The way to immediately close debate on a main motion is to call out "Question, question!"
exp: One proper form is "I move the previous question."

q: To take up a question out of its order on the agenda, you say, "I move to suspend the rules and take up..."
exp: This requires a two-thirds vote.

q: A Request for Information is in order when another member has the floor and needs no second.
exp: It may interrupt if urgent.

q: A member who has been given the floor may be interrupted to raise a question of privilege.
exp: Urgent privilege matters may interrupt.

q: An Objection to the Consideration of a Question is out of order when another member has the floor (but hasn't begun speaking) and needs a second.
exp: It is in order then and needs no second.

q: An Appeal is never in order when another member has the floor, and it needs no second.
exp: It is in order then and needs a second.

q: Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes is in order after another member has been given the floor but before they start speaking.
section: Reconsider and Enter on the Minutes
exp: That timing is allowed.

q: Take From the Table is debatable and amendable.
exp: It is neither debatable nor amendable.

q: Limit or Extend Debate is amendable but not debatable.
exp: Those are its rules.

q: Postpone Indefinitely is amendable but not debatable.
exp: It is debatable but not amendable.

q: Debate on Discharge a Committee and on Postpone Indefinitely may go into the merits of the underlying question.
exp: Both open the main question to debate.

q: A secondary amendment does not require a two-thirds vote.
exp: It needs a majority of those present and voting.

q: Without previous notice, Amend Something Previously Adopted requires a two-thirds vote.
exp: Or a majority of the entire membership.

q: Close Nominations and Raise a Question of Privilege both require two-thirds.
exp: A question of privilege is ruled on by the chair.

q: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn may be reconsidered.
exp: It may be reconsidered.

q: Lay on the Table may be reconsidered.
exp: It may not be reconsidered.

q: On Postpone Indefinitely, only an affirmative vote may be reconsidered.
exp: A negative vote can't be, since the motion can be made again.

q: An affirmative vote may be reconsidered on Consider Informally and on Rescind.
exp: Only a negative vote may be reconsidered on these.

q: Which of these is NOT a feature of a deliberative assembly?
exp: Deliberative assemblies are usually larger than a handful of people; the other three are defining features.
choices: The group has fewer than six people.
Members take part freely and use their own judgment.
The group meets and decides what to do after full and free discussion.
Every member's vote counts the same.

q: In a deliberative assembly, questions are normally decided by the
exp: Decisions are made by the members present at a legal meeting, and they bind the whole body.
choices: members present at a properly called meeting.

q: An assembly is best described as a
exp: An assembly is the body of people gathered to act as a group, not a single meeting or session.
choices: meeting of a larger organization's executive board.
special meeting of an organization's members.
body of people who come together to act as a group.

q: In parliamentary terms, a member of an assembly is someone entitled to
exp: Membership means the right to participate fully: make motions, debate, and vote.
choices: see every record the organization keeps.
take full part in the assembly's proceedings.
debate a motion in detail before anyone makes it.

q: Members of a deliberative assembly
exp: These are the basic rights of membership; shouting "Question" does not close debate.
choices: are required to debate every motion.
can vote only if their dues are current.
have the right to make motions, take part in debate, and vote.
can end debate on any motion by shouting "Question!"

q: If a deliberative assembly has not adopted any rules of its own, it is governed by the rules and customs
exp: Without adopted rules, an assembly follows common parliamentary law.
choices: written by the officers before the first meeting.

q: The actions of any deliberative assembly must follow
exp: An assembly is bound by its own rules and by any law that applies to it.
choices: whatever a majority decides, without notice.
its bylaws and other rules plus all applicable local, state, and federal laws.
whatever the president and secretary decide.

q: The basic rule for making decisions in a deliberative assembly is that
exp: Majority vote is the basic principle of decision.
choices: a proposal is adopted by a majority vote.
two members can demand a rising vote.
every amendment needs a two-thirds vote.
a two-thirds vote can overturn any ruling of the chair.

q: A majority vote means a motion is approved by
exp: A majority is more than half of the votes cast by members entitled to vote, not counting blanks or abstentions.
choices: more than half of the members present and voting.
exactly half of the organization's members.

q: The "call" of a meeting is
exp: The call is the written notice of the time and place sent to members in advance.
choices: a notice of a special meeting only.
the chair's demand that the meeting begin.
a written notice of the meeting's time and place, mailed or given to members.
a spoken notice of the time and place given at least a year ahead.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the main types of deliberative assembly?
exp: The main types are the mass meeting, local society, convention, legislative body, and board; a committee is not one of them.

q: A meeting of an unorganized group, open to anyone interested, held to discuss a particular problem is a
exp: A mass meeting is called for a specific purpose and is open to everyone interested.

q: Attendance at a mass meeting
exp: The sponsors may limit attendance, for example to people who support the meeting's purpose.
choices: depends on membership in the sponsoring society.

q: Membership in the assembly of an organized local society is limited to people who are
section: Local Assembly of an Organized Society
exp: Only voting members in good standing on the society's rolls make up its assembly.
choices: on the society's rolls as voting members in good standing.

q: The bylaws of an organized local society usually call for
exp: Local societies normally hold regular meetings at stated intervals, such as monthly.
choices: a fixed number of meetings each year.

q: In which type of deliberative assembly is each meeting normally its own separate session?
exp: In an organized local society, each regular meeting is usually a separate session.

q: An assembly of delegates, usually chosen for one session only, is a
exp: A convention is made up of delegates typically chosen for a single session.

q: Which statement about a convention is true?
exp: Convention voting members are normally delegates; the Credentials Committee certifies delegates, not non-delegates.
choices: A convention is never called to form an association.
Its voting members are usually delegates.
A typical convention lasts a month.
The Credentials Committee certifies all non-delegates.

q: When a convention ends,
exp: A convention normally dissolves at the end of its session.
choices: the official delegates must meet to elect new officers.
the alternates start their own convention.
the officers may meet to adopt new bylaws.

q: Law-making bodies such as Congress are called
exp: Bodies that make law, like Congress or a state legislature, are legislative bodies.

q: A board is an administrative body whose members are
exp: Board members may be elected or appointed, depending on the rules.
choices: appointed by the chair at a general meeting.

q: In general character, a board resembles a
exp: A board has the character of a deliberative assembly.

q: A board within an organized society
exp: All three describe a board inside a society.
choices: may be given a particular function, like a board of education.
has powers given to it by an authority outside itself.
answers to the society's full assembly.

q: Large boards and large committees use parliamentary procedure
exp: Large boards and committees follow regular procedure; the relaxed small-board rules apply only to small bodies.
choices: the same way as any other assembly.
less strictly than other deliberative assemblies.
only for business held over from the last meeting.
whenever the chair thinks it will help.

q: An organized society needs certain rules in order to
exp: Rules set out how the society is structured and operates.
choices: set up its basic structure and how it operates.
make sure it is different from other societies.
let its officers act against its bylaws.
protect its officers from liability for their actions.

q: The corporate charter of a society that wants to incorporate should include
exp: A charter states the name and object plus whatever the state's law requires.
choices: any information the state of incorporation requires.

q: A main advantage of incorporating a society is that its officers and members
exp: Incorporation shields members and officers from personal liability for the organization's debts.
choices: can deduct their service expenses from state income taxes.
can change the bylaws without a membership vote.
are protected from personal liability for the organization's obligations.
can use the organization's facilities for personal profit.

q: A corporate charter should be drafted by
exp: Because it is a legal document, a charter should be drafted by a lawyer.

q: In an incorporated organization, which document outranks all its other rules?
exp: The corporate charter is the highest document of an incorporated society.

q: The document containing a society's own rules about itself as an organization is its
exp: The bylaws (or constitution) hold the society's rules relating to itself.

q: The first two articles in the bylaws of an unincorporated society are usually
exp: Bylaws normally open with Article I, Name, and Article II, Object.

q: Which article is generally NOT found in an organization's bylaws?
exp: Membership lists are kept as records, not written into the bylaws.
choices: A list of every member's legal name and address

q: For an incorporated society, the best practice is to
exp: RONR recommends a single bylaws document; an incorporated society's charter fills the role a separate constitution would.
choices: combine the charter, bylaws, and constitution into one document.
treat it no differently from an unincorporated society.
keep a separate constitution and bylaws.
not keep a constitution separate from the bylaws.

q: Apart from the corporate charter of an incorporated society, the highest-ranking rules are the
exp: Among a society's own rules, the bylaws rank highest after any charter.

q: The term "rules of order" refers to
exp: Rules of order are written rules of parliamentary procedure.

q: Most societies adopt their rules of order by naming a parliamentary manual (and edition) in their bylaws. That manual is called the organization's
exp: The manual named in the bylaws is the parliamentary authority.

q: Rules that add to or change the rules in an organization's parliamentary authority are called
exp: Special rules of order supplement or modify the parliamentary authority.

q: In a mass meeting or a body that is not yet organized, a parliamentary authority
exp: A new or unorganized body can adopt a parliamentary authority at the beginning of its meeting.
choices: may be adopted at the start of the meeting.
must be adopted by the second meeting.
is not needed if there are fewer than 100 members.
may be adopted at the end of the meeting.

q: If a special rule of order conflicts with the parliamentary authority, which one governs?
exp: Special rules of order take precedence over the parliamentary authority.
choices: Neither; a backup manual is consulted.

q: An organization's bylaws name Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised as its parliamentary authority. If another manual disagrees on a rule, which is binding?
exp: The manual named in the bylaws is binding; other manuals are only persuasive.
choices: The assembly picks one by majority vote.
Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised
The officers decide in executive session.

q: Special rules of order should be
exp: RONR advises adopting special rules of order separately from the bylaws so they can be suspended.
choices: adopted as part of the bylaws.
voted on by the officers before going to the members.

q: Ordinary standing rules generally contain
exp: Standing rules cover administrative details like meeting start times.
choices: rules that can only be changed with notice and a two-thirds vote.
the society's object and standing committees.
procedure rules about the presiding officer.

q: Which is an example of a standing rule?
exp: A guest register is an administrative matter; the others belong in the bylaws.
choices: Listing duties of every standing committee chair

q: What is the minimum vote to adopt a standing rule at any business meeting?
exp: Standing rules are adopted like any main motion, by majority vote with no notice needed.
choices: A majority, with required previous notice

q: A standing rule stays in effect until it is
exp: A standing rule continues until rescinded or amended.
choices: withdrawn by the member who proposed it.

q: At a meeting, without notice, an assembly may temporarily suspend its
exp: Standing rules can be suspended for a meeting by majority vote; bylaws and charters cannot be suspended.

q: An assembly's quorum is
exp: A quorum is the minimum number of members needed to transact business.
choices: two-thirds of the members at a meeting.
the most members you can count on to attend.
the number of members who must be present to do business legally.
the number of members who always vote.

q: If the bylaws don't set a quorum, the quorum of an organized society is
exp: Without a bylaw provision, the quorum is a majority of all members.
choices: a majority of the entire membership.
a majority of those answering roll call.

q: The minimum officers needed to conduct business in a deliberative assembly are a
exp: An assembly needs at least someone to preside and someone to take the minutes.
choices: presiding officer and a secretary or clerk.

q: Which term refers both to the presiding officer and to the place where that officer presides?
exp: "The chair" means both the person presiding and the presiding station.

q: How is a vice-president addressed while presiding, if the president is not on the platform?
exp: Check against RONR: the vice-president presiding is addressed by the presiding officer's title.
choices: "Mr. or Madam President pro tem" or "Chair member"

q: With very few exceptions, a member never speaks
exp: In formal meetings, members rise to speak except in a few cases.
choices: more than once on a main motion.

q: During a meeting, the presiding officer refers to himself or herself as
exp: The presiding officer speaks of himself or herself in the third person as "the chair."

q: Which is a proper way for the chair to call a meeting to order?
exp: The standard form is "The meeting will come to order."

q: What sets the sequence in which general types of business are taken up at a meeting?
exp: The order of business fixes the sequence of classes of business.

q: A society that has adopted Robert's Rules of Order Newly Revised as its parliamentary authority
exp: A society may adopt its own order of business as a special rule; otherwise the standard order applies.
choices: can use a different manual at each meeting.
must use the manual's order of business.
can adopt its own order of business.
can change any rule in the manual by majority vote without notice.

q: After the meeting is called to order, the next item of business is usually
exp: In the standard order, the minutes come first after the call to order (and any opening ceremonies).
choices: reading and approval of the minutes.

q: In the standard order of business, officers' reports come
exp: Reports of officers follow approval of the minutes.
choices: right after the minutes are approved.

q: In the standard order of business, what comes right after special orders?
exp: The order is minutes, reports, special orders, unfinished business and general orders, then new business.

q: In the standard order of business, new business is taken up
exp: New business follows unfinished business and general orders.
choices: after unfinished business and general orders.
whenever members want to make main motions.

q: A mass meeting usually doesn't need an order of business because
exp: A mass meeting has no previous business, so all business is new.
choices: the officers write an agenda once the meeting starts.
only new business can come up.
a committee runs a panel discussion instead.

q: A member's motion is brought before the assembly by

q: A meeting that continues the previous regular or special meeting is a(n)
exp: An adjourned meeting continues the earlier meeting's session.

q: A society meeting on September 21 can't finish its business. It votes to adjourn to October 21. The October 21 meeting is a(n)
exp: It continues the September session, so it is an adjourned meeting.

q: Another name for a special meeting is a
exp: Special meetings are also called called meetings.

q: Which is true about an adjourned meeting?
exp: An adjourned meeting begins with the minutes of the preceding meeting, then picks up where it left off.
choices: It is the same as a called meeting.
The minutes of the meeting before it are read.
It is the same as adjourning a regular meeting.
It always starts with new business.

q: Some societies hold only one business meeting of the members per year. It is called the
exp: That is the annual meeting.

q: In a group that meets regularly all year, the annual meeting's minutes are approved at the next
exp: They are approved at the next regular meeting.

q: A meeting, or part of one, whose proceedings are secret is called a(n)
exp: Secret proceedings are held in executive session.

q: Which is true about executive session?
exp: Going into executive session is a question of privilege adopted by majority vote.
choices: Members may discuss it freely with anyone.
Its minutes are approved at a regular open meeting.
A motion to go into executive session is a question of privilege needing a second and a majority vote.
It is always limited to officers.

q: If a member breaks the secrecy of an executive session,
exp: Violating secrecy is grounds for discipline.
choices: the president has the secretary publish the secret information.

q: How should a society usually handle executive session minutes?
exp: Executive session minutes are read and approved only in executive session.
choices: The president appoints a committee to approve them.
Read and approve them in another executive session.
Approve them like any open meeting minutes.

q: An original main motion is one that
exp: Original main motions introduce new substantive subjects.
choices: brings up a substantive question as a new subject.
relates to the assembly's business or past or future action.
lets the maker chair the committee if referred.

q: An incidental main motion
exp: Incidental main motions have parliamentary names, like adopting a recommendation or ratifying.
choices: can only be made with the assembly's permission.
is in order while an original main motion is immediately pending.
proposes an action defined in parliamentary law and named by a parliamentary term.
is a main motion that can only be made while an incidental motion is pending.

q: An incidental main motion differs from an original main motion because it
exp: Incidental main motions relate to business or procedure, not new subjects.
choices: is always made while a main motion is pending.
can be made anytime, even while someone is speaking.
never brings up a new substantive subject.

q: Which is an example of an incidental main motion?
exp: Each of these is a procedural main motion made when nothing is pending.
choices: A motion to recess when no business is pending
A motion setting a special speech-length limit for the whole meeting
A motion to adopt a committee's recommendations

q: The main difference in the rules for original and incidental main motions is that incidental main motions
exp: Objection to the Consideration applies only to original main motions.
choices: can't have an Objection to the Consideration applied to them.
can be debated only once per member.

q: A main motion is a motion that
exp: A main motion applies to no other motion.
choices: can't be applied to any other motion.
can be made at any time.

q: All subsidiary motions can be applied to
exp: Every subsidiary motion can be applied to a main motion.

q: A general rule for wording a main motion is
exp: Motions should be worded positively; a "don't do" motion is confusing.
choices: to just say "I so move" after informal discussion.
not to propose that the assembly refrain from doing something.
never to start with "I move that..."

q: Which motion is worded best?
exp: A clear positive statement of opposition is better than a negative motion.
choices: "I move that this organization declare its opposition to the recent dues increase."
"I move that this organization go on record as not favoring the proposed dues increase."
"I move that our delegates be given no instructions on the dues proposal at next week's convention."
"I move that we give no response to the proposed dues."

q: A resolution should always be submitted
exp: Resolutions are written out.

q: In a written resolution, what word begins each clause of a preamble that gives reasons for adopting it?
exp: Preamble clauses begin with "Whereas."

q: When considering a resolution with a preamble, when is the preamble amended?
exp: The preamble is amended last, after the body.
choices: At the same time as the resolving clauses

q: After the Previous Question is ordered on a resolution that has a preamble,
exp: The Previous Question on the resolution doesn't cover the preamble, which can then be debated and amended.
choices: debate is allowed on the resolution.
debate is allowed on the preamble.

q: Which statement about main motions is FALSE?
exp: Renewing a rejected question in the same session is out of order (except by Reconsider).
choices: They bring business before the assembly.
They can be made only when nothing else is pending.
They may raise the same question already rejected in the same session.

q: Which main motions are out of order?
exp: All of these make a main motion out of order.
choices: Those that conflict with national law
Those that conflict with or repeat a question temporarily but not finally disposed of
Those outside the scope of the bylaws or charter unless authorized by a two-thirds vote

q: After a main motion is made but before the chair states it,
exp: Before it is stated, the motion belongs to the maker, and others may suggest changes.
choices: members may informally suggest changes to the maker.
the chair can force changes without a vote.
no changes are allowed because it belongs to the assembly.
any member can change it without the maker's consent.

q: After the chair states the question, the maker can change the motion by asking
exp: Once stated, the maker needs the assembly's permission, usually by unanimous consent.
choices: the chair to accept an amendment without a vote.

q: If a motion clearly needs time or study to perfect, a member should move to
exp: Referral sends it to a committee for study.

q: A main motion is pending, an amendment is moved and seconded, then a member moves to refer both to a committee. Which is voted on first?
exp: The last motion stated, Refer, is voted on first.

q: When a main motion and a motion to postpone it indefinitely are pending, the first vote is on
exp: The higher-ranking subsidiary motion is voted on first.
choices: None; the chair decides by the merits.

q: Scheduled main motions can be brought up even though another motion is pending by
section: Call for the Orders of the Day
exp: A Call for the Orders of the Day can bring up a scheduled order whose time has come.
choices: Calling for the Orders of the Day.

q: When debate seems to be over, the chair checks that no one else wants to speak by asking
exp: "Are you ready for the question?" or "Is there any further debate?"
choices: the maker for permission to vote.

q: What is it called when members are told ahead of time that a certain motion will be brought up at a meeting?
exp: That is previous notice.

q: Rescind, Amend Something Previously Adopted, and Discharge a Committee can be adopted by a simple majority only if there was
exp: With previous notice they need only a majority; otherwise two-thirds or a majority of the entire membership.

q: Adopting special rules of order requires
exp: Special rules need notice and two-thirds (or a majority of the entire membership).
choices: previous notice and a two-thirds vote.

q: Previous notice can be given
exp: Any member may give notice.
choices: by any member at a meeting.
by anyone present at a meeting.

q: Previous notice of a motion can be given aloud at a meeting
exp: Notice may be given when no one has the floor, even with a question pending.
choices: when no one has the floor, even if a question is pending.
after the chair has declared adjournment.
after the chair has stated a motion.

exp: Notice can be given in any of these ways.
choices: given aloud at a meeting even while a motion is pending.
given aloud when another member has been recognized but hasn't started speaking.

q: The motion to Ratify is a(n)
exp: Ratify is an incidental main motion.

q: The motion to Ratify is a motion to
exp: Ratify confirms action already taken.

q: The motion to Ratify
exp: Ratification validates action already taken.
choices: can be made with no quorum present.
is usually made by someone on the winning side.
if adopted, makes valid action already taken.
is only in order while a main motion is pending.

q: Ratify should NOT be used to confirm
exp: An assembly can't ratify something it couldn't have done, like violating a bylaw ballot requirement.
choices: a local unit's action needing national approval.
a voice-vote election when the bylaws require a ballot.
emergency action taken without a quorum.
emergency action by a committee beyond its instructions.

q: The motion to Postpone Indefinitely is used by

choices: the chair to schedule a motion for next meeting.
a member to send a motion to a standing committee.
members who want to change the main motion.
the assembly to decline to take a position on the main motion.

q: Which motion would kill a pending main motion and avoid a direct vote on it?

q: A member uses Postpone Indefinitely to avoid
exp: It disposes of the question without a direct vote.
choices: a direct vote on the question.

choices: nothing but the main question it applies to.

q: The motion to Postpone Indefinitely can be

choices: laid on the table by itself.
applied only to the main question.

choices: is in order when someone else has the floor.
is debatable, and debate may go into the merits of the main question.

q: Postpone Indefinitely can be reconsidered only if the vote on it was
exp: Only an affirmative vote on it can be reconsidered.

q: At a multi-meeting convention, a motion postponed indefinitely stays suppressed

for the whole series of meetings (session).

choices: more debate on the main question.
debate to close if it fails.

Get the floor and say, "I move that this motion be postponed indefinitely."
Get the floor and move the previous question.
From your seat, move to lay it on the table.

choices: change the wording of the main motion.

q: A member who voted for an amendment, when the amended motion comes to a vote,

exp: Debate is confined to the amendment.

debate must stay on the amendment, not the main motion as a whole.
debate may range over the full merits of the main motion.
another primary amendment may be offered.

exp: Replacing a paragraph or more is a substitution.

only the maker of the main motion can propose it.

accept it and ask for a second.

ask the maker to withdraw it.

get the floor and move to amend by adding "from 9 p.m. to 11:30 p.m."

laid on the table by itself.

the whole clause containing them and insert a new clause.
the whole motion and substitute a new one.

get a friend to move it.
declare a blank and fill it.
leave the chair to move it.

q: One rule for filling a blank with a name is that

a majority vote adopts a name.

q: Commit (Refer) sends a pending question to a committee so that

it can be studied carefully and put in better shape.

even after a motion is adopted.
as many times as they like.

To go into a quasi committee of the whole

a committee uses to postpone its work.

q: Commit (Refer) takes precedence over
exp: Commit ranks just above Amend.

Whether it should hire an expert

q: A committee given "full power" may be authorized to

q: If the presiding officer appoints a committee, who names its chair?

Rise without the floor and object to consideration.
Get the floor and say, "I move to refer the main motion to a committee appointed by the chair."
From your seat, move to rescind it.

q: Postpone to a Certain Time can be moved while

q: One rule of Postpone to a Certain Time is that

can be postponed past the next session.

exp: It can be postponed to the next regular session but no further.
choices: can be postponed beyond the next session.
cannot be postponed beyond the end of the next session.
cannot be postponed beyond the end of the current session.

q: Which motion, if adopted, makes a postponed question an order of the day for a future meeting?

q: If a main motion is postponed while an amendment is pending, the amendment is

q: When a question is taken up on a different day from when it was moved, each member

q: A pending main motion should wait until the next meeting. What should you do?
exp: Postpone to a certain time is the correct motion.

Get the floor: "I move to table it to our next meeting."
Get the floor: "I move to rescind it to our next meeting."

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate can be used to
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It can do all of these.
choices: close debate at a set time.

q: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: It ranks above all debatable motions (needs two-thirds).

q: The motion to Limit Debate can be

exp: It applies to any debatable motion.

laid on the table by itself.
applied to any immediately pending debatable motion.

q: When Limit Debate has been ordered on a main motion, the limit

q: Which motion is NOT debatable but IS amendable?

exp: Limit Debate is undebatable but amendable.

q: The privileged motion to Recess:
exp: It requires a second.

q: What's a difference between the privileged and main-motion forms of Recess?
exp: The main-motion form is debatable.

q: A motion to Recess made with no question pending is a:
exp: With nothing pending, it's a main motion.

q: If a member moves to Recess with no other business pending, it:
exp: It still requires a second.

q: The motion to Reconsider, used to bring a question back:
exp: All are true.

q: Which is an incidental main motion?
exp: These are all names for Rescind.

q: The motion to Take from the Table is classed as a(n):
exp: It's one of the motions that bring a question back.
choices: motion that brings a question again before the assembly

q: To be adopted, the motion to Rescind needs:
exp: Any of the three.
choices: a majority of the entire membership

q: The incidental motion to Suspend the Rules:
exp: It usually takes two-thirds.

q: The minimum vote to suspend an ordinary standing rule is:
exp: Ordinary standing rules can be suspended by majority.
choices: a majority of the entire membership

q: The motion to Take from the Table must always be:
exp: It requires a second.

q: After the chair states a motion, a motion to grant permission to withdraw it must be seconded if:
exp: Source answer: made by the member asking permission.
choices: it's made by the member asking permission

q: A motion about voting made with no question pending:
exp: With nothing pending it's a main motion, so it's debatable.

q: To amend a pending main motion by putting words at the end, you'd say:
exp: Words at the end are "added."
choices: "I move to amend by inserting the word..."
"I move to amend by striking out..."

q: A member disagrees with the chair's ruling on a point of order. The proper form for an appeal is:
exp: That is the correct form.
choices: "I appeal from the decision of the chair."

q: What would you say so members could speak as often as they get the floor?
exp: Informal consideration removes the speech limit.
choices: "I move that the question be considered informally."
"I move that debate on the question be unlimited."

q: A motion to "give the president $500 to attend a leadership workshop" is pending. How would you create a blank for the $500?
exp: That is the form for creating a blank.
choices: "I move to create a blank by striking out $500."

q: If the chair doesn't order a counted vote on a division, a member may say:
exp: Any of these forms works.
choices: "I move that the vote on this motion be counted."
"I move that the vote be counted."

q: The correct form for a request for information is:
exp: All are acceptable.
choices: "I rise to a request for information."
"Will the member yield for a question?"

q: With no business pending, how would you have the minutes read later than scheduled?
exp: Dispensing with the reading delays it.
choices: "I move to reconsider the minutes later."
"I move that the reading of the minutes be dispensed with."
"I move to lay the reading of the minutes on the table."
"I move to postpone the reading of the minutes indefinitely."

q: To take up a question out of order, you'd say:
exp: Suspend the rules.
choices: "I move to postpone indefinitely to consider..."
"I move to suspend the rules and take up..."

q: Which is in order when another member has the floor and needs no second?
exp: A request for information fits.

q: A member who has the floor may be interrupted to:
exp: A question of privilege can interrupt.

q: Which is in order when another member has the floor (but hasn't begun speaking) and needs no second?
exp: Objection to Consideration fits.
choices: Objection to the Consideration of a Question

q: Which is in order when another member has the floor but must be seconded?
exp: An appeal may interrupt but needs a second.
choices: Objection to the Consideration of a Question

q: Which motion is debatable and amendable?
exp: Refer is both.

q: Which motion is neither debatable nor amendable?
exp: Take from the Table is neither.

q: Which motion is amendable but not debatable?
section: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate
exp: Limit or Extend Debate is amendable but undebatable.

q: Which motion is debatable but not amendable?
exp: Postpone Indefinitely is debatable but unamendable.

q: Which motions allow debate on the merits of the main question or the matter they act on?
exp: All open the merits to debate.
choices: Discharge a Committee and Amend Something Previously Adopted
Postpone Indefinitely and Reconsider a debatable motion

q: Which motion does NOT need two-thirds?
exp: A secondary amendment needs a majority.
choices: Limit or Extend Limits of Debate

q: Which motion may require two-thirds to adopt?
exp: Without notice, it needs two-thirds (or a majority of the entire membership).

q: All of these need two-thirds EXCEPT:
exp: A question of privilege is ruled on by the chair.

q: Which motion may be reconsidered?
exp: Fix the Time may be reconsidered.
choices: Fix the Time to Which to Adjourn

q: Which motion may NOT be reconsidered?
exp: Lay on the Table can't be reconsidered.

q: Only an affirmative vote may be reconsidered on the motion to:
exp: Only a yes vote on Postpone Indefinitely may be reconsidered.

q: A negative vote may be reconsidered on the motion to:
exp: For all three, only a negative vote may be reconsidered.
